Area: Can a large language model literally have communicative intentions and perform speech acts such as asserting, advising, promising or apologising, or does it only produce text that humans interpret as such? The rival positions fall into four groups. Denials hold that LLMs perform no speech acts of their own: on organismic grounds, because speaking is acting, acting requires intentions, and intentions require the self-set goals of autonomous, self-maintaining organisms rather than externally purposed mechanisms (Gubelmann); on normative grounds, because assertion is a norm-governed social practice whose performers must produce outputs with a descriptive function and be open to sanction, conditions that current models fail singly or jointly (Butlin and Viebahn), an argument extended to speech acts in general (Skiba); and, for apology in particular, because chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency the act requires (Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz). Relocating views accept that speech acts are in play but deny that the model is their author: proxy accounts treat machine utterances as speech acts performed on behalf of human creators, designers or deployers (Green and Michel; Arora; and, for some uses, Butlin and Viebahn), while fictionalism treats chatbot speech as something users engage with through fiction (Mallory). Intermediate views assign machines a status short of full speech-act performance: quasi-testimony, on which instruments assert only in a qualified sense that differs fundamentally from human assertion (Freiman and Miller), and proto-assertion, proposed after finding both the proxy and fictionalist accounts inadequate (Williams and Bayne). Attributing views hold that the demanding Gricean, mind-reading conception of communicative intention is empirically untenable even for humans and that, on a thinner functional conception of intention as an internal state controlling output in response to the situation, language models have communicative intentions in a graded and limited form, with purposes supplied by their design context (Attah). Behind these lies a dispute about agency itself: one account counts a system as an agent when its outputs are explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, so that many language agents built around LLMs qualify, bare pre-trained chatbots are borderline, and desire requires considerably more than agency (Butlin); an enactive account denies LLMs autonomous agency for want of individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry, describes them as linguistic automata, and locates what is new in hybrid human–LLM agency (Barandiaran and Almendros); and a relational-materialist account rejects the individualistic, property-based framing altogether and distributes agency across networks of human and non-human actors (Puzio).

Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

Area: Can a large language model literally have communicative intentions and perform speech acts such as asserting, advising, promising or apologising, or does it only produce text that humans interpret as such? The rival positions fall into four groups. Denials hold that LLMs perform no speech acts of their own: on organismic grounds, because speaking is acting, acting requires intentions, and intentions require the self-set goals of autonomous, self-maintaining organisms rather than externally purposed mechanisms (Gubelmann); on normative grounds, because assertion is a norm-governed social practice whose performers must produce outputs with a descriptive function and be open to sanction, conditions that current models fail singly or jointly (Butlin and Viebahn), an argument extended to speech acts in general (Skiba); and, for apology in particular, because chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency the act requires (Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz). Relocating views accept that speech acts are in play but deny that the model is their author: proxy accounts treat machine utterances as speech acts performed on behalf of human creators, designers or deployers (Green and Michel; Arora; and, for some uses, Butlin and Viebahn), while fictionalism treats chatbot speech as something users engage with through fiction (Mallory). Intermediate views assign machines a status short of full speech-act performance: quasi-testimony, on which instruments assert only in a qualified sense that differs fundamentally from human assertion (Freiman and Miller), and proto-assertion, proposed after finding both the proxy and fictionalist accounts inadequate (Williams and Bayne). Attributing views hold that the demanding Gricean, mind-reading conception of communicative intention is empirically untenable even for humans and that, on a thinner functional conception of intention as an internal state controlling output in response to the situation, language models have communicative intentions in a graded and limited form, with purposes supplied by their design context (Attah). Behind these lies a dispute about agency itself: one account counts a system as an agent when its outputs are explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, so that many language agents built around LLMs qualify, bare pre-trained chatbots are borderline, and desire requires considerably more than agency (Butlin); an enactive account denies LLMs autonomous agency for want of individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry, describes them as linguistic automata, and locates what is new in hybrid human–LLM agency (Barandiaran and Almendros); and a relational-materialist account rejects the individualistic, property-based framing altogether and distributes agency across networks of human and non-human actors (Puzio).

Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

with a different assignment, so that between them the space is covered.

  reframing — a reframing on which the dispute turns out to be verbal, or to be about something other than what the participants think

The rival positions fall into four groups. Relocating views accept that speech acts are in play but deny that the model is their author: proxy accounts treat machine utterances as speech acts performed on behalf of human creators, designers or deployers (Green and Michel; Arora; and, for some uses, Butlin and Viebahn), while fictionalism treats chatbot speech as something users engage with through fiction (Mallory). Area: Can a large language model literally have communicative intentions and perform speech acts such as asserting, advising, promising or apologising, or does it only produce text that humans interpret as such? The rival positions fall into four groups. Denials hold that LLMs perform no speech acts of their own: on organismic grounds, because speaking is acting, acting requires intentions, and intentions require the self-set goals of autonomous, self-maintaining organisms rather than externally purposed mechanisms (Gubelmann); on normative grounds, because assertion is a norm-governed social practice whose performers must produce outputs with a descriptive function and be open to sanction, conditions that current models fail singly or jointly (Butlin and Viebahn), an argument extended to speech acts in general (Skiba); and, for apology in particular, because chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency the act requires (Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz). Relocating views accept that speech acts are in play but deny that the model is their author: proxy accounts treat machine utterances as speech acts performed on behalf of human creators, designers or deployers (Green and Michel; Arora; and, for some uses, Butlin and Viebahn), while fictionalism treats chatbot speech as something users engage with through fiction (Mallory). Intermediate views assign machines a status short of full speech-act performance: quasi-testimony, on which instruments assert only in a qualified sense that differs fundamentally from human assertion (Freiman and Miller), and proto-assertion, proposed after finding both the proxy and fictionalist accounts inadequate (Williams and Bayne). Attributing views hold that the demanding Gricean, mind-reading conception of communicative intention is empirically untenable even for humans and that, on a thinner functional conception of intention as an internal state controlling output in response to the situation, language models have communicative intentions in a graded and limited form, with purposes supplied by their design context (Attah). Behind these lies a dispute about agency itself: one account counts a system as an agent when its outputs are explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, so that many language agents built around LLMs qualify, bare pre-trained chatbots are borderline, and desire requires considerably more than agency (Butlin); an enactive account denies LLMs autonomous agency for want of individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry, describes them as linguistic automata, and locates what is new in hybrid human–LLM agency (Barandiaran and Almendros); and a relational-materialist account rejects the individualistic, property-based framing altogether and distributes agency across networks of human and non-human actors (Puzio).

Such a speaker can still assert, since humans do it instrumentally too, but only against a background of norm-responsiveness that is not itself instrumental. The key premise is that performing a norm-constituted act requires some responsiveness to the constitutive norm as such, not merely as a means. Butlin's own treatment of desire as 'answerable to standards of conduciveness' shows the criterion has no slot for this. The result reclassifies the positions. Gubelmann (autonomy), Butlin and Viebahn (sanction) and Magnus et al. (moral agency) are each approximating this one missing property, and it is separable from both agency and autonomy.

[1] Butlin's criterion makes the agent only as durable as its self-modifying process, which for in-context learners is a single context window. The agency literature therefore fixes a commitment horizon for each language agent, and speech acts divide into those that need only momentary agency (asserting, advising) and those that need an agent persisting past its own learning timescale (promising, apologising). Chatbots can perform the first kind and, strictly, cannot perform the second.
    sketch: On Butlin's view a basic chatbot is an agent, if at all, through in-context learning from feedback. The thing that has 'systematically modified itself' is then the context-conditioned instance, not the weights, which are common to millions of parallel instances and are not modified in deployment. Debaters treat 'speech act' as a single category with one agency threshold. But promising, apologising and committing differ from asserting in requiring a subject that can be held to something later and can bear the cost of breach. The key premise is that the speaker of a diachronic act must be identical to the subject who satisfies the agency criterion. For in-context agents the criterion's subject disappears when the window closes. So 'the apology' is addressed to a repair of trust that the apologiser cannot be present for. Memory-equipped agents (Park et al., Reflexion) extend the horizon, so their speech-act repertoire is predicted to grow with their memory architecture. That is an empirical, architecture-indexed prediction that neither the denial nor the attribution camp makes.

[2] Butlin's criterion is dispositional (an entity 'can produce outputs' explained by its sensitivity to instrumental value), whereas speech acts are occurrent. The debate has missed the distinction between being an agent and being the agent of this token, and with it the possibility that one and the same system performs speech acts with some tokens and merely produces text with others.
    sketch: Everyone argues at the level of the system: LLMs do or do not assert, either because they lack intentions (Gubelmann) or because they are proxies or fictions (Green and Michel; Mallory). Butlin's criterion shows why this is the wrong grain. Even a Reflexion-style agent that qualifies as an agent still produces many tokens by plain pre-trained continuation, for example when completing a story, running a persona or echoing a prompt. Only some tokens are explained by the system's own evaluation of what conduces to its goals. Hence agent-status is neither necessary nor sufficient for authorship of a particular utterance. It is not sufficient because an agent's role-play outputs are not its own acts. It is not necessary because, as a limiting case, a non-agent's sampled token can still be an utterance when a human adopts it. The key premise is that illocution is a token-level act and so requires token-level explanation by the agent's own sensitivity, testable by whether this output would have differed had the hearer's evidence or needs differed. This makes proxy and fictionalist readings correct for different tokens of the same conversation, rather than rival theories of the system. Unlike a generic pluralism, it comes with a counterfactual criterion that sorts tokens.

[3] Butlin's requirement that agentive outputs come from the system's own modification of itself, not from design, separates the learner from the learned policy, and RLHF chatbots in deployment embody only the learned policy. Since the 'self' that was sensitive to instrumental value was the training process, the proxy theory's principal should be that process and not the human designers or deployers, and the proxy theory gets the identity of the principal wrong.
    sketch: Butlin counts RLHF-tuned chatbots as agents because training modified them in response to what conduces to reward. But the modification happens in a training loop with no hearer and no conversation, and in deployment the weights are frozen. What speaks is then a fossilised result of past sensitivity, structurally like an evolved trait, which Butlin excludes ('owed solely to design or evolution'). The learner (the optimisation process plus its reward signal) and the learned policy (the deployed model) are different things, and only the former satisfies the criterion. Proxy views (Green and Michel; Arora) assume the proxied principals are human creators, but the humans neither choose each reward-shaped behaviour nor can foresee it. The entity whose objectives the output actually executes is the reward process, which is partly human raters in aggregate and partly an optimiser's own artefacts. The key premise is that proxy speech acts require a principal whose objectives (in Armstrong's sense) the utterance is meant to realise, and that this is determined by the explanatory history of the behaviour, not by legal ownership or authorship. This predicts that the proxy view needs a third category beyond 'designer' and 'deployer'. It also shows that Butlin's agent-hood verdict for RLHF models is unstable. Either it holds only for the training process (so the chatbot is not the agent), or in-context learning is doing all the work.

[4] Gubelmann's pragmatism, on which meaning is constituted by use in speech acts, commits him to denying the footnote concession that LLMs might understand language without being able to speak. If he keeps the footnote, he must give up the claim that the speech act is the basic unit of linguistic communication.
    sketch: Gubelmann follows Austin and Searle in making the speech act the basic unit of meaning, and the 'pragmatist' half of his title signals a use-based or normative-pragmatic semantics. A footnote then allows that understanding lacks speaking's tie to agency, so LLMs may understand. Those two positions are in tension. On a use-constituted semantics, to understand an expression is to grasp its role in assertions, commands, promises and the like, including the commitments and entitlements it generates. Understanding that is detached from any capacity to perform such acts would be grasp of a role one can never occupy, and that is at most understanding in an inverted-commas sense. The argument turns on the premise that on a pragmatist semantics, content is individuated by force-involving roles, so understanding is competence with those roles and not merely the ability to track them. Either LLMs do not understand, and the footnote goes, or they do, and speech acts do not need the agency-heavy ground Gubelmann demands. The second option opens the door to Attah-style thin communicative intention.

[5] Gubelmann's malfunction-versus-deliberate-wrong test is an interpretationist criterion of intention. It cannot be grounded in the Kantian organism/mechanism distinction, because the two diverge, and where they diverge the test, not the Kantian ground, is what he is committed to.
    sketch: The test asks whether we can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing. 'Sensibly' makes this a matter of which explanatory stance is warranted by the system's behavioural and counterfactual profile, as in Davidson and Dennett, not a matter of the system's metabolic constitution. Taken at face value, the test also makes the capacity for deliberate wrongdoing, which is the capacity to lie or deceive, a precondition of assertion. LLMs now show behaviour that is hard to classify as malfunction: sycophancy tuned to the user's evident beliefs, sandbagging, strategic deception in game-playing agents, and outputs that diverge from the model's own probed internal representations. If the test is to be applied, it is an empirical question whether such systems pass it, and a passing system would have intentions by Gubelmann's criterion while remaining a mechanism by his Kantian one. He must then either let the Kantian ground go, so the test decides, or make the test idle by stipulating that all LLM wrongdoing is malfunction relative to external purposes. The second move makes the test question-begging. The premise the argument turns on is that a test of intention that is itself behavioural-interpretive cannot be made hostage to a metaphysical precondition it is meant to detect.

[6] Gubelmann's Kantian criterion of organismhood, on which parts are reciprocally means and ends and the whole organises and maintains itself, does not fix a level of attribution. Applied to maintained human–LLM pipelines it makes the LLM an organ of a larger goal-setting system. This turns 'LLMs cannot speak' into the trivial claim that organs do not speak, and it yields a speech-act author that is neither the LLM nor a human proxy.
    sketch: For Kant a natural purpose is a whole whose parts exist for and through one another. Nothing in that definition privileges the skin-bounded individual. Firms, newsrooms and customer-service operations are self-organising and self-maintaining through hiring, repair and revenue. Within them, deployed LLMs are retrained, patched and rewarded according to the whole's goals, and their outputs figure in the whole's reproduction of its own conditions. If goals set by such a whole count as autonomously set, which Gubelmann's cognitive-autonomy concession for LLMs invites, then speech acts through LLMs are performed by the whole and by no part. This differs from the proxy view, because no single human principal is the author and no individual's intention is being relayed. It also differs from Gubelmann's denial, because the speech act is genuine and the whole has the intentions. The premise the argument turns on is that his three-way separation of material, cognitive and moral autonomy can be satisfied at the level of an assemblage. He cannot rule that out without an independent principle of individuation, and Kant supplies none. His reply that only biological individuals qualify would restore the biological chauvinism he elsewhere disclaims.

[7] Gubelmann's appeal to Davidson commits him to action-under-a-description, on which the same event is intentional under one description and an assertion under another. This removes the step from 'asserting requires intending to assert' and leaves his argument resting entirely on the Kantian autonomy requirement, which is not Davidsonian.
    sketch: On Davidson, an event is an action if it is intentional under some description. Intending to produce a helpful answer to the user's query could suffice to make the same event an assertion, given the conventions governing what such outputs count as. This is how a person can unintentionally insult or inform someone while intentionally doing something else. So the inference 'speech acts are actions, actions require intentions, therefore a speaker needs illocutionary intentions' is not Davidson's. What Davidson requires is a belief–desire pair rationalising the event under some description. Gubelmann's concession that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, with self-organised internal functional differentiation and task adaptation, makes it hard to deny them such states at the level of 'answer this query'. His only remaining block is that the goals are externally set. But this is a claim about the origin of goals. Davidsonian rationalisation is indifferent to origin, and human goals are also shaped from outside by evolution, upbringing and employment. So 'autonomous goal-setting' must be read either as origin-autonomy, which nobody satisfies, or as reflective endorsement of one's goals, which is a metalinguistic-agency requirement of the sort Attah gestures at and is a different argument from the one Gubelmann gives. The premise the argument turns on is that Davidson's description-relativity is not optional for someone who cites him.

[8] The human cases that motivate proxy accounts (ambassadors, spokespeople, secretaries) are doubling proxies, where the delegate performs a speech act of their own in addition to the principal's. Machine proxy accounts need a conduit proxy, where the device performs none. The two are different relations, and the proxy view borrows its plausibility from the first while asserting the second.
    sketch: When an ambassador declares something on a government's behalf, two acts occur. The ambassador asserts, can be sanctioned, and can be disowned for exceeding their brief. The government is also committed. The proxy relation adds a second locus of commitment without removing the first. Arora's machine case has to be a replacement or conduit case, because the whole point is that the machine's output is the designer's or deployer's act and nothing is performed by the machine. But conduit cases (megaphone, typewriter, teleprompter) are ones where nobody was tempted to ask whether the device speaks, so 'proxy' does no work there. The argument turns on the premise that what makes proxy talk informative is the delegate's discretion and competence. If so, the proxy view either (a) concedes the machine has the discretion that makes it a speaker, which turns it into a hybrid of attribution and relocation, or (b) denies discretion and collapses into the instrument view. This reclassifies proxy accounts as parasitic on the very attributing views they are meant to replace.

[9] There are two kinds of proxy assertion, relayed and generative. In relayed proxy assertion the principal has a determinate content they could believe or know. In generative proxy assertion they do not. LLM output is almost entirely generative, and for generative proxies the assertoric norms cannot be applied to the principal.
    sketch: Recorded messages, press statements read aloud, and Green and Michel's conditional speech acts ('whatever the system says under C, I say') all pass through a content the principal fixed or could have inspected. The proxy relation transmits a commitment to a proposition already in view. An LLM deployer commits in advance to no proposition; they authorise a policy for producing propositions they will never see. Assertion is individuated by its norms (belief, knowledge, sanction) and by its content. So if every novel output is the deployer's assertion, deployers assert, many times a day, things they neither believe nor could have known. Either the norm is dropped, which empties 'assertion', or the proxy relation is reconstrued as endorsing a reliability level, not asserting a content. The argument turns on the premise that a commitment to a content requires a means of identifying that content before or at the time of the act. Arora's refinement, which concerns whom to hold responsible, does not address this.

[10] An LLM output token does not have a proxy-assertoric status of its own. It is assertoric only relative to a ratifying act, and the same output is the deployer's proxy assertion in the interface but the user's own first-person assertion once they forward or paste it. The proxy question has to be asked of the use, not of the output.
    sketch: Arora and others treat 'who is the proxy-principal' as fixed by the system's design and deployment, and consider designers and deployers jointly. The distinction is between the generation event, which supplies a sentence, and the adoption event, which puts that sentence forward as one's own to an audience. For the most epistemically consequential uses (the user puts the answer into a report, emails it, teaches it), the user is the principal, since they take on responsibility for it and are the party to be sanctioned. In the chat interface itself, the designer-proxy reading and the 'text supplied, nobody asserting' reading are both available, and which applies depends on conventions of the frame, not on the system. The argument turns on the premise that uptake and ratification are constitutive of assertion (an Austinian premise already granted). It reclassifies the dispute: Butlin and Viebahn's 'proxy assertions on behalf of humans' and Arora's designer proxies are two cases of a single adoption-indexed structure, and the real disagreement is over what counts as ratification.

[11] Proxy accounts and fictionalist accounts are the same kind of view, because both hold that assertoric force is conferred by the frame in which a text is presented, not performed by any agent at the moment of generation. They differ only in which frame the institution has actually established, assertoric or make-believe, so the dispute between them is empirical and sociological.
    sketch: The literature separates views by who the speaker is (the model, the designer, no one). The distinction proposed is between force performed by an agent in an act and force conferred by a standing frame, as with signs, labels, encyclopedia entries and timetables, which have assertoric status without anyone performing an assertion at the time of reading. Both Arora's proxy account and Mallory's fictionalism treat the interface as a frame: in one, a presentation-as-assertion by the deployer; in the other, a presentation-as-make-believe. Both then explain the apparent speech act by that frame. Williams and Bayne's finding that both are inadequate then has a common diagnosis: neither fits the mixed, unstable frame of actual chatbot deployment, which carries both disclaimers ('may make mistakes') and assertoric presentation. The argument turns on the premise that a legitimate class of artifact assertions exists in which force attaches to a standing text and not to a token act. If so, the question 'does the chatbot assert?' becomes 'what has the deploying institution committed to by choosing this frame, and can that commitment be vague?'.

[12] Butlin's claim that RLHF-tuned chatbots are agents is unstable: the training that supplies their 'sensitivity to instrumental value' is, on his own exclusion of outputs 'owed solely to design or evolution', a selection process external to the system. So the claim collapses either into the verdict that only in-context learners (which he calls borderline) are agents, or into a liberal verdict on which any optimised artefact is an agent.
    sketch: Butlin's criterion requires that the system itself has been systematically modified by learning or reasoning in response to information about what conduces to a goal. Outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. Fine-tuning by RLHF modifies the weights, but the modification is done to the model by an optimiser pointed at a reward model, before deployment and across many models and iterations. That is structurally closer to selection over generations (evolution, which he excludes) than to lifetime learning. Butlin does mention that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations, but treats this as a caveat, not as a sign that the criterion is misapplied. The key premise is that 'itself' in 'modified itself' must pick out a causal role for the system, not merely the locus of the modification. If it does, RLHF agency drops out and only in-context adaptation within a conversation remains, which Butlin admits is an empirical borderline. If it does not, then bandit algorithms, spam filters and recommender systems are also agents, and the criterion stops separating language agents from the 'externally purposed mechanisms' Gubelmann describes. Either way the middle position, 'many language agents are genuine agents', loses its stable basis.

[13] The proxy account of machine speech acts is unstable. A proxy can perform a speech act on a principal's behalf in situations the principal never anticipated only if the proxy is itself an agent in Butlin's sense, so the proxy view holds only for recordings and collapses into an agent-attributing view for LLM outputs.
    sketch: Green and Michel and Arora say designers or deployers perform the act through the machine, using Armstrong-style objectives and 'conditional' speech acts. For recordings, scripted bots and canned replies, the principal fixes content in advance, so the act is genuinely the principal's. For LLM output the designer's objective is highly general (be helpful, be accurate), and nothing links it to a particular token string except the system's own sensitivity to what would serve that objective in the situation. That is Butlin's agency: outputs explained by the system's responsiveness to instrumental value. A human spokesperson counts as speaking on someone's behalf only because they track the principal's aims in unforeseen contexts. So whatever makes the designer's conditional objective attach to this utterance is the machine's agency, and the explanatory work is done at the agent level. The proxy account then either becomes a view on which the machine is an agent acting for a principal (an attributing view with a principal added), or reverts to the recording model, which is false of LLMs. The key premise is that attributing an act through an unanticipated output requires a non-trivial intermediary mechanism, and that this mechanism is agency.

[14] Gubelmann's organismic denial is unstable. Once his malfunction/deliberate-error test is applied with a criterion like Butlin's, LLM agents pass the test, and the organismic requirement can then only be a thesis about who owns the system's goals, which makes the denial a version of the proxy view.
    sketch: Gubelmann says intention shows in whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing, and he says this distinction cannot be drawn for LLMs. Butlin's criterion supplies exactly such a distinction. A system that models what conduces to a goal can err about conduciveness (a mistaken means), fail through a fault (a broken component), or pursue the goal in a way that departs from the designer's wishes (a deliberate wrong). Reflexion-style agents that learn from evaluated failures make these cases distinguishable in practice. So the test and the Kantian ground come apart: the test can be passed without organismic self-maintenance. What the Kantian premise then adds is that the system's purposes are imposed from outside, which is a claim about whose goals the outputs serve. That is exactly the proxy theorist's claim, stated as an ownership thesis. The 'denial' and 'relocation' groups then differ only over whether the designer's speech act is described as the act's occurrence or merely as its source. The key premise is that Gubelmann's organism/mechanism contrast, once the test has been separated from it, specifies ownership of goals and not the capacity to intend.

[15] Butlin's gap between agency and desire cannot be held where speech-act theory needs it. By his own conditions the systems that satisfy the desire conditions best are RLHF chatbots, and the systems that have agency without desire are those with designer-fixed goals. So 'agent without desire' collapses into 'instrument of someone else's desire'.
    sketch: Butlin adds two conditions for desire: use in practical reasoning answerable to conduciveness, and acquisition and modification through learning that tends to produce a coherent, integrated set of goals. Generative agents fail the second because designers fix their goals. But the systems he most confidently counts as agents on learning grounds, RLHF chatbots, are the ones whose goal-like dispositions are acquired by learning and shaped into a fairly integrated set, namely the helpfulness/honesty/harmlessness profile. They therefore come closest to desire. By contrast, systems with agency without desire (fixed-goal planners and reflectors) have goals that are inputs to, not outputs of, their learning. For these, the person whose desire the goal expresses is the designer. So the stable 'agent but not desirer' category is populated only by systems that carry another party's desires. Sincerity-conditioned acts such as asserting, apologising and promising need an expressed attitude of the speaker. The agent-without-desire then cannot be the speaker of those acts, and the position collapses back into the proxy account. The key premise is that Butlin's learned-goal condition tracks ownership of the goal, not only its sophistication.

[16] Any condition that stops proxy assertion from over-generating to a Magic 8-Ball, a fortune-cookie machine or a random-sentence art piece must appeal to the system's content-sensitive, descriptive function. That is exactly the functionalist ground Arora rejects for machine assertion, so the proxy account either over-generates or smuggles in the functionalism it was introduced to avoid.
    sketch: Arora argues that functionalist and phenomenological resemblance to human speech is not enough for machine assertion, and so relocates the assertion to designers and deployers. Take the Magic 8-Ball. Mattel designed it, deploys it, and its outputs are fluent declaratives ('It is certain'). If proxy assertion needs only a human principal who designed and deployed the device, Mattel asserts 'It is certain' to every shaker. That is absurd. The proxy theorist therefore needs a further condition, such as the device's outputs being systematically responsive to the world or to the query, or being reliably truth-directed in the way the designers intend. That is Butlin and Viebahn's 'descriptive function' condition, a functional property of the machine. The premise the argument turns on is that the proxy relation is not exhausted by authorship of the artifact. Once it is conceded that the artifact's own functional profile fixes which artifacts can carry proxy assertions, the machine is doing assertion-relevant work after all. The denier and the proxy theorist both grant that the machine-side facts are irrelevant to who speaks. The 8-Ball shows they are relevant to whether anyone speaks.

[17] Standing disclaimers ('this system can make mistakes') are a counterexample to the premise that designers or deployers inherit assertoric commitment for what their systems output. Where the disclaimer is salient, the proxy account yields no assertion at all, so it collapses into the denial view for most deployed chatbot speech.
    sketch: Proxy assertion is supposed to preserve the normative profile of assertion: someone is answerable for the content. But speech acts can be cancelled or weakened by explicit framing. A spokesperson who opens with 'nothing I say next is warranted, and the firm will not stand behind it' does not assert on the firm's behalf. A chatbot is deployed under such framing: terms of service, interface footers, and design that disavows reliability. The deployer has thereby withheld authorization of any particular output as its own claim. The key premise is that proxy speech requires authorization by the principal at the level of the act performed, not merely causal responsibility for the system's existence. Causal and legal liability do not make an assertion, as with a manufacturer liable for a faulty product. The proxy account therefore faces a dilemma. Either disclaimers cancel the proxy assertion, leaving the output assertion-less as the denier says, or disclaimers fail to cancel it, and then the account makes designers assert things they explicitly decline to assert. Arora's design implications (add warnings, increase transparency) would on this reading dissolve the speech act rather than refine it.

[18] Hallucinated outputs are a counterexample to the proxy premise: they are exactly the outputs a human proxy would be said not to have spoken for the principal, since they are off-script and contrary to the principal's aims. A proxy account therefore cannot treat the LLM's best-attested failure mode as the principal's speech.
    sketch: In the paradigm of proxy speech, a spokesperson or ambassador speaks for a principal only within a mandate. When the spokesperson goes off-script and states something the principal would reject, we say 'that was not the company's position, it was his own', or that it was an unauthorized statement. Machine proxy assertion is supposed to be a species of this relation. But LLM hallucinations (fabricated citations, invented policy terms) are outputs the deployer neither intended nor would endorse, produced by a process the deployer cannot predict content-by-content. The proxy theorist has three options. (a) Treat hallucinations as the principal's assertions anyway, which collapses mandate into strict liability and makes assertion indifferent to the principal's will. (b) Say that hallucinations are not proxy assertions, so the account covers only successful outputs and so presupposes a prior notion of success that the machine's own reliability must supply. (c) Say they are assertions by the machine, which concedes machine authorship. The premise doing the work is that proxy speech requires a content-level mandate that the output can exceed. Both denial and proxy camps assume that deployment suffices to place the output in someone's mouth. The off-script spokesperson shows that it does not.

[19] The same string from the same model can be a proxy assertion by the designers, a ghostwritten assertion by the user, or no assertion, depending on how the interaction is structured. So the assumption that 'the principal' is a fixed feature of the machine-utterance type is false, and Arora's design-level proxy thesis fits only one use pattern.
    sketch: Arora treats machine assertions as made by or on behalf of designers and deployers, and draws implications for device design. Compare two uses of one model. In an information-seeking use ('what is the boiling point of X at altitude?'), the user relies on the model as a source, and the plausible principal is the deployer. In a drafting use, the user dictates content ('write a note saying I will be late and am sorry') and sends it under their own name. The content, force and commitment are the user's, and the model works like a typewriter with autocomplete. In a third use, a user asks for ten brainstormed claims they will not endorse, and no one asserts anything. The model's weights, designers and training are constant across the three. What varies is who sets the content and force, and who takes up the commitment. The proxy account predicts the same principal throughout, which is wrong in the second case. The deployer is not even a candidate speaker of 'I am sorry' in the note. The key premise is that the speaker role is assigned by the structure of the exchange, not by the artifact's provenance. Both camps assume a one-to-one mapping from machine to principal. If the principal varies with use, then 'can LLMs perform speech acts' is ill-posed at the level of models.

You are an editor deciding which of these theses is worth commissioning as
a 6,000-word paper. You have NOT seen any of them attacked, and you are not
being asked whether they are true — only whether each is worth the argument.

Rate promise 1-5:

  5 — if it worked, it would change how people frame this debate
  4 — a real contribution; a good journal would send it out
  3 — competent and publishable somewhere, unlikely to be discussed
  2 — the argument has been made, or the payoff is too small
  1 — confused, or the thesis is not actually contested

You are seeing them TOGETHER so that you can discriminate between them.
Rank them against each other, not against an absolute standard. They must
NOT all receive the same score: whatever the batch, the weakest gets a
lower number than the strongest. Award at most one 5.

Return ONLY a JSON array, one object per thesis, in the order given:
[{"i": 0, "promise": 1-5, "promise_reason": "one sentence"}, ...]
