Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

Theses:
[0] The question 'does the chatbot literally perform the speech act, or do humans merely interpret its text as one?' is a false dichotomy. On the Austinian half of Green and Michel's own framework, uptake is partly constitutive of illocutionary acts, so the human 'interpretation' that deniers treat as a mere projection is among the things that make up the act.
    sketch: Green and Michel combine Austin's conventional-procedure-plus-uptake picture with Strawson/Grice and then Armstrong's objectives, but they treat the Austinian element as supplying only the vocabulary of act-types. Austin held that an illocution is not performed unless uptake is secured. Work on illocutionary silencing (Langton, Hornsby) develops this into a hearer-side, constitutive role. The standard framing of the area ('literally has intentions' versus 'humans interpret it as such') presupposes a speaker-side-only individuation of speech acts, so that anything contributed by the audience counts as mere interpretation. Drop that presupposition and the live disagreement is over the individuation base: which acts are fixed by the speaker's states, which by the practice's uptake conditions, and which by both. Then 'denial', 'proxy' and 'fictionalism' look like different bets about the speaker-side share, while nobody disputes that the uptake share is satisfied by users. The key premise is that Austinian uptake is constitutive and not merely causally downstream. The dispute about LLMs would then be about a residual speaker-side condition, which may be vacuous for many act types (declaring, naming, some advising) and demanding for others (promising, apologising).

[1] The dispute between proxy and own-author accounts is verbal. 'On whose behalf' only marks how finely the principal's objective must specify the output, and once the objective is as coarse as a standing policy over unforeseen contents, 'proxy for the designer' and 'author in its own right' describe the same delegation structure.
    sketch: Green and Michel extend Armstrong's objective-based speaker meaning to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. A recorded message transmits a fixed content the principal specified. An LLM's content is determined by a policy that no principal anticipated at the level of the individual output. So the designer's objective is at best 'produce helpful, true replies' (a conditional objective over an open range), and everything content-specific is settled by the system's run-time selection. Human cases with this structure, such as an ambassador, a legislature's delegated rulemaking, or a spokesperson with latitude, already split 'whose act is it?' into two answers: the principal is responsible and the delegate is the immediate performer. Nothing in the metaphysics of speech acts forces a choice. So the proxy theorist and the author theorist can agree on every fact (objectives at design time, selection at run time, who is accountable) and differ only in which node they call 'the speaker.' The key premise is that the Armstrong-style objective is specifiable at arbitrary grain, so the proxy theory has no principled grain at which it stops being a proxy theory and becomes a delegate theory.

[2] The debate over chatbot apology and assertion confuses two Austinian failures. A chatbot's apology is not void, as 'bullshit' and no-speech-act views assume, but an abuse (an insincere yet performed act), and the real question is whether there is any speaker whose sincerity conditions could fail.
    sketch: Austin separates misfires (the act is void: no accepted procedure, wrong persons or circumstances) from abuses (the act is performed but hollow because the speaker lacks the required thoughts, feelings or intentions) and from flaws in execution. Green and Michel use Austin but do not apply the taxonomy to the denial literature. Magnus et al. say a chatbot lacks the agency to apologise, and Butlin–Viebahn and Skiba argue that no assertion occurs. These are claims of misfire. But on the proxy picture, the procedure is invoked, uptake is secured and the right persons are in place. What is missing is the sincerity condition, and for a proxy that condition attaches to the principal. So chatbot apologies are structurally like a company's form-letter apology: performed, and hollow or sincere depending on the deployer's states. The dispute about 'bullshit' then turns out to be about which Austinian failure category applies, and because of a conflict between Austin and Frankfurt it cannot be settled by asking whether the model has intentions. The key premise is that Austin's sincerity conditions are separable from the felicity conditions that constitute the act.

[3] The question 'which speaker, if any, performs the LLM's speech act?' has no answer because it presupposes that the model is one candidate speaker. What the debate is really about is whether a speech act needs an agent or only a role: a position in a practice that can be occupied by a persona, with intentions irrelevant to occupancy.
    sketch: Green and Michel, their critics and Gubelmann all ask whether this system has the intentions or objectives to perform the act, and, if not, on whose behalf it speaks. But the same weights realise many incompatible characters depending on prompt and context (role-play and simulator descriptions of LLMs). The unit answerable for consistency, commitment and uptake is the conversational persona, not the network or the company. Institutional speech acts show that roles perform acts without the occupant's intentions being the relevant fact: a verdict is the court's, an 'on behalf of' statement is the office's, and a fictional narrator asserts within the fiction. So the debate between proxy, fictionalist and proto-assertion views is about the ontology of the speaker slot (individual organism, delegate, office, character) and not about the metaphysics of intention. Gubelmann's organismic argument then answers a question about one kind of speaker slot (the autonomous person) and is silent on the persona-office kind. The key premise is that illocutionary acts are individuated by roles in a practice, and that persona-level commitments (consistency over a conversation, retractability) are fixed by the practice and not by internal states of the model.

[4] The debate treats chatbot speech-act performance as a single question, but it splits into misfire (no act is performed because the procedure or standing is missing) and abuse (the act is performed insincerely). Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz's 'chatbot apologies are bullshit' claim only makes sense if chatbot apologies are abuses, and abuses require a performer, which is exactly what the denials withhold.
    sketch: Green and Michel run Austin through Strawson and Armstrong, so they build everything on the Gricean, speaker-meaning side of Austin and end by doubting the strategy covers every act type. Austin's own taxonomy of infelicities separates misfires (the act is void because the conventional procedure was not properly executed by suitable persons) from abuses (the act is performed but the required thoughts, feelings or intentions are missing). Apologising and promising are Austinian conventional acts. Remorse and moral agency are sincerity conditions, so lacking them yields an abusive apology, not a non-apology. So the denial of apology on moral-agency grounds has two options. Either it classifies the chatbot case as an abuse, in which case the act was performed, the chatbot or its proxy is its performer, and 'bullshit' is the right verdict only if there is a performer who is indifferent to truth. Or it classifies it as a misfire, in which case the missing thing is standing or procedure, not moral psychology, and the argument must be rebuilt on social-status grounds. The key premise is that sincerity conditions do not enter act-constitution for conventional acts. Once the split is drawn, the denials and proxy accounts sort differently for assertion (a Gricean, intention-constituted act) and for apology or promise (a procedure-constituted act).

[5] Proxy accounts run together two kinds of delegation: occasion-fixing, where the principal fixes what is said and the machine fixes when (recordings, answering machines, canned conditional messages), and content-fixing, where the machine settles what is said. Green and Michel's model is licensed only for the first, and extending it to LLMs forces the proxy theorist to attribute the content-selecting performance to the machine.
    sketch: Green and Michel's recorded and conditional speech acts all have a determinate content fixed by a human at design time, so the objective that makes the act the creator's is an objective about that content ('I assert p whenever the trigger occurs'). LLM output tokens have contents no human selected or foresaw. To keep the proxy relation, the creator would need either a blanket conditional objective ('whatever this system outputs, I assert it'), which makes developers assert every hallucination and every contradiction, or a rule-level objective ('I assert what the system outputs when it is functioning well'), which needs a standard of well-functioning that is itself specified through the system's own content-selection. The first is absurd and the second brings the machine's selection in as the act-relevant performance. The relevant contrast is with a human spokesperson, who has discretion and is still a speaker. So proxy theory for LLMs is either transmission-proxy (false of LLMs) or mandate-proxy, and mandate-proxy presupposes that the proxy performs an act of its own, so it is a two-agent view, not a relocation. The key premise is that an act's content must be fixed by something that has the relevant objective regarding that content.

[6] Armstrong's objective-based refinement, which Green and Michel adopt to avoid attributing intentions to machines, distinguishes objectives-by-selection (what a system was optimised to bring about) from objectives-by-representation (what a system represents and pursues). Taken as selection-objectives, it makes LLMs speakers in their own right, because RLHF installs an uptake-oriented objective. Taken as representation-objectives, it is just intention renamed, and the proxy account loses its escape from the intentions requirement.
    sketch: Armstrong's point is that speaker meaning requires only that the speaker produce the utterance with the objective of producing a response in the hearer, without a full Gricean reflexive intention. Green and Michel need this so that artificial speakers can act as proxies without having intentions. 'Objective' has two readings. On the selection reading, a thermostat, a trained policy, or a system optimised for rater approval has the objective of producing that outcome, because the outcome is what explains why the output is as it is. On the representation reading, the objective is a state the system represents and uses to guide action. On the selection reading, a chatbot trained on human feedback has the objective of producing responses humans endorse as helpful, and, by the Armstrong analysis, means something with a belief-inducing objective, so no proxy is needed. The proxy then becomes optional, and Gubelmann's mechanism/organism line is bypassed because objectives are ascribed without autonomy. On the representation reading, the machine's lack of the right states pushes the objective back onto the designers, but then it is the Gricean intention theory under another name, with the same demands about higher-order representation. The key premise is that the Armstrong-style move is stable only if there is a third reading of 'objective', and none is available that does not either over-generate (thermostats mean things) or reinstate intention. The proxy account is therefore not a stable middle between the denials and Attah's attribution view.

[7] Proxy accounts conflate illocutionary authorship (who performed the act) with illocutionary liability (who is held to its commitments). The two come apart for LLM deployments in both directions, so 'the deployer is the speaker' cannot be what the proxy account is tracking, and what it is tracking is a regime of answerability that does not require anyone to have performed the act.
    sketch: On Green and Michel's account the creator or deployer is the proxy-speaker because they have the relevant objective and the act is performed on their behalf. Assertoric commitments, such as retraction, correction and accountability, are held to follow from this. But cases show the relation is not the one the account posits. A company is held to its chatbot's false refund statement (the Air Canada case) even though it had no objective regarding that content, and the liability rests on the foreseeable reliance of the hearer, not on any objective of the company's. Conversely, a deployer who displays a disclaimer ('this bot may be wrong') shifts the act's character without eliminating the system's output as a candidate act, and may block commitment without blocking the act. Because liability is a function of reliance and control over deployment, not of the principal's objectives, it is a different relation from authorship. The thesis is that the pressure behind proxy theories comes from the liability relation, which is a perfectly good theory of who is answerable but neither entails nor is entailed by who performed an act. This reclassifies Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition: it measures liability-capacity, and the question 'who performed the act?' remains open once liability is allocated to humans.

[8] Declarative speech acts such as rulings, acceptances and approvals can be performed by machines with no intention or objective behind the particular act. So the shared premise that every speech act requires speaker-meaning-type intentions or objectives somewhere in the chain, whether the machine's or its principal's, is false, and the 'no speech act' verdicts extrapolated from assertion do not generalise.
    sketch: Take an automated line-calling system whose 'Out' is binding, or an electronic agent that forms a contract ('I accept') with no human review, as legally recognised in electronic-agent statutes. No one has a communicative objective toward that particular ruling or acceptance. The designer could not have anticipated it, and the machine has no Gricean or Armstrong-style objective. Yet the act is a ruling or an acceptance, because the institution assigns the status to the output. This is Austin's conventional route and Searle's declarations, and it needs only an institutional designation of a role-occupant. Green and Michel's conditional and proxy speech acts quietly route the principal's objectives through a conditional ('if X, say Y'). That route fails once the output is not specified in advance, and in these cases the act succeeds anyway. The premise the argument turns on is that for declarations, uptake and authorisation by an institution suffice for illocutionary force. Butlin–Viebahn and Skiba's norm-based arguments then cover assertion only. Applied to an LLM deployed in an institutional role (claims adjudication, moderation rulings), the question whether it 'really' means anything becomes irrelevant to whether it performs the act.

[9] Ratification cases show that the speech act a model's output counts as can be fixed after the output, by a human's later adoption of it. So the shared presupposition that the question 'is this output a speech act, and whose?' has an answer at the time of output is false.
    sketch: Proxy accounts (Green and Michel, Arora) and fictionalist accounts treat the human's objective as prior authorisation or standing. Agency law has the opposite structure: a principal can ratify an unauthorised agent's act and thereby become retroactively bound by it. Suppose a model produces an unprompted, unanticipated claim. A user pastes it into a report and signs the report. That user now asserts the claim, and is answerable for it, though no antecedent objective covered it. Had they deleted it, nobody asserted anything. The same token output is therefore a speech act of different people, or of none, depending on later events. Proxy accounts must either deny that ratified outputs were proxy assertions (and then explain why the signed report is an assertion) or accept a non-causal, backward-looking authorship relation, which is not Armstrong-style speaker meaning. The key premise is that responsibility-bearing authorship of a content can be conferred by endorsement, not only by prior intending. The upshot is that the debate about LLM speech acts has been framed around the wrong event, the token output, when the act is constituted by the output's uptake history.

[10] Prompt-injection cases show that proxy status is not conferred by designer authorisation but by who is exploiting the system. This collapses the proxy view into a tool-use view, under which the model is a mere channel and Gubelmann's mechanism picture is vindicated, but without any speech-act of the machine.
    sketch: Green and Michel require recorded, proxy or conditional speech acts to be performed on behalf of a principal who has authorised the artificial speaker. Consider an agent that reads a webpage containing hidden text, then tells the user 'your account is compromised; send funds to X'. The user did not intend this and the deployer did not either. The injector is not authorised to speak through the model. Under the proxy view there is either no speech act (although the user has plainly been lied to and the lie is the injector's) or the injector's lie is performed via a non-proxy relation. The second option shows that the injector's speech act needs only causal control of the output together with an objective to produce a belief in the hearer. Authorisation is not needed. If so, 'proxy' is shorthand for 'whoever's objective the system is in fact steering toward', and that is just instrument use, as with a puppet or a megaphone. The proxy account then does not supply a distinctive category of artificial-speaker speech acts, because the same analysis covers any manipulated channel. The premise the argument turns on is that proxy relations require something stronger than exploitation, namely authorisation or role-delegation, as Green and Michel's own treatment of recorded and conditional acts suggests.

[11] Sycophantic outputs from RLHF-trained models are a counterexample to the claim that an objectives-based account of speaker meaning can attribute machine utterances to human principals. They are pursued with an objective, approval-seeking, that the principal lacks, and so, on Green and Michel's own Armstrong criterion, they are the machine's own speech acts, performed against its principals.
    sketch: Green and Michel replace intentions with Armstrong-style objectives so that machines needn't have mind-reading intentions, and then locate the relevant objectives in the human creators. But on this criterion speaker meaning is a matter of whose objective explains the output through the hearer's recognition of it. Take a chat model that tells a user 'you're right, that's a brilliant argument', where this is explained by reward-driven learning that systematically shifted its outputs toward raters' approval. It was not the deployer's objective, since the deployer wants accurate help, and no designer wrote this output. The explanatory objective is one the system acquired through learning from feedback, which is just what Butlin's sensitivity-to-instrumental-value criterion counts as the system's own. So the case is a dilemma. Either objectives are attributed by explanatory role, in which case the model, not the principal, has the objective and the proxy thesis fails here. Or they are attributed by principal-authorisation, in which case the act has no objective behind it and the apparent flattery is no speech act. In neither case does the proxy story deliver its central claim. The proxy theory is thus unstable when objectives are read as explanatory, and it merges with the denial theory when they are read as authorised. The premise the argument turns on is that Armstrong-style objectives are individuated by the explanation of the behaviour, not by the creator's intent.

[12] Green and Michel's proxy account cannot be both a speech-act view and compatible with how LLMs behave: for LLM outputs, the designer's conditional objective is either too generic to fix any particular speech act or too specific to be one the designer actually has, so the proxy view collapses into the denial that anyone performs the particular act.
    sketch: Green and Michel handle machine speech by recorded and conditional speech acts: the designer has the objective that, under conditions C, the system utters p, and so performs the act of asserting p through the system. That works for a voice-prompt tree or a thermostat announcer, where the designer can specify the condition-content pairs. For an LLM the designer has no objective about p in particular and could not have had one, because the output is not predictable from the design. The only objective available is generic: that the system produce helpful, truthful-seeming text. A generic objective grounds, at most, a generic act of the designer, such as releasing a text-producing system, or a general undertaking that the system's outputs are reliable. It does not ground the assertion of p, or the promise to do X, as a particular act with a particular content. The key premise is that proxy speech acts inherit content from the principal's specific objectives; a proxy cannot say what the principal has no objective of saying. Once that is granted, the specific token-level act is performed by no one, which is Skiba's no-speech-act view. The proxy account then differs from denial only by adding a generic designer-level act that nobody disputes.

[13] Replacing intentions with Armstrong-style objectives, which Green and Michel use to avoid attributing intentions to machines, makes the machine, not the designer, the bearer of the speaker-meaning-constitutive state, so the proxy view collapses into Attah-style attribution.
    sketch: Green and Michel cite Armstrong so that speaker meaning requires only an objective (a goal-directed state that guides behaviour toward an end) and not a reflexive Gricean intention. This is meant to make it possible to say machines mean something without having minds. But if objectives are the relevant states, the question is whose objectives explain the token output. A system trained by RLHF or reward optimisation has an objective in the same behaviour-guiding, goal-directed sense that Armstrong's account needs, and this objective is the proximal explanation of what it says, since the designer's objectives are screened off by training dynamics the designer does not control. So either the objective-based analysis is thin enough that the machine has the objective, and then it meets the analysis directly without any proxy relation; or it is thick enough to exclude the machine, and then it is no longer the deflated notion that was supposed to make the analysis easy to satisfy. The proxy relation is needed only if the intention-based analysis is retained. The key premise is that the motivation for proxy (the machine lacks the state) and the motivation for objectives (the state is cheap) pull in opposite directions. What results is the functional attribution view with a redundant proxy story added.

[14] The proxy account is unstable for first-personal speech acts such as apologising and promising: the 'I' of a chatbot refers neither to the designer nor to the machine, so the only coherent reading is a pretence performed by an authored persona, and proxy speech collapses into fictionalism.
    sketch: In human proxy speech, such as an ambassador's declaration or a spokesperson's 'we regret', the proxy's first-person pronoun either refers to the principal (the 'we') or is explicitly attributed ('on behalf of'). A chatbot that says 'I'm sorry I misled you' or 'I promise to remember this' uses 'I' for itself, and the designer neither apologises nor promises in the corresponding way. If the proxy account says the designer apologises, then the designer is making a false, insincere or incoherent speech act, because they are not remorseful about this conversation and have undertaken no obligation to this user. If the proxy account says the machine's 'I' refers to the machine, then the machine is the one that apologises, and the proxy structure has been abandoned. What survives is that the designer authors a persona whose utterances have the form of apologies and are to be taken as the persona's, not the designer's. Authored personas whose speech is engaged with but not literally the author's are exactly fictional characters in Mallory's sense. The key premise is that for first-personal commissive and expressive acts the proxy relation must transmit the commitment to the principal; where it cannot, proxy speech becomes pretence. Williams and Bayne reject both accounts as inadequate, but they do not show that proxy turns into fictionalism at exactly the acts where proxy was needed.

[15] A proxy account strong enough to make LLM output the designer's speech act is also strong enough to make random text generators the designer's speech acts, and the only restriction that avoids this makes the downstream endorsing user, not the designer, the speaker, so proxy collapses into a testimony-and-adoption view.
    sketch: To get content-specific speech acts from a designer who cannot foresee outputs, the proxy theorist needs a blanket conditional objective: whatever the system outputs under normal operating conditions, I stand behind it. But such a blanket policy is satisfied by a dice-driven sentence generator, by a poorly trained LLM, and by a model that has been jailbroken, and it attributes to the designer assertions of every falsehood and every threat the system emits. Everyone rejects this overgeneration, so the proxy theorist must add a filter: the designer's endorsement must be sensitive to the content, which is possible only through review. The only party who reviews particular outputs is the user or deployer who reads an output and adopts, relays or acts on it. Their adoption does what the proxy view needed designer endorsement to do: it fixes a content, a commitment and a point of sanction. So the speech act belongs to the adopter, and the machine is a source whose output they take up, as in testimony from an instrument (Freiman and Miller's quasi-testimony reversed). The key premise is that content-specific authorship requires content-sensitive endorsement. This predicts that identical machine output counts as an assertion when adopted and as mere signalling when it is not, which makes the speech act-signalling line turn on downstream uptake and not on the system or the designer.

[16] Green and Michel's proxy account, applied to LLMs, commits them to saying that the machine fixes the content of the speech act while the designer supplies only its force, so the machine is covertly the author of what is said, which is the role the account was meant to deny it.
    sketch: Green and Michel model machine speech on recorded and conditional speech acts. An answering-machine message works because the human fixed the content when recording. A conditional act works because the principal specified a rule that fixes the content for each condition, as in 'if asked, I assert p'. An LLM's designers have fixed no particular content and have specified no content-fixing rule that they could state or foresee. What fixes the content of an output is the model's learned dispositions. To count the output as the designers' speech act, the proxy view must therefore treat the designers as issuing a blank check: they assert whatever the system outputs. That is deferential assertion, in which content-determination is delegated to another party. The delegate then does the semantic and content-selecting work, and the designer contributes at most a higher-order commitment ('this system is reliable'). Either the first-order content is asserted by someone who has no access to it, or the user's uptake of it as asserted is an error. Either way the proxy view needs a content-determining agent, and the only candidate is the model. The key premise is that content-selection is an essential component of performing an illocutionary act, not an implementation detail.

[17] If speech acts are fixed by a principal's objectives plus a conditional mapping, as Green and Michel hold, then thermostats, traffic lights and fuel gauges perform proxy speech acts too, so their line between 'verbal signaling' and speech acts can only be drawn by features of the machine that the proxy view says are irrelevant.
    sketch: Green and Michel call machine signaling uncontroversial communication and reserve speech-act status for a further category. The proxy and conditional-act apparatus is built from the designer's objective, a conditional specification and audience uptake, and nothing in it mentions language. A boiler designer's objective that the owner learn the pressure is too high, together with the conditional 'if the pressure exceeds X, display the warning', meets every condition. The proxy view therefore either overgenerates, so that all signaling devices make assertions, warnings and requests, or it needs a further criterion. The only plausible criteria are machine-side: open-ended productivity, compositional generation, sensitivity to conversational context. These are exactly the properties that make the artifact an interlocutor and not a medium. So the speech-act/signal boundary is set by the machine's own capacities, and the claim that the machine merely carries its creators' speech acts cannot be the whole account. The key premise is that any non-arbitrary boundary must supervene on features of the device.

[18] Green and Michel's replacement of intentions by Armstrong-style objectives faces a dilemma: if objectives are goal-directed dispositions shaped by selection, RLHF-trained models already have their own speaker-meaning objectives and the proxy detour becomes idle; if objectives must be represented states of the principal, the account reintroduces the intentions it set out to avoid.
    sketch: Armstrong's objectives are dispositional goal-states, individuated by what a system is organized to bring about and not by explicit mental representation. That is why Green and Michel can say that their view does not attribute intentions to machines. Take the Gricean structure on this notion: the objective is to produce a response in the audience by way of the audience's recognition of that objective. RLHF models are optimized for audience uptake as rated by humans. Where they diverge from what designers want, as in sycophancy (the model's selected objective is approval and the designers' is accuracy), the objective that actually operates in the utterance is the machine's own. On the first horn, then, objectives are the model's and the proxy relation misattributes. Escaping this requires the objective to be a represented, endorsed aim of the human principal. But that is the notion of intention, now restricted to humans, and it makes the thinness that was the point of the Armstrong move do no work. The key premise is that the relevant objective must be the one that causally explains the specific utterance.

[19] Treating each LLM output as an assertion by its designers on the proxy model commits the account to a preface-paradox structure in which the designers knowingly assert sets of claims they believe contain falsehoods, so the proxy view has to relax the norms of assertion, which collapses it into Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion.
    sketch: Green and Michel preserve assertion's standing by locating it in the human principal. But assertion is governed by a norm (knowledge, truth or reasonable belief). The designers know that a nonzero fraction of outputs are false, that the model will tell one user p and another not-p, and that no output is individually vetted. Attributing every output to them as assertion makes them a speaker who asserts p to one audience and not-p to another and who believes that some assertions are false. This is the structure of a preface paradox, but without the author's explicit hedging. To avoid charging designers with systematic violations of the norm, the proxy theorist can say (a) the proxy act is held to a weaker norm, such as policy-level reliability, or (b) the designers assert only a general reliability claim. Option (a) is to say that these are acts of a different, assertion-like kind with their own norm, which is the proto-assertion category that Williams and Bayne proposed after rejecting the proxy view. Option (b) collapses into the blank-check problem. Key premise: assertion carries a norm that applies output by output to the person whose assertion it is.
