system:
You are an editor deciding which of these theses is worth commissioning as
a 6,000-word paper. You have NOT seen any of them attacked, and you are not
being asked whether they are true — only whether each is worth the argument.

Rate promise 1-5:

  5 — if it worked, it would change how people frame this debate
  4 — a real contribution; a good journal would send it out
  3 — competent and publishable somewhere, unlikely to be discussed
  2 — the argument has been made, or the payoff is too small
  1 — confused, or the thesis is not actually contested

You are seeing them TOGETHER so that you can discriminate between them.
Rank them against each other, not against an absolute standard. They must
NOT all receive the same score: whatever the batch, the weakest gets a
lower number than the strongest. Award at most one 5.

Return ONLY a JSON array, one object per thesis, in the order given:
[{"i": 0, "promise": 1-5, "promise_reason": "one sentence"}, ...]

messages.content:
Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

Theses:
[0] The debate's verdicts differ largely because each camp tacitly picks a different candidate for 'the speaker' (the weights, the simulated persona-type, the running instance, or the deployed product), and once the candidate is fixed the disagreements shrink and the positions regroup.
    sketch: Mallory's fiction supplies a unified character, 'the Assistant', and that character is a type instantiated across millions of parallel conversations. Gubelmann's organismic argument is about the trained network as a mechanism. Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition makes sense only for a product line that can be retrained, reputationally damaged or withdrawn. Attah's control conception applies to the model's internal pipeline. These are four different entities with different persistence conditions, so 'does the LLM assert?' is four questions. The premise the argument turns on is that speech-act performance requires a bearer of commitments with diachronic identity. The persona-type and the product have that identity, and the weights and the single forward pass do not. Fixing the candidate then reclassifies the views. Organismic denial may be right about weights and irrelevant to personas. Fictionalism becomes a thesis that the persona-type is a real institutional speaker whose status is mistaken for fictional. The proxy view says the product is a speaker whose principal is the company.

[1] Chatbot fictionalism needs users to imagine a speaker, but the best evidence about how people use chatbot output supports a speakerless 'says', as in 'the map says' or 'the gauge says', in which no one is imagined to speak, so the fiction posited is not the one users engage in.
    sketch: Distinguish (i) pretend-speaker engagement, where one imagines that someone is telling one things and takes the stances proper to that (trust, resentment, 'you misled me'), from (ii) speakerless representational engagement, where one reads a prop for information and blame is directed at its maker or at the calibration. Walton's own paradigm representational props, such as maps and instruments, work in mode (ii) without any imagined narrator. Mallory's fictionalism, like quasi-testimony, runs these together. The premise is that the pattern of reactive attitudes diagnoses which mode is operative. Users often say 'it hallucinated', which locates the fault in a malfunction, and in other contexts say 'it lied to me'. If the first pattern dominates for information-seeking and the second for companionship uses, then fictionalism is correct only for a sub-practice and the assimilation to Freiman and Miller's quasi-testimony is wrong. This reclassifies the middle positions: quasi-testimony is the speakerless view with a misleading name.

[2] Fictionalism cannot account for performative speech acts such as promising and apologising unless it adds an 'export rule' that converts fictional normative upshots into real ones, and the choice between ex ante authorisation (Green and Michel's proxy) and ex post ratification (adoption) is a distinction that sorts fictionalist and proxy views differently from how the debate sorts them.
    sketch: A promise's force is normative: it creates an obligation. If the chatbot's 'I promise' is a move in a game of make-believe, the obligation is fiction-bound. Yet a tribunal can hold an airline to its chatbot's stated refund policy, so real obligations do accrue. Something must export them. The proxy view says export happens through ex ante authorisation: the deployer had objectives that the act would serve. But with LLMs the deployer has no objective regarding the particular act, only a standing policy over a distribution of outputs. What actually happens is ex post ratification or adoption, where the institution takes the output as its own after the fact, or refuses and calls it a malfunction. So there are three categories: authorised proxy, adopted output, and fiction-bound output with no export. The premise is that Green and Michel's Armstrong-style objectives condition fails for the individual token act, whereas adoption doesn't require it. Fictionalism plus adoption is then a theory that the speech act is the institution's retrospective act, which neither fictionalism nor proxy theory, as stated, predicts.

[3] Fictionalism is a theory of the audience's uptake, whereas denial, proxy and attribution views are theories of the system's production, so the 'relocating' group is misclassified: fictionalism is consistent with every production-side verdict, including full attribution of communicative intention.
    sketch: Distinguish a theory of what the producer does from a theory of what the consumer does when treating the output as speech. In other domains fictionalism about a discourse is compatible with the speaker's performing a real act. A person can make believe that a statue 'watches over' the town while a sculptor really intended a protective symbol. So if Attah is right that models have thin communicative intentions, the user could still be imagining a richer speaker than the one that exists, and the fiction would be about the persona's depth, not about whether any speech act occurs. The premise is that 'engaging through fiction' answers the question 'what is the user imagining?' and not the question 'what is the system doing?'. Mallory's non-assertion verdict therefore needs an extra production-side premise that he does not obviously supply. The thesis also predicts that arguments against fictionalism from user sincerity (Williams and Bayne) strike a different target than arguments against it from the system's capacities.

[4] Both the literalist and the relocating camps grant that a speech act's force is fixed by the psychology of some producer, whether the model or its principal. Cases in which a chatbot's output was held to bind a deployer with no content-specific intention show that force can be fixed by the normative practice of adoption and reliance, with no producer-side intention at all.
    sketch: Take Moffatt v. Air Canada, where a tribunal held the airline to its chatbot's statement of a bereavement-fare policy. No designer or deployer had any objective regarding that content, so Green and Michel's Armstrong-style 'objectives' condition for proxy speech acts fails. The tribunal also did not treat the utterance as fiction or as mere signalling, so Mallory's fictionalism misdescribes the practice. The objective theory of contract and of representation gives the general pattern: an utterance counts as a promise or assertion by an agent because of the agent's role, the uptake, and the allocation of risk, whatever the agent intended. The key premise is that this is a case of illocution and not merely of liability. The evidence is that the standard felicity vocabulary applies: the statement is 'a misrepresentation', 'a promise', and so on. If that holds, the question 'who is the author of the model's speech act?' is badly posed. Authorship is conferred by the practice and not discovered in the producer's mind. The result is a non-psychological, deontic-status view that proxy accounts approximate only by accident.

[5] Speech-act talk about chatbots ('it advised me', 'it promised') is neither evidence for literal speech acts nor evidence of make-believe, because the same talk is licensed where pretence is demonstrably absent and withheld where pretence is demonstrably present.
    sketch: Fictionalism, like its literalist rivals, takes the ordinary practice of describing chatbots as saying, telling and apologising to be the explanandum that needs either a literal or a pretence-based reading. But users say 'autocomplete told me to use a semicolon' and 'the translator apologised for the delay' with no pretence, in the way they say 'the gauge says empty'. This is an indicator-idiom of 'says'. Conversely, users who deliberately immerse themselves in a companion-bot fiction often describe the output as 'what the character says', and decline to credit anyone with advising. So pretence is neither necessary nor sufficient for speech-act vocabulary, and the data fictionalism is built to explain are not specifically fictional. The key premise is that the idiom's applicability tracks reliability and conventional signification, not make-believe. The consequence is that Mallory's evidence supports a third category of non-assertoric 'saying'. It also leaves open whether anything beyond signalling occurs when users take advice from a chatbot.

[6] In multi-agent LLM pipelines where one model's output is consumed, accepted and acted on by another model with no human reading it, there is uptake of exactly the kind speech-act theories require. Fictionalism, proxy and quasi-testimony accounts all presuppose a human interpreter, so none can say whether anything is asserted there. The question 'do LLMs perform speech acts' therefore cannot be settled by facts about human interpretation.
    sketch: Every relocating and intermediate view locates the speech act in a human relation: users pretend, designers speak by proxy, or instruments testify to human knowers. Consider an orchestrator model that receives a sub-agent's report ('the tests pass; the file is unchanged'), updates its state, and issues further actions, with an audit trail and with penalties in training or deployment for unreliable reports. No human is engaged in make-believe, and no designer has objectives about this token string. The proxy account is silent, since the principal never knows the content. The fictionalist account is idle, since no one imagines. If the denials hold, nothing is asserted, yet the structure of report, acceptance and reliance, with sanctioning in the Butlin–Viebahn sense, is all present inside the machine ecology. The key premise is that Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition can be met in such pipelines, because reward signals sanction unreliable reporters. This pressures both camps: the proxy view must say the sub-agent's report is no assertion and no proxy, and the denial view must explain why the sanctionability condition is not met.

[7] Make-believe engagement with an utterance is compatible with, and sometimes the vehicle of, genuine assertion, so fictionalism and the speech-act question are not rivals; the chatbot case then shows the live question is which acts pass through the fiction, not whether the fiction excludes them.
    sketch: Mallory and Williams and Bayne treat fictionalism as an alternative to a speech-act analysis. That presupposes that if an utterance is engaged with as fiction, no genuine illocution occurs through it. Counterexamples abound. An actor in character on stage shouts 'Fire, get out!' and means it. A tabletop game master in the voice of an NPC conveys a real rules ruling. A satirist's persona issues real accusations. A hypnotherapist's role-played 'guide' gives real instructions. In such double-voiced utterances, the in-fiction speaker is pretended, but a real speaker advises or asserts through the pretence. Applied to chatbots: even if the 'assistant' is a fictional character played by the model or sustained by the user, the pretence does not entail that no one asserts. This shifts the dispute to who is the real voice behind the character. For a base model playing characters that author is arguably nobody, and for a fine-tuned assistant it is arguably the training process or the developer. The key premise is that fiction frames are transparent to illocution when the uttering party has non-fictional objectives. The upshot is that fictionalism is not a rival to proxy accounts but a layer compatible with them, which makes Mallory's view collapse into a neighbour.

[8] Fictionalism about chatbots and the proxy view are not rival theories of chatbot speech but one theory described twice. In Walton's framework, what is true in the fiction ('the bot promised p') is fixed by a principle of generation, and the best principles of generation just are the proxy account's rules for when a deployer is committed. Disagreement between them concerns only whether users represent that structure by pretence or by direct belief.
    sketch: Walton's props generate fictional truths through principles of the form 'if the prop has feature F, it is fictional that P'. For a chatbot, the output string is the prop. For the fictional truth 'the bot asserted p' to be useful and not arbitrary, the principle must track something real. The candidates are who is answerable for p, who can be corrected, and who bears reputational or legal cost. Those are the facts proxy theorists (Green and Michel, Arora) cite as making the deployer the speaker. A fictionalist who withholds the proxy facts gets arbitrary fictions, and a proxy theorist who adds that users hear the output as 'the bot says p' has added a representational layer, which is the fiction. The key premise is that principles of generation are individuated by what they track, not by the attitude users take to the output. So the two views assign the same truth-makers to the same speech-act ascriptions. What remains is a psychological question about whether users make-believe or believe, and it does not bear on whether any speech act occurred. Williams and Bayne's claim that both views are inadequate then gets reread: they fail for the same reason, because neither says what the generation principle is when no deployer stands behind the output.

[9] The fiction in chatbot speech sits on the production side, not the consumption side. A model completing an assistant-persona transcript is in the position of an author writing a character's dialogue. Searle's pretended illocutions are therefore the right base case, and users' engagement with chatbots need not be fictional at all.
    sketch: Mallory locates the make-believe in users, who pretend that the chatbot says things. But a base model trained on text is a continuer of documents, and the 'assistant' is a character in a transcript it is extending. This is the role-play picture (Shanahan) read in speech-act terms. Searle and Austin treat an author's writing of a character's assertion as a non-serious illocution that commits the author to nothing. If so, the realist-versus-denier debate has been looking for the wrong thing. 'Does the model assert?' presupposes a serious frame, whereas the model's default frame is authorial. The real question is whether post-training (RLHF, groundedness tuning) shifts the system from authorial pretence to serious performance, or only makes the pretence more stable. The key premise is that the serious/non-serious distinction applies to the producer's mode of speech act, and that distinction can be asked of a system without asking whether it has intentions. Users can then be perfectly literal consumers of what is, on the producer side, fiction. That is a structurally odd and so far undescribed situation, like reading a very reliable novel as a reference book. It also explains why the intention and sanction conditions seem unsatisfied: they are conditions on serious performance, which was never the model's default mode.

[10] For conventional speech acts such as promising, apologising and advising, fictionalism about chatbots is unstable. Collective make-believe that a bot promised, backed by uptake and enforced norms, is how such acts come to exist, so the 'literal versus interpreted' dispute reduces to a question about whether the practice has yet become sanction-bearing.
    sketch: Fictionalism needs a contrast between pretending that X is F and X's being F. For institutional facts that contrast fails. Money, promises and offices exist because of collective acceptance, which began as 'treat this as' (Searle's status functions, Austin's uptake). If users are collectively invited by designers to hold 'the bot promised' true, and they resent, complain, demand redress and reward consistency, then the make-believe has acquired the constitutive role that makes a promise a promise. Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz say chatbot apologies are bullshit because the bot lacks moral agency. Mallory-style fictionalism can say the apology is only pretended. But if pretended apologies reliably restore trust and attract complaint when breached, the denial is only about a stage in a developing practice. The key premise is that for conventionally constituted acts, sustained, norm-backed make-believe is sufficient for the real thing. The debate is then about the stage of social uptake, and it cannot be settled by looking at the model's properties. Butlin and Viebahn's sanction condition becomes the empirical hinge.

[11] Once fictionalism is stripped of the claim that the pretence is dispensable, it is Dennettian interpretivism with a different label, and the speech-act debate is the old realism-versus-instrumentalism dispute about intentional states. Mallory, Attah and the proxy theorists differ only in how much 'literally' they pack into the word 'speech act'.
    sketch: Fictionalism (Yablo, Walton) gets its bite from the idea that the make-believe vocabulary could in principle be replaced by literal talk and is kept for convenience. For chatbots, the literal replacement would be a description in terms of weights, sampling and training distributions. No user can use that description to predict, trust or correct what the system will say, so the speech-act vocabulary is not dispensable at the grain at which users operate. An indispensable, predictively powerful vocabulary applied on the basis of real patterns is what Dennett calls the intentional stance, and for him it is not pretence. Attah's graded control-based intention reads the same patterns as inner states, and Gubelmann's malfunction-versus-wrong-doing test is an interpretivist test. The key premise is that the fictionalism the literature has in mind, with a pretence-ascribing user and a literally speechless system, requires dispensability, which fails here. Hence the 'literal speech act versus mere interpretation' question is a choice about how much realism to read into pattern-based ascription, as in the long-running debate over beliefs, and nothing specific to speech acts is at stake.

[12] Fictionalism about chatbots is unstable because every way of saying who authors the fiction turns it into another view: a designer author gives the proxy view, a model author gives the attributing view, and no author gives quasi-testimony.
    sketch: In Walton's framework, a fiction needs prescriptions to imagine. These come either from an agent who intends the prop to be used that way (an author) or from a natural prop, such as a stump taken for a bear. Option (a): the designers and RLHF pipeline fix the persona and the prescription to imagine 'the assistant says p'. The fiction is then authored by the deployer, and the make-believe sits on top of what is functionally a proxy speech act. Option (b): the model itself generates the fiction, as in role-play-simulator pictures. Making-up fictional utterances is itself an intentional, illocutionary activity (Currie-style fictive utterance), so the model has the communicative intentions the fictionalist wanted to deny, and this is Attah's graded attribution. Option (c): no one authors it, and the output is a natural prop. Then users learn from it only because it reliably covaries with the facts, as with a thermometer, and the make-believe does no epistemic work. This is the instrument or quasi-testimony picture with a cosmetic interface story. The key premise is that prescriptions to imagine require either an intending source or a purely causal-reliabilist source, and that Mallory's fictionalism needs neither.

[13] Fictionalism about chatbots is stable only if make-believe sanctioning of chatbots stays make-believe, but feedback loops make the sanctions real. This satisfies the Butlin–Viebahn sanction condition and collapses fictionalism into a thin attributing view.
    sketch: Fictionalists say users only pretend the chatbot asserts, advises or apologises, so no genuine speech act occurs. Butlin and Viebahn deny assertion to current systems partly because the system cannot be sanctioned by its interlocutors. But users do 'hold chatbots to account'. They complain, downvote and reprompt, and these acts feed into fine-tuning, system prompts and product decisions. They are thus pretend-reprimands with real downstream effects on future outputs, the way a pretend-reprimand of a person would. Once the practice has this structure, the claim that it is merely a game is strained. Games are insulated from consequences, and this one is not. Following Searle-style status-function thinking, a practice in which outputs are collectively treated as assertions, with commitments tracked and sanctions applied that causally shape the producer, is the kind of institution that makes something an assertion. So fictionalism must either insulate the pretense, which is false of actual deployment, or accept that the pretense has become the practice that constitutes the speech act. The key premise is that speech-act status is fixed by sanction-involving social practice, a premise the normative deniers themselves accept.

[14] A fiction whose success condition is truth in the actual world, which is what users need to treat hallucination as a defect, is not a fiction, and fictionalism about chatbots collapses into Williams–Bayne's proto-assertion.
    sketch: Fictionalism's advantage is meant to be that it explains why users can take on chatbot content without the chatbot asserting. But users appraise outputs as accurate or hallucinated, trust them for medical, legal and factual purposes, and revise beliefs on that basis. So the pretense is governed by a norm of actual-world correctness, unlike the norm of internal coherence that governs standard fictions. Walton's cases of this kind (the map, the textbook, the museum model) are representations used non-fictionally, with truth in the world as the standard. A practice of 'pretending that S says p' whose point is to be corrected against reality, and whose participants update on p, differs from assertion only in the non-assertoric label. That is just what the proto-assertion category was introduced to capture. The key premise is that a make-believe practice individuated by its correctness norm is a truth-norm-governed practice, so it cannot be told apart from proto-assertion except by labelling.

[15] Fictionalism about chatbots is stable only given robust realism about human communicative intention, and on the interpretivist or functional theories that make deflationary views attractive it collapses into literalism.
    sketch: The contrast the fictionalist draws, between users pretending the chatbot speaks and humans really speaking, needs a fact about human speakers that chatbots lack, namely real intentions. Mallory's motivation is to avoid committing to chatbot mental states. But the live accounts of intention that make machine attribution tractable are interpretivism (Dennett), the functional control conception (Attah), and the claim that Gricean mind-reading is empirically untenable even for children and animals. On these accounts, intention-ascription is licensed by predictive and explanatory success of the stance. If chatbot-directed pretense is predictively and explanatorily indispensable, with users anticipating, correcting and cooperating, then by the same criterion that makes human intentions real, the 'fictional' intentions are real, though thin. Fictionalism about X requires that the stance toward X be dispensable in principle without loss of truth-tracking. The key premise is that the fictionalist's pretended-to-literal contrast has no principled location unless intentional states are realistically distinguished from stance-relative ones. The people who most want to deflate machine speech acts are also usually the ones who deny that realism.

[16] Gubelmann's malfunction-versus-deliberate-wrong test does not detect intention. It detects whether the system itself holds the standard against which its outputs count as successes or failures, so his organismic argument and the proxy accounts are one thesis, that LLM outputs are answerable to standards owned by someone else.
    sketch: The test asks whether we can sensibly separate 'it broke' from 'it did the wrong thing on purpose'. That separation is available only if the system has its own standard of success, which it can fall short of by accident or flout deliberately. In his cases (ChatGPT, the order-translating assistant, RoboCop) the only standards in play are the designers' or deployers'. So the test shows that standard-ownership is external. Intention is then an intermediate label that adds nothing. Proxy theorists (Green and Michel, Arora) say the same thing about the ownership of the act. The apparent split between 'denial on organismic grounds' and 'relocation to the human' is therefore one claim about standard-ownership, stated once in metaphysical vocabulary and once in social-normative vocabulary. The real dispute is whether a speech act requires its performer to own its success standard. Illocutionary success conditions are plausibly set by convention and uptake, not by the speaker's own goals, so Gubelmann's premise is the contestable one.

[17] On Gubelmann's own Kantian source, organismic purposiveness is a regulative maxim of reflective judgment, not a constitutive property. His organism/mechanism criterion is therefore itself an interpretive stance, and the literature's contrast between 'literally has intentions' and 'is merely interpreted as having them' is not available on his grounds.
    sketch: In the Critique of Judgment, Kant says we must judge organisms as natural purposes, as if their parts were reciprocally cause and effect, because our understanding cannot otherwise grasp them. He denies that this is a constitutive claim about things in themselves. Gubelmann takes over the organism/mechanism contrast as if it marked an ontological line between systems that have goals and systems that are given them. If the line is regulative, then 'LLMs lack goals of their own' means that we are not rationally compelled to judge them teleologically. That is a claim about our explanatory needs, which is exactly what the 'interpreted as' side of the headline question says. The dispute is then not literal versus interpretive. It is about whether the best explanation of LLM output requires the teleological stance, which is an empirical question about the explanatory economy of intentional versus mechanistic descriptions. Attah's graded functional notion of intention then lands close to a Kantian position.

[18] The question 'can an LLM perform speech acts?' is ill-posed until the speaker is individuated, and Gubelmann's cognitive-autonomy concession attaches to the training process while his speech-act denial attaches to the deployed frozen artefact, so his two claims are about different candidate subjects.
    sketch: Gubelmann grants LLMs cognitive autonomy because they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks. But the self-organisation happens in the training loop, which includes data, optimiser, reward signal and engineers. At deployment the weights are frozen, and any adaptation is in-context. 'The LLM' can denote the training-and-deployment pipeline, the weight file, a running instance, a session, or the persona simulated in a conversation. Each has a different profile for autonomy, persistence and answerability. The organism-style autonomy he concedes belongs to the pipeline, which is not what utters tokens. The thing that utters tokens is a static function with no self-organisation at the time of speaking. The persona that appears to promise or apologise is not the thing that was trained. The debate looks like one dispute over 'the model', but it is several disputes over different subjects. Verdicts can then diverge systematically: the pipeline-level subject may meet autonomy conditions but not speaker conditions, while the persona-level subject may meet speaker conditions but not autonomy. The area's positions would then be answers to different questions.

[19] Gubelmann's thesis that LLMs cannot speak 'for now' is close to analytic. He defines the artificial as what has externally fixed purposes and concedes that a system with self-set purposes would no longer be artificial, so what is at stake is the artificial/autonomous boundary and not speech acts.
    sketch: His argument has three parts. Speech needs intention. Intention needs purposes that the system sets for itself. A mechanism is by definition a system whose purposes are imposed from outside. His conclusion that future non-biological speakers 'would no longer be artificial' shows that artificiality has been defined so as to exclude autonomy. 'Artificial things cannot speak' is then true by stipulation, and the empirical content is carried entirely by the question when a trained system's purposes cease to be externally fixed. That question is not one about language. It is whether reinforcement learning, self-generated objectives and long-horizon learning (the conditions Butlin discusses for agency) move a system across the line. The speech-act literature is therefore a proxy debate for the agency debate. The 'for now' is redundant because the criterion is non-linguistic, and a system's passing it would entail speech-act capacity with no further argument. This predicts that on his view no further linguistic evidence could bear on the matter.
