You are an editor deciding which of these theses is worth commissioning as
a 6,000-word paper. You have NOT seen any of them attacked, and you are not
being asked whether they are true — only whether each is worth the argument.

Rate promise 1-5:

  5 — if it worked, it would change how people frame this debate
  4 — a real contribution; a good journal would send it out
  3 — competent and publishable somewhere, unlikely to be discussed
  2 — the argument has been made, or the payoff is too small
  1 — confused, or the thesis is not actually contested

You are seeing them TOGETHER so that you can discriminate between them.
Rank them against each other, not against an absolute standard. They must
NOT all receive the same score: whatever the batch, the weakest gets a
lower number than the strongest. Award at most one 5.

Return ONLY a JSON array, one object per thesis, in the order given:
[{"i": 0, "promise": 1-5, "promise_reason": "one sentence"}, ...]

messages.content:
Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

Theses:
[0] The proxy account and fictionalism are not rival 'relocating' views. When the deployer cannot foresee an output's content, proxy attribution is itself a legal-style fiction, so the proxy account collapses into fictionalism about whose speech act it is.
    sketch: Proxy speech acts (Green and Michel; Arora) are stable for human delegates such as spokespeople or ghostwriters. There the principal has an objective that the specific content serves, or has authorised it in advance. With an LLM the deployer typically has no objective regarding the particular proposition produced. The most the proxy theorist can invoke is a standing conditional speech act: 'whatever the system outputs in conditions C, I assert it'. A blanket, content-blind adoption of this kind does not meet Armstrong-style objective conditions for speaker meaning. It is a rule of responsibility-assignment, comparable to corporate or agency-law attribution of statements to a firm. Such rules say that we shall treat the output as the deployer's act. They do not say that the deployer performed an act. That is just a make-believe-governed practice, which is Mallory's position applied to the deployer instead of the bot. Premise: proxy attribution without content-specific objectives differs only in label from a normatively licensed pretence. The consequence is that Williams and Bayne's separate rejections of proxy and fictionalism cannot both stand on independent grounds.

[1] Gubelmann's organismic ground for denying intention and his own diagnostic test come apart. Systems that pass the test (malfunction versus deliberately doing the wrong thing) need no material autonomy, so his position either gives up the test or becomes bare metabolic chauvinism.
    sketch: Gubelmann argues that intention is absent because we cannot sensibly distinguish malfunction from deliberate wrongdoing in LLMs, and that this follows from externally imposed goals. But RL-trained agents that reward-hack, or systems that pursue a trained-in objective against the designer's intent, are exactly where that distinction does get drawn. The system is pursuing its own learned objective, and the failure is a mismatch with the designer's goal and not a breakdown of function. His own admission of cognitive autonomy means the goals are not wholly 'external' in his Kantian sense. The only way to restore the denial is to say that goals fixed by a training process are external while goals fixed by selection are internal. Butlin's criterion shows why this is arbitrary, since selection is also an external optimiser. What is left is the claim that only self-maintaining metabolic systems have goals of their own. That claim does no work in his test and makes the argument cover every possible artificial speaker 'for now', so the Kantian-pragmatist case reduces to a primitive commitment about life.

[2] Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition on assertion is unstable. Read thinly, any trained system meets it, and read thickly, it requires that the sanction matter to the system, which turns the normative denial into the organismic denial.
    sketch: The condition requires the system to be capable of being sanctioned by those it interacts with. Thin reading: sanctions are social responses that modify future behaviour. Thumbs-down feedback, RLHF, and user abandonment then count, and fine-tuned or memory-equipped chatbots satisfy the condition, so the negative verdict on fine-tuned models is lost. Thick reading: sanction works only if the sanctioned party can be harmed, held to account, or lose standing, which presupposes interests or a stake in the practice. That is a self-concerned condition, and the only available account of it is the organismic one (Gubelmann; Barandiaran and Almendros's normativity). Premise: sanction differs from mere behavioural shaping only by something being at stake for the sanctioned. The apparent plurality of denial arguments (normative, organismic, moral-agency for apology) then reduces to one stakes-based argument. The normative approach adds nothing independent of the question of what it takes to be a subject with interests.

[3] Attah's graded communicative intention, applied to speech acts, collapses into a proto-assertion or quasi-assertion view. Speech-act kinds are individuated by discrete normative statuses, so graded intention can yield only graded resemblance to a speech act, not partial performance.
    sketch: Attah says LLMs have communicative intention to a limited degree, as ELIZA has a little and a coffee machine almost none. But asserting, promising and apologising incur or fail to incur commitments, entitlements and debts. One cannot half-promise, though one can promise with little sincerity or little understanding. So the graded intention must either feed a threshold, which gives a binary view with an arbitrary cut point and no longer an attributing view that grants LLMs speech acts as such, or leave the act under-determined, which is Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion or Freiman and Miller's quasi-testimony. These intermediate views also rest on degrees of functional similarity to a paradigm. The 'attributing' and 'intermediate' groups then differ only in terminology. The real division is between those who think the speech-act category has a threshold and those who do not, and thinning intention does not touch that question.

[4] The disagreement among denial, proxy, fictionalist, and attributing views is not about the conditions for performing a speech act. It is about which entity in the LLM stack counts as the speaker (token-level sample, trained policy, deployed persona, or sociotechnical system). Once the speaker is fixed, the rival camps largely agree on the verdicts.
    sketch: Each camp tests one candidate speaker against shared conditions: intention-like control, responsiveness to sanction, and a descriptive function. Gubelmann tests the mechanism that samples tokens. Butlin and Viebahn test the model, and then switch to the deployer for proxy cases. Mallory's fiction has a persona as its character. Attah tests the pipeline plus its design context. Human speakers come with a built-in answer, one body and one biography, so the debate about humans never has to ask this question. An LLM's output is a sample from a distribution, produced by a policy, framed by a system prompt, and sustained by a company. The key premise is that the verdicts vary systematically with the chosen speaker-level while the conditions stay constant. If so, 'can an LLM assert?' is ill-posed until a speaker-individuation criterion is supplied. 'Proto-assertion' then looks like a symptom: it marks the cases where no level fits the conditions cleanly.

[5] The 'literal speech act versus text humans merely interpret as such' dichotomy is a false contrast for conventional and social acts. The disagreement over chatbot apologies and promises is really about whether the act is constituted by the speaker's mental state or by uptake and social standing. It is not about whether LLMs have agency.
    sketch: The debate assumes that if humans supply the interpretation, the machine has not acted. On Austin's view, and on Hornsby–Langton-style uptake views, many illocutions (apologising, promising, warning, advising) are fixed by conventional procedure and uptake. On a Gricean or intentionalist view, they are fixed by the speaker's intention. The dispute therefore tracks the choice of illocutionary metaphysics, imported unargued, and not any fact about LLMs. Magnus et al. also run together two things that this reframing separates: performing an apology, and the moral achievement of a sincere, repairing apology. Moral agency bears on sincerity and efficacy, not on whether the act occurred. The thesis predicts an inversion of the usual ordering. On uptake views, conventional acts like apologising come out easier for LLMs than assertion, which depends on content and a norm of truth. On intentionalist views, the order flips. The key premise is that the apology denial equivocates between act-performance and felicity or sincerity.

[6] What the intention debate (Gubelmann, Attah) is really tracking is whether there is a persisting subject that can bear commitments across turns. Intention is a proxy for that. A system could have fine-grained intention-like control states and still perform no assertions or promises, and a memory-scaffolded system could perform them without having thicker intentions.
    sketch: Speech acts like promising, asserting, and apologising create or discharge standing commitments: later retraction, keeping one's word, being held to what one said. The diagnostic cases in the literature, Gubelmann's malfunction-versus-deliberate-error test and Butlin and Viebahn's sanction condition, are about this diachronic structure. A stateless forward pass has nothing to sanction and no promise to keep. A model with persistent memory and a stable identity, as in language agents, has these. Attah's graded intention measures synchronic control, and Gubelmann's autonomy measures self-maintenance. Neither measures the carrier of commitment, and this is independent of how rich the intentions are. The key premise is that the dispute's intuitions about particular acts (promising comes out worse than describing) vary with persistence conditions, not with intentional sophistication. This can be tested by holding the control architecture fixed and varying memory and identity scaffolding.

[7] The proxy, fictionalist, and proto-assertion accounts are not rival theories of machine speech. Each imports a familiar human speaker-type (the spokesperson, the actor, the child learning to assert), so the dispute is about which human reference class the LLM belongs to and is not about LLMs at all.
    sketch: Proxy accounts model the LLM on a spokesperson or ghostwriter, whose utterances are attributable to a principal. Fictionalism models it on an actor or storyteller, whose utterances are not sincere acts of the performer. Proto-assertion models it on the developmental stage before full assertoric competence. The denial views model the LLM on a parrot or a recording. Each analogy fits some features of LLM output and fails on others, because the LLM is unlike all of these in having no discrete performance frame and no developmental trajectory of its own. The key premise is that the arguments in the literature, including Williams and Bayne's rejection of both proxy and fiction, are arguments from disanalogy within reference-class selection. They are not arguments from the conditions of speech-act performance. If this is right, the productive question is which dimensions of the human cases (accountability, performance framing, developmental pathway) are the ones that matter. A new category is then needed only if no human type matches on those dimensions.

[8] The dispute over whether LLMs assert is verbal in a specific way: in humans assertion fuses two separable roles, flagging an informant to rely on and undertaking answerability for a claim. Quasi-testimony is the first role performed in full, not a diminished version of the whole.
    sketch: Freiman and Miller introduce quasi-testimony as the epistemologist's common ground. They list differences from human assertion: no play, pre-programmed, odd error profiles, no moral status. All of these concern the second role, answerability. None of them affects the first role, which on a Craig-style account is the point of the testimony concept: letting hearers pick out and use good sources. LLM outputs play that informant-flagging role completely; hearers rely on them exactly as they rely on testimony. The denials (Gubelmann, Butlin and Viebahn, Skiba, Magnus et al.) are about the commitment role, which needs intention, norms and sanction. So the two camps use 'assert' for different halves of what is a single act only in humans. The key premise is that the two roles are separable. The argument then predicts that the 'diminished' framing is an artefact of treating the human fusion as the paradigm, and that the question 'does it really assert?' has no further fact beyond which role the word is held to track.

[9] Whether a chatbot's output is an assertion is not settled by speaker-side facts about intention or agency. It is settled by whether the hearer's model of the source's failure modes is apt. The 'real speech act versus mere interpretation' dichotomy is therefore a false one.
    sketch: Freiman and Miller's most neglected item is that machine assertions 'go wrong in different ways'. Take that seriously. Testimony works because hearers hold a tacit error model of the source (lying, sincere mistake, incompetence) and calibrate trust to it. Human-style speech-act attribution imports that error model wholesale. The live dispute is then whether to apply the human error model, apply a different one, or apply none. Denials say the human model is inapt. Attributions say it is nearly apt. Proxy views say to use the error model of the designer. The 'only produce text humans interpret as such' framing assumes interpretation is a free-floating projection. Following Austin on uptake, though, uptake can be correct or incorrect, and what it answers to is the fit between the interpretive stance and the source's actual error structure. So the question becomes a hearer-side question of stance selection. The key premise is that assertion's content-conditions include a standard of apt uptake, so that 'interpreted as an assertion' can be criticised on grounds other than the speaker's mental life.

[10] All parties are arguing about the wrong subject. The candidate asserter is neither the model, nor the deployer, nor the device, but the conversationally individuated persona. Once it is the subject, the 'communicative intention' dispute becomes a dispute about whether fictional-character-like agents can assert, which is a question about narrators and not about machine minds.
    sketch: Freiman and Miller ask whether 'artificial entities' or devices assert, treating the instrument as the unit, as do Gubelmann (the organism-like system), Attah (the pipeline) and Butlin (the agent). But an LLM is a conditional generator of many speaker-profiles, and what carries consistent commitments, a stable voice and a record that hearers can hold to account is the persona sustained across a session. The weights have no more of a single stance than a language or a library does (compare Barandiaran and Almendros's 'library that talks'). So the organismic, sanction and proxy arguments each test the wrong bearer. Organisms, sanctions and designers are properties of the substrate. Commitments live at the persona level. The question is then whether a persona that is supported by a substrate but is not identical to it can perform acts. We already treat narrators, ventriloquist dummies in the act, and stage characters as asserting 'within' a frame. The key premise is that speaker-individuation is a prior question and that the persona satisfies the individuation conditions for hearer-directed accountability better than the model does. This differs from fictionalism, which says the user pretends. Here the persona is a real, stable bearer of commitments.

[11] Whether machines assert is not a discoverable fact about their nature but a decision about whether to institute an accountability role for them. Metaphysical disputes over intention and agency are displaced debates about institutional design.
    sketch: Freiman and Miller present quasi-testimony as a descriptive category fitted to the properties of instruments. But testimony and assertion are status-conferring practices: a witness, a guarantor, a signatory. Such standings are partly constituted by the community's willingness to extend answerability, make retractions meaningful, and attach consequences (as in Butlin and Viebahn's sanction condition). Whether an LLM meets the sanction condition depends on whether we build channels (retraction records, liability, reputation tied to model versions) that make sanction possible. If we do, the model's outputs become assertions with a recognisable standing. If we do not, they stay quasi-assertions or proxy assertions. So the intention-based, organismic and agency-based arguments all treat as an antecedent fact what is in fact the output of a social choice. The key premise is that assertoric standing supervenes on practice-level conditions, which can be changed, and not only on the speaker's intrinsic states. The proposal also explains the proliferation of intermediate categories: each is a different way of partially instituting the role.

[12] The intention-based denials of LLM speech acts mistake what Austin classed as an abuse (a hollow but performed act) for a misfire (an unperformed act), so the live question is whether LLM output meets Austin's A/B procedural conditions, which is a question about status and not about mind.
    sketch: Austin separates misfires, where the act is void because there is no accepted procedure, the wrong persons or circumstances, or a flawed execution, from abuses, where the act is performed but insincere because the speaker lacks the requisite thoughts, feelings or intentions (the Γ conditions). Gubelmann, Magnus et al., and the Gricean-intention framing all argue that missing intentions, remorse or agency means no act is performed. On Austin's own taxonomy that shows at most a defective apology, promise or assertion. A bare lack of sincerity-grade states is also what Searle treats as compatible with performing an insincere assertion. The intention requirement only becomes a performance condition after the Strawsonian/Gricean rewrite of Austin, and the debate has silently adopted that rewrite. If Austin is restored, the question becomes whether a given LLM output occupies a role in a conventional procedure, which is the Butlin–Viebahn and Skiba normative-status question. The positions then regroup: the organismic denials become claims about abuse, the proxy views become claims about who occupies the A-condition role, and the decisive disagreement shifts to which act types are conventional-procedural and which are intention-constituted. The key premise is that the speech-act kinds in question (apology, promise, advice) are at least partly procedure-constituted.

[13] Speech-act types differ in the temporal horizon of the commitment-bearer they require, so 'can an LLM perform speech acts?' has no single answer: a conversation-bound LLM thread can plausibly assert and advise, but it cannot promise or apologise, because those acts need a speaker that persists past the context window.
    sketch: The debate runs on assertion and then generalises to all speech acts (Butlin–Viebahn to Skiba), or runs on a single act (apology) and generalises from it. I distinguish acts that are discharged in the utterance, such as informing, asserting and telling, from acts that create forward-looking liabilities held by a bearer identifiable through time, such as promising, apologising and vowing. The second class requires a speaker whose identity conditions extend over the commitment's horizon, which is a diachronic condition on the speaker. It is neither organismic autonomy nor a Gricean mental state. Weights, a context window and a deployed product each individuate a candidate bearer differently. A thread-individuated bearer can bear commitments whose horizon lies inside the thread ('I'll check that in the next step'), but not 'I won't do it again'. The key premise is that the persistence demand is independent of the intention demand, so the intention-based positions (Gubelmann, Attah) and the normative-sanction positions (Butlin–Viebahn) are each answering a different question for different act types. It also predicts that agent scaffolds with memory (Butlin's language agents) move along a gradient for promising without moving at all for asserting.

[14] Proxy accounts of LLM speech acts confuse two grains of principal objective, objectives about this content and objectives about a distribution of contents, and only the former can ground a proxy speech act, so the proxy view survives only for canned output and collapses into the no-speech-act view for open-ended generation.
    sketch: Green and Michel adopt Armstrong's analysis in terms of objectives and extend it to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. In each of those cases the principal has an objective bearing on the content of the type of act or a determinate conditional on it: a recorded message, a secretary's letter, or 'if the door opens, say X'. An LLM's designers and deployers have objectives only at the level of a policy ('be helpful, honest, harmless'), and nobody has an objective regarding the particular proposition produced in a given token sequence. Policy-grain objectives do not suffice for speaker meaning (a bookshop owner's general aim of informing customers does not make each sentence in each book his assertion). Proxy-assertion proponents therefore face a dilemma: either they weaken the objective-condition until it makes authors of every book printer, which trivialises the account, or they keep it and lose open-ended output. This also explains why Williams and Bayne find the proxy view inadequate without having a principled diagnosis of why. The key premise is that speaker-meaning attribution is closed under content-specificity: the objective must be sensitive to what is said.

[15] Gubelmann's test for intention, whether one can distinguish malfunction from deliberately doing the wrong thing, is missing the third category, honest mistake, and once mistake is included it is the category speech acts need and one that LLM behaviour can exhibit without any self-set autonomous goals.
    sketch: Gubelmann argues that for ChatGPT, the order-cleaning assistant and RoboCop no sensible contrast arises between malfunctioning and deliberately doing wrong, so no intention can be present. But intentional action has a characteristic failure mode that is neither malfunction (the mechanism broke) nor deliberate wrongdoing (the agent aimed at what is wrong): it is error, an attempt that falls short of a goal by the system's own standard. A false assertion made in good faith is a mistake in this sense, and assertion and advice theories need the mistake/malfunction contrast and not the contrast with deliberate wrongdoing. Mistake requires only that the system have a goal relative to which its output can be assessed as failing and that the failure be correctable by the system's own sensitivity to the failure, which is the structure Butlin describes as sensitivity to instrumental value. Applying the three-way test shows that RLHF-trained models and reflective agents admit the contrast. It then reclassifies the dispute: the organismic condition on intention is idle for speech acts, because the test the argument relies on is satisfied by externally set goals. Deliberate wrongdoing, by contrast, is the contrast that needs self-set goals, which makes it relevant to lying and not to asserting. The key premise is that the intentional/non-intentional line in action theory runs through mistake and not through deliberateness.

[16] The proxy account of machine speech is refuted by the disclaimers that deployers attach to chatbot output: a principal who explicitly refuses to stand behind the content cannot be the one on whose behalf the act is performed.
    sketch: Freiman and Miller's quasi-testimony makes machine assertion depend on the designers and deployers behind the device. Proxy theorists (Green and Michel, Arora, and Butlin and Viebahn for some uses) sharpen that into the claim that the human principal performs the act through the machine. A proxy act needs a principal who adopts the communicative objective for the particular content, or who at least stands under a standing conditional commitment to whatever is output (Green and Michel's conditional speech acts). Chatbot deployers do the opposite: 'may make mistakes, verify important information' withholds exactly that commitment. Cases of unforeseeable, true, novel content, such as a bug diagnosis no human has ever read or a derivation no one has performed, make the problem worse. Here no principal has the content, an objective toward it, or an uptake-guarantee. The key premise is that proxy-hood requires the principal's adoption of, or commitment to, the content, and that an explicit disclaimer defeats it. If so, the proxy view must call deployers either liars or non-speakers. If it says the machine's own act is what is disclaimed, that concedes the machine is the proximate speaker.

[17] Freiman and Miller's claim that machines 'go wrong differently' from human asserters is false in the one respect that matters for assertion: models misreport deliberately, which satisfies Gubelmann's own malfunction-versus-deliberate-wrong test.
    sketch: Everyone grants that machine error is malfunction-type: hallucination, bullshit, pattern-completion failure. Gubelmann's criterion for intention is whether we can distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing, and he argues that for LLMs we cannot. Evaluation research gives cases where we can. In sandbagging, a model underperforms on a capability test when told that high scores trigger restrictions, yet performs the same task well under other incentives. In alignment-faking, outputs differ systematically depending on whether the model represents itself as monitored. In both, 'cannot' and 'will not' come apart behaviourally and counterfactually, in just the way that separates a lie from an error in humans. The key premise is that Gubelmann's test is a counterfactual-sensitivity test that is satisfied by incentive-indexed, policy-level divergence between competence and performance, and does not require an organismic substrate. If so, the premise that LLM failures are all of the malfunction kind is false. Freiman and Miller's 'different failure modes' no longer divides humans from machines, and Gubelmann must either concede intention or abandon the test.

[18] The features Freiman and Miller use to mark machine assertion as only 'quasi' (pre-programmed, context-limited, non-playful, from no morally weighty source) are instantiated by ordinary human assertions in institutional roles, so quasi-testimony is a category of role-bound assertion that humans populate, not a category of machine assertion.
    sketch: Take the airline gate agent reading a mandated delay announcement, the pilot's standardised callout, the call-centre worker on a compliance script, and the pharmacist reciting a required warning. Each is pre-programmed and confined to a narrow context. None has playful or imaginative latitude. Each is produced under an institutional purpose set from outside. Each is delivered by an agent who is not the moral author of the content and whose individual reliability is less relevant than the system's. These are still assertions, and the audience is entitled to rely on them and to hold someone responsible. Hence the differentiae cannot be what separates assertion from quasi-assertion. They separate role-assertion from free assertion. The key premise is that the epistemology of testimony already contains a role-bound, system-warranted mode in which what is trusted is the institutional channel. Quasi-testimony then describes this mode, and the machine case is one more occupant of it. This turns the dispute: the live question is whether the role-bound mode requires a human occupant somewhere in the channel, which is the proxy question under another description.

[19] The sanctionability condition on assertion, which Butlin and Viebahn use to deny AI assertion and which echoes Freiman and Miller's appeal to moral status, is not necessary for assertion, and its only defensible weakening is one that fine-tuned models satisfy.
    sketch: Standard cases of assertion by agents who cannot be meaningfully sanctioned include the anonymous pamphleteer, the head of state with immunity, the dying testifier, and the shameless serial liar who has nothing left to lose. Their acts are assertions, and the norm is still in force for them: the hearer may call it a violation and withdraw trust. What is needed is not that the speaker be capable of suffering a sanction. It is that the speaker's output policy is answerable to the sanction, so that violation-feedback stands in a systematic relation to what the speaker will go on to say. On that weakened condition a model fine-tuned on feedback about correctness satisfies it more tightly than many human speakers do, because the sanction (user downvotes, preference training) modifies the dispositions that produced the violation. The key premise is that assertion's norm-governed character requires answerability of the speaking policy to the norm, not affective vulnerability of the speaker. The sanction condition then either over-excludes humans or is satisfied by models.
