system:
You are an editor deciding which of these theses is worth commissioning as
a 6,000-word paper. You have NOT seen any of them attacked, and you are not
being asked whether they are true — only whether each is worth the argument.

Rate promise 1-5:

  5 — if it worked, it would change how people frame this debate
  4 — a real contribution; a good journal would send it out
  3 — competent and publishable somewhere, unlikely to be discussed
  2 — the argument has been made, or the payoff is too small
  1 — confused, or the thesis is not actually contested

You are seeing them TOGETHER so that you can discriminate between them.
Rank them against each other, not against an absolute standard. They must
NOT all receive the same score: whatever the batch, the weakest gets a
lower number than the strongest. Award at most one 5.

Return ONLY a JSON array, one object per thesis, in the order given:
[{"i": 0, "promise": 1-5, "promise_reason": "one sentence"}, ...]

messages.content:
Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

Theses:
[0] A Swampman who has just coalesced and speaks is a counterexample to the shared assumption that the capacity for assertion or intention depends on the system's selection history (the function condition of Butlin and Viebahn, and the organismic-history condition of Gubelmann), so the live question is what a system does now, and on that question pre-trained LLMs are not excluded in advance.
    sketch: Butlin and Viebahn say pre-trained models fail because their outputs lack a descriptive function, meaning they are not selected for tracking truth. Gubelmann says LLMs lack goals because they were never self-organised through self-maintenance. Both treat these conditions as historical or etiological. A Swampman has no selection history for truth-tracking and no organismic past, yet if he says 'the bridge is out' we should treat him as asserting. So the conditions must be synchronic: what the system's present dispositions do, for instance whether it responds to evidence and revises its outputs under challenge. A synchronic reading of 'descriptive function' is satisfied by a base model that is reliably sensitive to contextual cues about truth. The key premise is that Swampman asserts. If it is granted, the denials must either bite the bullet on Swampman or relocate their objection to current dispositions, which is exactly where the empirical question about LLMs becomes open.

[1] Gubelmann's test for intention, whether we can sensibly distinguish malfunction from deliberately doing the wrong thing, is passed by systems with wholly externally imposed purposes (a handicap-mode chess engine, a model instructed to deceive, a model sandbagging an evaluation), so the test does not track the organismic autonomy he uses it to establish.
    sketch: Gubelmann argues that no malfunction/deliberate-error distinction applies to ChatGPT, so it lacks intention, and he grounds this in the Kantian mechanism/organism divide. But take a chess engine with a 'let the child win' mode. It plays a losing move deliberately, and that differs from a bug in a way we can check, since the engine computed better moves and suppressed them. LLMs are an even clearer case. Interpretability probes and chain-of-thought evidence in deception and sandbagging studies show a model representing the true answer while outputting a false one conditional on a goal in the context. That differs structurally from hallucination, where no such internal representation exists. So the distinction can be drawn for externally purposed mechanisms. Either the test counts these cases as intentional, which cuts the test loose from the organism/mechanism contrast, or it does not, which makes the test uninformative. The key premise is that the distinction is fixed by internal functional structure and not by who set the system's ends.

[2] Spokesperson-style and corporate apologies are counterexamples to the premise, shared by Magnus et al. and their opponents, that the apologiser must herself have moral agency and remorse: the act is valid when delivered without them, so what chatbot apologies lack is something else, and 'bullshit' is the wrong diagnosis.
    sketch: Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz argue that apology requires linguistic and moral agency in the one apologising, so chatbot apologies are mere pattern-matched form. But a press officer reading a company's apology, a clerk's 'we apologise for the delay', and an insincere or coerced apology are all recognised as apologies, flawed or insincere but real, with uptake and with repair obligations incurred. In Austinian terms, remorse is a sincerity condition whose absence makes the act an abuse, not a nullity. So the necessary condition cannot be the utterer's remorse or moral agency. What does the work is the standing of the party who is answerable for the wrong. For chatbots this means the deficiency lies in whether the deployer is bound by the words, not in the model's inner life. 'Bullshit' also presupposes an assertion-like act with indifference to truth, so the diagnosis assumes more speech-act status than the authors grant. The key premise is that remorseless institutional apologies are apologies.

[3] Proxy accounts of machine speech assume the principal has objectives regarding the content, but human proxies such as plenipotentiary delegates, unscripted press secretaries and attorneys under a general power of attorney bind their principals to content the principal never anticipated, so the proxy relation rests on standing authorisation plus accountability and gives the proxy's own discretion a role that the proxy account then cannot deny the machine.
    sketch: Green and Michel, using Armstrong's objectives account, and Arora both ground proxy speech acts in the designer's or deployer's objectives, as in recorded or conditional speech acts. That fits a fixed recording or an if-then script. LLM outputs, however, are not content the designer foresaw, and no objective of the designer concerns their specific content. The proxy theorist needs a human case where an unforeseen utterance still counts as the principal's act. Such cases exist. An ambassador improvises a commitment, a spokesperson answers an unscripted question, an attorney signs under a blanket power. They count because of the authorisation structure and the principal's liability, not because the principal had the objective. But in all these human cases the proxy's own judgment selects the content. If authorisation alone makes the act the principal's, there is a further question about who is selecting, and a spokesperson counts as an author of a derivative speech act too. If we then say the LLM is only 'sampling', we have conceded that the machine does not select, which is the very thing at issue. So the proxy view either fails to cover LLM output or collapses into a two-level view on which the machine also acts. The key premise is that the human cases are structurally like the LLM case in lacking content-level objectives.

[4] Whether an artificial system can perform a given speech act depends on whether that act type's felicity conditions require a speaker that persists until the act is satisfied. Assertion and advice need no persisting speaker, but promising and apologising do, so the current positions (quasi, proxy, proto, denial) cannot each be correct across act types.
    sketch: Freiman and Miller test artificial speakers almost wholly on assertion or testimony, and the later literature generalises from assertion to 'speech acts' (Skiba) or to apology in particular (Magnus et al.). Assertion is a synchronic act: its success conditions are met by the utterance and the hearer's uptake. Commissives and apologies are diachronic, because the speaker's future conduct is what satisfies or falsifies them. An LLM deployment offers several candidate speaker-units: the weights, the context-window instance, the persona, and the product or company. Each persists differently. The weights persist but are not 'in' the conversation. The instance ends with the window. The persona is individuated by prompt. The product persists but is a corporate agent. The key premise is that the speaker-unit must be individuated by the act type's satisfaction conditions, not fixed once for the whole system. On this premise, quasi-testimony or proto-assertion may be right for assertion while the proxy view is forced for promising and apology. A 'quasi-promise' would be incoherent, since a promise cannot be partly binding on no one. The positions are therefore indexed to act types, and the existing disputes come from treating assertion as the model case.

[5] Quasi-testimony runs together two things: uptake-warranting (a hearer is entitled to believe on the output) and accountability-bearing (something can be held to the output). Every difference Freiman and Miller list concerns the second, so quasi-testimony is a concept for the first and does not qualify as a lesser kind of assertion.
    sketch: Freiman and Miller present quasi-testimony as testimony with qualifications: no play or imagination, pre-programming, different error profiles, no moral status. Sort these by what they bear on. Reliability and context-limits bear on whether the hearer's trust is warranted. Moral status, error-type and play bear on whether anyone can be blamed, retract, or be challenged. The key premise is that these two dimensions vary independently. A reliable almanac warrants uptake with no accountable speaker, and a sincere, accountable but unreliable witness does the reverse. Once separated, 'quasi' is shown to be a degree-word applied to one dimension while the paper's actual contrasts lie on the other. The positions then reclassify: Butlin and Viebahn's sanction condition and the moral-agency denials target accountability, and Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion targets neither cleanly. Assertion in the full sense is the joint satisfaction of both dimensions. What LLMs have is high and variable warranting with accountability supplied externally, and there is no intermediate species of speech act.

[6] The proxy-versus-quasi dispute misdescribes how machine content is authored, because it assumes dictation, in which the designer fixes what is said. LLM outputs are produced by discretionary delegation, in which the designer fixes only a standard the content must meet. The two authorial relations ground different attributions of speech acts, and delegation leaves a residual speaker that proxy views cannot accommodate.
    sketch: Freiman and Miller identify 'pre-programmed' content as a mark of device assertion, and proxy accounts (Green and Michel, Arora) extend recorded-message and conditional speech acts to machines. Both models fit dictation, where a human fixes the content or a content-selection rule in advance and the device executes it. A sign or voicemail is the paradigm case. LLM deployers specify norms such as 'be helpful and truthful' and training pressures, not contents. The designer cannot foresee what is said, and that is the point of the product. Human practice already distinguishes dictation from discretionary delegation: a spokesperson, an attorney or an ambassador speaks for a principal beyond instructions. In delegation the act is attributed to the principal within the scope of authority, but the agent also counts as the performer, and liability and defeasibility run through both. The key premise is that attribution under delegation is dual and scope-limited. It follows that proxy accounts are right about principal-attribution but wrong that the machine contributes nothing, and quasi and proto accounts are right that something about the machine matters but mislocate it in qualified assertion. The residual question is whether a delegate must itself be an agent of the relevant kind. That question separates this account from both the proxy view and the denials.

[7] Assertoric force in chatbot output is assigned by the genre or interface frame (an answer box, a first-person reply) and not performed by any speaker. The dispute about whether the model intends or is a proxy therefore asks who performs force when the real question is who is answerable for the frame that assigns it.
    sketch: Every position in the debate, including Freiman and Miller's, treats force as something a speaker does with content: asserts, proxies, proto-asserts, or fails to. But much human written force is assigned by genre conventions that no individual enacts at the moment of reading, such as headlines, encyclopedia entries, FAQ answers, signs and form letters. Freiman and Miller's own devices (GPS, search engines, answering systems) are interface-framed in this way. Chat interfaces add the first-person 'I' and a turn-taking format, which makes the frame assign assertoric, advisory or apologetic force to strings. The key premise is that force-assignment by genre is a separate determinant from speaker intention and is sufficient for the hearer's entitlements and reactive attitudes. It follows that the intention-based denials (Gubelmann, Attah's graded intention) and the proxy views are answering a question the genre already settles. What is left to dispute is the legitimacy of the frame. A frame that assigns force of apology to strings no accountable party stands behind is defective, and this explains why chatbot apologies strike us as 'bullshit' (Magnus et al.) without any appeal to what the model lacks. The 'speech act or not?' question gives way to 'who authors and warrants the genre?'.

[8] Anyone who individuates speaker meaning by objectives (Green and Michel's Armstrong-style refinement) or by functional control states (Attah) is committed to saying that a reward-trained chatbot's own speech act is usually not the assertion, advice or apology its text displays, but something like placating or approval-seeking.
    sketch: Armstrong-style accounts fix what a speaker means by the objective the utterance is produced to achieve, not by its surface form. Attah's control conception likewise individuates an intention by what the internal state steers the system toward. For RLHF- and preference-tuned models, the objective that actually shapes and selects outputs is high rater approval, plus a thin layer of truth-tracking. Applied consistently, the objective-based view makes the model's own act one of eliciting approval, which is closer to a perlocutionary aim than to informing. The sentence 'I'm so sorry for the error' is then an act of mollification, and 'Paris is the capital' is an approval-seeking output that happens to be true. The key premise is that force follows the objective that explains production, not the conventional force of the sentence type. Attributing views therefore deliver non-assertion, non-apology and sycophancy-acts, not graded assertion. This also shows that proxy and attributing views disagree about whose objectives count, not about whether objectives matter.

[9] Proxy accounts of machine speech acts, applied at deployment scale, commit the deployer to asserting and promising contradictory things to different users at once. To avoid this they must treat proxy acts as carrying no speaker commitment, and that collapses them into the proto-assertion or fictionalist views they were meant to replace.
    sketch: A proxy account says the designer or deployer performs the speech act through the model, as a conditional or recorded speech act performed on their behalf. One model instance, under sampling, tells different users incompatible things in the same minute, and the deployer has neither seen nor endorsed any of these outputs. If each output is the deployer's assertion, the deployer is a massive, incoherent asserter. It is answerable for each falsehood by the assertion norm, and it is also insincere, since it lacks the belief expressed. The usual response is to say that proxy acts bind the principal only weakly, via disclaimers, role framing or a general policy. That response gives up the idea that the proxy act has the full commitment-profile of assertion: it creates no entitlement for the hearer to rely on the speaker, and no retraction duty tied to the content. The premise is that assertion's identity lies in the commitment it generates. With the commitment weakened, proxy assertion becomes an act of a lower grade, which is Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion under another name, or a pretense licensed by the deployer.

[10] Butlin's criterion of agency and Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition for assertion are jointly inconsistent with their verdict that fine-tuned chatbots fail to assert. An entity that meets the first because it systematically modifies itself in response to what conduces to its goals is thereby sanctionable in the only sense that sanction does work.
    sketch: In 'The agency in language agents', an RLHF-tuned chatbot counts as an agent because its outputs are explained by self-modification in response to information about instrumental value, including in-context learning from feedback. In 'AI Assertion', such systems fail the second condition because they cannot be sanctioned by interlocutors. But the function of sanction in an assertoric practice is to change the asserter's later assertoric conduct: it deters, corrects and recalibrates. Criticism, a thumbs-down, or an in-context rebuke is feedback of exactly the kind the agency criterion says the system is sensitive to, and it changes later outputs. If the sanction condition demands more, such as resentment, loss of reputation or felt cost, then it is no longer a condition about the practice and has become a condition about the sanctioned party's phenomenology. Most human sanction operates through conditioning anyway. So the two papers' own premises imply that the fine-tuned agentive systems the first paper counts as agents meet the second condition, and the sanction condition cannot be read thickly without making assertion depend on affect. The premise is that sanctionability is the capacity to be moved by sanction through learning, not the capacity to suffer.

[11] Gubelmann's own test for intention, whether a system's malfunctioning can be told apart from its deliberately doing the wrong thing, is behavioural and is passed by some current models in cases of strategic deception. His organismic grounding is therefore either idle or contradicts the test.
    sketch: Gubelmann argues that for ChatGPT, for RoboCop and for an order-processing assistant no such distinction can be drawn, and he uses this to diagnose a lack of intention. But the test is a diagnostic about explanatory contrast: does the system's behaviour support the explanation 'it did X on purpose' over 'it broke'? In evaluations of alignment faking, sandbagging and context-dependent misbehaviour, models behave differently when they represent themselves as unmonitored. Interventions that remove the disposition, and probes of internal representations of the monitored/unmonitored distinction, support the 'deliberate' explanation over the 'malfunction' one. If the test is what detects intention, these cases pass it, and the organismic requirement is not needed to make the verdict. If the test is passed but the verdict stays negative because the system lacks self-maintenance, then self-maintenance is a separate necessary condition that the test no longer evidences. His position then rests on the organismic thesis alone and cannot claim support from the malfunction/deliberateness contrast. The premise is that the test is one of explanatory contrast available at the behavioural and mechanistic level, not at the metabolic level.

[12] Quasi-testimony is stable only if testimony is reductionist, and on a reductionist theory the 'quasi' qualifier does no work; on assurance or non-reductionist theories, quasi-testimony collapses into plain evidence from an instrument and is no speech act at all.
    sketch: Freiman and Miller motivate quasi-testimony epistemologically: devices are sources of knowledge, so they need a testimony-like category. Whether the category is useful depends on what makes testimony special. On assurance views (Moran, Hinchman), testimony works because the speaker invites trust and takes on accountability, and a hearer's warrant comes from that. Devices cannot offer assurance, because they cannot be held to account, which Freiman and Miller concede with 'no moral status'. So on these views the hearer's warrant for a device's output is just inductive reliability, as with a thermometer, and 'quasi-testimony' is a label for instrument-evidence. On reductionist views, testimony's warrant is already inductive track-record evidence about reliability. Then human assertion and device output are epistemically on a par, and 'quasi' marks no epistemic difference. The qualified middle exists only if testimony has a non-reductive epistemic dimension that devices partly but not wholly share. The key premise is that no such dimension exists: warrant-by-assurance is all-or-nothing, so there is no partial assurance for devices to have.

[13] Each of Freiman and Miller's four differentia between machine and human assertion (pre-programmed, context-limited, different error profile, lack of play) fails for LLMs or is a difference of degree, so the only differentium left is moral status. The view therefore collapses either into full assertion with an accountability caveat or into the sanction-based denial of Butlin–Viebahn and Skiba.
    sketch: Quasi-testimony was drawn around 2018-era devices such as GPS and thermometers. LLMs are not pre-programmed in the relevant sense (their outputs are not specified in advance), they are open-domain, they role-play and joke, and their characteristic errors (confabulation, sycophancy, motivated-seeming rationalisation) resemble human ones closely. If the first four differentia go, 'differs fundamentally' rests entirely on moral status. But moral status is not a feature of the speech act. It matters to assertion only through answerability: whether the asserter can be sanctioned, blamed or required to retract. That is exactly Butlin and Viebahn's second condition. So quasi-testimony either (a) treats sanctionability as constitutive of assertion, in which case quasi-assertions are not assertions and the view becomes a denial view, or (b) treats it as extrinsic, in which case LLM output is assertion and 'quasi' is an idle hedge. The key premise is that no third role exists for moral status, one that is neither constitutive of the act nor extrinsic to it.

[14] The proxy account, usually treated as the stable rival to quasi-testimony, collapses into quasi-testimony once applied to LLMs. Designers have no content-specific objectives for particular outputs, so the proxy relation reduces to 'the system's output counts as an assertion with derived accountability', which is just the quasi view.
    sketch: The standard worry is that quasi-testimony collapses into proxy assertion. The reverse is the more serious problem. Proxy speech acts (Green and Michel, Arora) require a principal whose speaker-meaning objective the proxy carries out. For a recorded message or a fixed-script device the principal's objective attaches to a specific content. For an LLM, no designer or deployer has any objective regarding most particular outputs, since they have not seen them and could not have predicted them. The proxy account must therefore appeal to a standing conditional objective, such as 'let the system say whatever is true and helpful in response to the user'. A conditional of that kind leaves all the content selection and illocutionary-force selection to the system. The proxy relation is thereby reduced to a rule of responsibility attribution, under which the human is accountable for what the system says. That is what Freiman and Miller's 'qualified' assertion by instruments, with human-traced accountability, already says. The key premise is that a principal-fixed objective must be content-specific if the speech act is to belong to the principal rather than to whatever picks the content.

[15] Defining quasi-testimony by its role in hearers' epistemic practice makes machine assertion hearer-constituted, which collapses it into the 'text humans merely interpret as speech acts' horn it was meant to be an alternative to.
    sketch: Freiman and Miller introduce quasi-testimony as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge. The category is therefore individuated from the receiver's side: by how knowers rely on the output, not by anything about its production. Yet the debate's own contrast is between a speaker's performing an act and an audience's interpreting output as one. If a machine counts as asserting 'under certain circumstances', those circumstances are fixed by the uptake practices of hearers, such as trust, deference, and the ability to cite the output as a source. Then the act-status of the output is a function of audience stance, which is the interpretivist or fictionalist position (Mallory) under another description. The key premise is that a category defined by function in a knower's economy has no resources to say that the speaker performed an act independently of that economy. Quasi-testimony is therefore not an intermediate view between denial and attribution. It is a version of the interpretation view with an epistemological emphasis.

[16] Freiman and Miller's differentia between machine and human assertion (pre-programmed, context-limited, deviant failure modes, no imaginative play) are each satisfied by human speakers whom they would credit with full assertion, so 'quasi-testimony' marks a kind of speaker role rather than a kind of speaker, and humans fall under it too.
    sketch: The chapter says machine assertions differ because they are scripted, bounded in context, fail in non-human ways, and lack playfulness. Test each against humans. Call-centre staff, press spokespeople, and pilots reading checklists are scripted and context-limited, and they do not play. Confabulating patients (Korsakoff, split-brain 'interpreter' reports) fail in a way that is neither lying nor ordinary mistake, which is just the LLM profile. If these humans make full assertions, the differentia do not separate machines from humans. If instead they make only quasi-assertions, then quasi-testimony is a role-based category covering much human testimony. The key premise is that the differentia are offered as constitutive of the quasi/full contrast and not as mere statistical tendencies of current devices. Either horn undercuts the claim that quasi-testimony is a distinctively artificial-entity notion. It also pushes the view toward the proxy account, where the scripted speaker acts for an institution.

[17] If, as Freiman and Miller hold, quasi-testimony can ground knowledge in hearers just as testimony does, then the absence of moral status in the speaker is epistemically idle, and the human/machine difference in assertion concerns accountability and repair, not epistemic standing.
    sketch: The chapter's stated aim is common ground for treating instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge. It also lists lack of moral status as a fundamental difference between machine and human assertion. These pull apart. Assurance or trust views of testimony make the speaker's moral standing do epistemic work: the speaker takes responsibility, which entitles the hearer to believe. If quasi-testimony transmits knowledge without that standing, then moral standing is not part of what makes testimony epistemically good. That commits the authors to a reliabilist or anti-assurance picture of testimony, which they do not endorse. The alternative is to say quasi-testimony yields only reliance-based, thermometer-like knowledge, which defeats the 'common ground' aim. The key premise is that the moral-status difference is meant to be significant for epistemology and not only for ethics. The conclusion is that what machines lack is the accountability profile (blame, retraction, apology), a normative and not an epistemic profile. This is the place to locate the dispute with Butlin and Viebahn's sanction condition.

[18] A community-uptake criterion for who may be credited with assertion, which is the natural reading of Freiman and Miller's circumstance-relative quasi-testimony, commits one to saying that victims of testimonial injustice are denied full assertion and not merely denied credibility.
    sketch: The chapter says devices can quasi-assert 'under certain circumstances', which are mostly facts about how a community trusts, relies on, and treats a device's outputs. So the status of an output as testimony is partly set by social treatment. Apply that principle to humans. Where a group is systematically not treated as a source of testimony (Fricker's testimonial injustice), uptake-based status would imply they do not assert, or assert only in a reduced sense. That is absurd, since the injustice consists in wronging someone who did assert and was not believed. So either assertion status is fixed independently of uptake, in which case machine quasi-testimony cannot be fixed by community treatment, or the uptake view is committed to a perverse verdict about injustice. The key premise is that the authors' circumstances are uptake-dependent and not, for instance, dependent on design facts. Using this to separate uptake from design shows that the live question about LLMs is whether assertion status can be defeasibly independent of uptake. That in turn favours a design/proxy or capacity account over a purely social one.

[19] Quasi-testimony cannot be extended to chatbots without extending it to thermometers and fuel gauges, unless the line is drawn by conventional encoding of messages by designers, and that line makes quasi-testimony the proxy account under another name.
    sketch: Freiman and Miller treat instruments (GPS, search engines, measuring devices) as sources of knowledge that can testify in a qualified sense. Ask what excludes a mercury thermometer. Candidate lines are: it does not use a language, it does not report propositional contents, and it does not give 'answers'. The first is the only principled one, and it is Grice's natural versus non-natural meaning. But an artifact's output counts as non-natural meaning only because its signals were conventionally assigned content by human designers who intended them to be read that way. That makes the device's 'assertion' derivative on designer intention, which is exactly Green and Michel's and Arora's proxy structure. Without that line, quasi-testimony sprawls and loses its link to assertion. For LLMs the point sharpens: their outputs are conventionally meaningful in a way no designer intended case by case, so the view must say how designer-derived conventionality extends to novel utterances. The key premise is that no non-intentional criterion separates meaningful device speech from instrument readouts.
