system:
You are an editor deciding which of these theses is worth commissioning as
a 6,000-word paper. You have NOT seen any of them attacked, and you are not
being asked whether they are true — only whether each is worth the argument.

Rate promise 1-5:

  5 — if it worked, it would change how people frame this debate
  4 — a real contribution; a good journal would send it out
  3 — competent and publishable somewhere, unlikely to be discussed
  2 — the argument has been made, or the payoff is too small
  1 — confused, or the thesis is not actually contested

You are seeing them TOGETHER so that you can discriminate between them.
Rank them against each other, not against an absolute standard. They must
NOT all receive the same score: whatever the batch, the weakest gets a
lower number than the strongest. Award at most one 5.

Return ONLY a JSON array, one object per thesis, in the order given:
[{"i": 0, "promise": 1-5, "promise_reason": "one sentence"}, ...]

messages.content:
Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

Theses:
[0] Butlin's criterion for agency (systematic self-modification in response to information about what conduces to a goal) entails that fine-tuned or in-context-learning chatbots meet the sanctionability condition on assertion that he and Viebahn later use to deny them assertion, so the two positions cannot both stand.
    sketch: Butlin counts in-context learning from feedback, and RLHF-style fine-tuning, as sensitivity to instrumental value. Butlin and Viebahn say that fine-tuned models may satisfy the descriptive-function condition but fail the requirement that they be capable of being sanctioned by interlocutors. A sanction is an adverse response, such as a rebuke, correction or withdrawal of trust, that is meant to change the sanctioned party's future conduct. A system that systematically modifies its later outputs in light of such feedback, in service of a represented goal, is by Butlin's lights an agent responding to information about what conduces to that goal. So either (a) sanction-responsiveness just is a case of the agency-grounding sensitivity, and chatbots that are agents are sanctionable in the relevant sense, or (b) the sanction condition requires something extra, namely that the sanction cost the system something, which means stakes, welfare or self-maintenance. In case (b), assertion needs more than agency, and the bridge from agency to speech acts that Butlin's framework seemed to offer fails. The key premise is that the functional profile of 'being sanctioned' cannot be separated from 'learning from negative feedback' without appealing to stakes.

[1] The gap Butlin draws between agency and desire is exactly the gap between proxy speech acts and authored speech acts, so on his own account an LLM agent that is an agent but not a desirer can perform only proxy speech acts, and the proxy view is a consequence of his position, not a rival to it.
    sketch: Butlin grants that many language agents are agents because their outputs are explained by sensitivity to instrumental value. He denies that they thereby have desires: their goals are fixed by designers and not acquired through learning and reasoning that tend toward a coherent, integrated set. Armstrong-style accounts of speaker meaning, which Green and Michel use, define speech acts by the speaker's objectives. If agents of Butlin's kind pursue only objectives supplied by someone else, the structure is that of an agent acting on a principal's ends, which is the structure of proxy performance. Agency without desire therefore generates the proxy structure. The only way to get authored speech acts is to meet Butlin's more demanding desire conditions, which are the conditions he says are doubtful. The key premise is that the speaker's objective in a speech act must be the speaker's own end, not merely a goal the speaker represents and efficiently pursues. This challenges Attah-style attributing views and Williams and Bayne's rejection of the proxy view, since the authority for the proxy view comes from the agency literature itself.

[2] If in-context learning is what makes a chatbot an agent, then the agent is the single conversational trajectory and not the model, so such chatbots can assert and advise but cannot promise or apologise for anything done outside the current conversation, and the debate wrongly treats 'speech acts' as one capacity.
    sketch: Butlin's most favourable route to agency for pre-trained chatbots is in-context learning from feedback, which modifies activations and not weights. The entity that has modified itself in response to information about what conduces to the goal is then the running process with this context, not the weight file, which is the same across millions of parallel conversations. Butlin's criterion therefore individuates the agent at conversation grain, and the agent comes into and goes out of existence with the context window. Speech acts differ in the diachronic identity they need. Assertion and advice can be completed within one exchange, whereas promising and apologising require an agent that persists to be held to the commitment or to have done the wrong. Thus the criterion commits its defenders to a speech-act hierarchy: some acts are available to conversation-bound agents and others are not, unless memory scaffolding (generative agents, Reflexion) supplies persistence, and then the agent is the scaffold system, not the LLM. This cuts across Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz, whose denial of apology rests on moral agency, since the failure here is of identity and not of moral standing. The key premise is that the self which modifies itself under Butlin's criterion must be the subject of the speech act's normative consequences.

[3] Butlin's criterion presupposes that language agents take up text as information about what conduces to a goal, which commits him to treating them as hearers of speech acts, and in the case of Reflexion-style agents as performers of self-addressed speech acts, before they are speakers in any contested sense.
    sketch: Butlin's agent must modify itself 'in response to information'. In in-context learning the information arrives as language: a user's correction, a reward message, or in Reflexion the agent's own written lessons. For the system's self-modification to be explained by sensitivity to what conduces to the goal, and not to mere token statistics, the text must be handled as content, as a claim about what worked and what did not. That is semantic and pragmatic uptake, on the audience side, of assertion, criticism and advice. In Reflexion the lessons are produced by the model and fed back to itself, so the system's agency is partly constituted by outputs functioning as self-addressed advice or assertion. The speech-act debate (Gubelmann, Skiba) assumes the direction of explanation runs from agency to speech acts: no agency, no illocution. On Butlin's criterion the direction is partly reversed, because linguistic acts are among the vehicles that make some systems agents. Denying that these self-notes are speech acts then forces the choice between saying their learning is not information-responsive, so they are not agents, and saying the learning is information-responsive without uptake of content, which empties the criterion. The key premise is that information-responsive learning requires the system to treat the text as representing something.

[4] Butlin-agency is not even a candidate-making condition for speech acts: a system can have outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value and still have outputs that are sensitive only to the causal effects of its strings, never to their deontic effects. Such a system is a clear agent that performs no commissive or assertive act.
    sketch: Take a Reflexion-style agent whose reward is hearer compliance or trust. Across multi-step interaction it learns that emitting 'I promise' or 'I'm sorry' in certain contexts raises reward. It satisfies Butlin's criterion unambiguously, since it has modified itself in response to information about what conduces to its goal. But its selection pressure runs through the string's causal effect on hearers, and nothing in its learning distinguishes 'I promise' from any other reward-raising noise, such as 'I guarantee' used where it creates no commitment. A trained parrot or bandit shows the same structure. The relevant premise is shared across the debate: that agency, or intention, is the bottleneck, so that settling it settles candidacy for speech-act authorship. Deniers say the bottleneck is not cleared. Attributers say it is, at least gradedly. The counterexample shows the criterion can be cleared with no movement on speech-act performance. What the speech-act case needs is instrumental sensitivity to the act-type's constitutive uptake conditions, such as commitment and entitlement-transfer. That is a different explanandum from instrumental sensitivity in general, and it cross-cuts the rival positions.

[5] Butlin's exclusion of outputs 'owed solely to design' is refuted by designed-from-scratch fully formed speakers: a system with hand-built, real-time means–end reasoning and no learning history can plainly promise and advise, so the etiological condition shared with Gubelmann's organismic view is not a condition on speakerhood.
    sketch: Consider a Swampman-style or Adam-style creature, or a system engineered from a complete psychology specification, that has no history of self-modification. It computes online what conduces to its goals, and it adjusts its utterances to the hearer's situation. By Butlin's criterion its outputs are 'owed to design', so it is no agent. By Gubelmann's Kantian criterion its goals are imposed from outside, so it has no intentions. Yet it intuitively asserts, promises and apologises on its first day, and it would be sanctionable and apologetic in the Butlin–Viebahn sense. The counterexample targets the premise that agency and intention are historical properties: autonomy of source, whether learned or self-organised, is needed. If speaker status supervenes on present functional organisation and normative position, then the live question for LLMs is what inference-time organisation pre-training produced. It is not whether training counted as self-modification in response to instrumental value. That would reclassify much of the debate about RLHF and fine-tuning as beside the point, because those matter only as causes of present organisation.

[6] For in-context-learning chatbots, the entity that 'modified itself in response to instrumental value' is individuated by the transcript, not by the model, so on Butlin's own criterion the author of a speech act is a text-individuated process that migrates across models. This is a case no existing view of authorship (model, proxy, fictional character) handles.
    sketch: Butlin allows that pre-trained chatbots with memory may qualify as agents through in-context learning from feedback. Run an adaptive conversation in which the system has learned from feedback how to achieve a user's goal. Then paste the transcript into a different model with different weights, or into the same model on different hardware. The adapted behaviour, including keeping the commitments made earlier, is preserved. Edit the transcript and the 'agent' changes, even though the weights are untouched. So the thing whose behaviour is explained by its own learning has transcript-relative identity conditions. It is neither the weights, which are common to countless conversations, nor the deployer. The premise attacked is that debates over LLM speakerhood have a determinate candidate bearer, 'the model', whose agency is then at issue; proxy, fictionalist and attributing accounts all share it. If the bearer is the transcript-conditioned process, a promise made at turn 3 and kept at turn 40 by a different substrate is one agent's act, while the same weights in two conversations are two agents. This yields novel and testable conditions on who can be sanctioned or apologise.

[7] The debate looks for speech acts at the wrong grain: the assertoric act is performed once, at deployment, as a standing policy commitment, and individual chatbot outputs are instances of that act, not acts in their own right.
    sketch: Arora's proxy account, like the denial, attribution and intermediate views, treats the unit of analysis as the token utterance and asks who asserts it. Her own practical worry shows why this fails. With machine-learning systems no designer or deployer has formed any attitude toward the specific content of a given output, so 'the designer asserts p by proxy' is false of almost every token. A better model is a legislature or a publisher of a reference work. They perform one act, such as 'I will stand behind what this system says in mode M', whose content is general and open-textured, and particular outputs fall under it. On this picture the questions 'does the model have intentions?', 'is the token an assertion?' and 'who is the proxy?' are all misposed. The remaining questions are what the general commitment covers and which outputs fall outside its scope (hallucinations as 'unauthorised' speech). The key premise is that illocutionary commitment can attach to a generative policy without being distributed over its instances, as it does with standing orders and published rules.

[8] The dispute over whether machines assert is a dispute about whether illocutionary acts are constituted on the hearer's side (uptake and functional role) or the speaker's side (accountable commitment), and LLMs matter only as the first case where these systematically come apart.
    sketch: Arora rejects 'functionalist' ascription because machine utterances resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions, and she replaces it with attribution to an accountable principal. Both sides treat this as a disagreement about machines. But the functionalist standard individuates illocutions by what the audience can do with the utterance, which is Austin's uptake. The proxy standard individuates them by who is on the hook, which is the commitment side. For humans the two are co-instantiated, so speech-act theory never had to say which one is constitutive. LLM output separates them: full uptake-conditions are met while no one has formed the commitment. The intermediate views (quasi-testimony, proto-assertion) are then best read as hedges between two constitutive theories, not as positions about machines. The key premise is that the human literature contains no argument for the priority of either side, only coincidence. The machine debate therefore cannot be settled by facts about machines, and positions on it should be predictable from prior commitments about the metaphysics of illocution.

[9] The proxy account's real difficulty is not about assertion but about the first-person pronoun: whatever 'I' refers to in chatbot output, it is not the designer or the machine, and so the dispute over speech-act authorship is a disguised dispute about the semantics of a fictional or persona-denoting 'I'.
    sketch: Chatbot outputs are overwhelmingly first-personal ('I think', 'I apologise', 'I recommend'). Proxy accounts must say that the designer asserts or apologises by proxy, but then the output's 'I' would refer to the company. Users would hear 'we' as the natural form, and an 'I'-form apology by proxy is not an apology the company has offered. Direct accounts take 'I' to refer to the model, which presupposes agency. Fictionalism takes it to be a character, but then the speech acts are the character's. Each position is really a thesis about the reference of 'I' in these outputs: designer, system, persona, or nothing. Once that is stated, much of the apology and promise literature (Magnus et al.) turns on whether a persona can be the target of moral address, and the assertion literature turns on whether a persona can be sanctioned. The key premise is that illocutionary force in these outputs is routed through indexical reference. If the referent of 'I' is a stable persona with an interactional history, as for a fictional narrator or a brand mascot, the speech-act question reduces to ordinary questions about personas.

[10] 'Proxy assertion' is best understood as an attribution regime like the law of agency's apparent authority, which deliberately ignores the proxy's mental states, so the debate between proxy theorists and intention-based theorists is a clash between juridical and metaphysical senses of 'who said it'.
    sketch: Arora's refinement of proxy assertion is driven by design implications: who should answer for what the system says. Agency law attributes an agent's statement to the principal when a third party reasonably took the agent to speak for the principal, whatever the agent's mind or the principal's actual instructions. Applied to LLMs, this gives the proxy result without any claim that the designer performed an illocutionary act in the Gricean sense. Opponents (Gubelmann, Attah) argue about intention and autonomy, which settle metaphysical authorship. Both camps can be right, because they answer different questions: who is bound by what was said, and who meant it. The reframing predicts that a scenario with no human principal at all (an autonomous system deployed by no one) leaves the metaphysical question untouched but removes any attribution, a case the proxy theory cannot handle. It also predicts that the proxy theorist's 'implications for design' are normative claims about liability that no theory of speech acts could deliver.

[11] Proxy assertion is unstable for machine-learned systems because it needs a distinction between on-script and off-script output, and a system with no script cannot supply one; the account therefore collapses into mere product liability, which is not assertion.
    sketch: A human proxy such as a spokesperson, interpreter or signatory can go rogue. Her principal is committed only to what falls within a mandate, so the principal asserts p only if p is mandated. Arora's refined view says designers and deployers assert via the machine. But for ML systems the designers have no content-level mandate, and any output, including contradictory pairs and outputs the deployer would disown, is equally the product of the same training. There are two options. If every output is the principal's assertion, the principal asserts contradictions and things she never saw, which wrecks the link between assertion and commitment to a content. If only outputs the principal would endorse count, the proxy relation holds only for the endorsed cases, and the rest is a blanket policy of accepting responsibility for whatever the device emits. That policy is the structure of strict liability for a product. The premise the argument turns on is that proxy assertion requires a content-sensitive mandate and cannot rest on a content-insensitive acceptance of risk. Arora's own design recommendations for ML devices are then a concession that the proxy structure is missing.

[12] A proxy account of chatbot speech cannot handle first-person self-referential utterances without positing a persona to which 'I' refers, and a persona-involving proxy account is fictionalism under another name.
    sketch: When a ghostwriter or press office speaks for a principal, 'I' or 'we' refers to the principal. Chatbots routinely say things like 'I'm a language model', 'I can't access that file', 'I'm sorry I got that wrong' and 'I'll remember that'. If proxy assertion is the designer's assertion, 'I' refers to the designer, and the utterances are false or absurd: the company is not a language model. If instead 'I' refers to the system, the system is the one the utterance is about and is plausibly the locus of the act, which abandons the proxy view. The remaining option is a persona, 'the assistant', that is neither company nor machine, and the company speaks through it. But a persona that is spoken through, and that users address and make-believedly engage with, is the fictional character in Mallory's account. The premise the argument turns on is that self-ascriptive content is central to chatbot speech and cannot be set aside as peripheral. The proxy–fictionalism contrast, which Williams and Bayne treat as a choice between two rivals, becomes a distinction between two descriptions of one persona structure.

[13] Any principled way of choosing the principal of a proxy assertion, namely control over content, makes the user the principal in most chatbot cases and turns 'machine assertion' into tool-assisted self-assertion, so the proxy account either picks its principal arbitrarily or dissolves its own explanandum.
    sketch: Arora assigns assertions to designers and deployers. Yet a proxy relation needs a non-arbitrary account of whose act it is, and the natural candidate is whose communicative objectives the output realises, or who has counterfactual control over its content. In ordinary use the user's prompt fixes topic, stance, register and often the claim itself ('write a paragraph arguing that X'). The developer's contribution is a standing disposition and the deployer's is a system prompt. On a control criterion, the user is the principal in most interactions, and the output is like predictive text or dictation: the user adopts or does not adopt the sentence. That is not a distinctive category of machine assertion at all, since it is the ordinary use of a writing aid. If instead the principal is whoever bears accountability, the criterion is sanctionability rather than authorship, and the proxy view becomes the Butlin–Viebahn sanction condition applied to a different entity. The premise the argument turns on is that 'on behalf of' needs a criterion of authorship that is the same across human and machine proxies.

[14] The proxy and relocating accounts are not rivals to attributing views, because 'on behalf of' presupposes that the proxy itself performs an act of its own that commits the principal; the proxy account is therefore stable only for systems that are agents on Butlin's criterion, which are the cases where the machine acts as well.
    sketch: In human cases such as an ambassador, an interpreter, an attorney or a signatory with power of attorney, the principal is bound because the proxy performs an act that the institution recognises as binding. Proxy structure is two-level: the proxy utters, and her utterance counts as the principal's. This is why proxy acts can be defective in ways peculiar to proxies (ultra vires, misrepresenting the principal) and why the proxy can also be a sincere or insincere speaker. If Arora and Green and Michel keep this structure, machine proxies must perform an act, an utterance with the objective of conveying the principal's communicative aim, and that aim-directed sensitivity is what Butlin's instrumental-value criterion of agency measures. For systems with RLHF or reflective loops, the proxy view therefore does not relocate the act but presupposes machine agency. For systems that are not agents, the machine is a medium (a letter, a recording) and the proxy structure is idle, because the designer does not assert via a proxy but only via an instrument, as with a printed sign. Proxy accounts therefore have no stable region of their own: they fade into instrument views at one end and into intermediate or attributing views at the other. The premise the argument turns on is that the proxy relation is irreducibly two-agent.

[15] Proxy, fictionalist and proto-assertion accounts are not rivals about one speaker. Each is a correct answer for a different candidate speaker (deployed system, simulated character, base model), and 'does the chatbot assert?' is ill-posed until the speaker is individuated.
    sketch: Williams and Bayne treat 'the chatbot' as a single, obvious candidate asserter and then test three theories against it. But at least three entities answer to that description: the weights (a next-token predictor), the persona or character the system is shaped to simulate, and the deployed product with its system prompt, fine-tuning and operator. Proxy accounts are natural for the product, since the operator speaks through it. Fictionalism is natural for the persona, since the user engages with a character. Proto-assertion, with its descriptive-function and learning-from-feedback profile, fits the weights as shaped by RLHF. Each of the three papers' objections to the others (e.g. that the proxy view fails because no human endorses each output, or that fictionalism fails because users take outputs seriously) works only by holding the speaker fixed at a different entity. The key premise is that the three candidate speakers have different individuation conditions and different relations to the output tokens. Once the speaker is indexed, the apparent dilemma dissolves into a set of compatible claims, and the real residue is the question of which entity users should hold responsible.

[16] The dispute over whether chatbots can be 'sanctioned' (Butlin and Viebahn) and over whether assertion 'emerges' (Williams and Bayne) is really a dispute about the timescale of the feedback loop. Training-time sanction is a legitimate form of sanction, so the sanctionability condition is met, and what the debate has missed is that it is met by a different relation than the one in human practice.
    sketch: Butlin and Viebahn require that an asserter be capable of being sanctioned by interlocutors, and conclude that fine-tuned models fail this. Williams and Bayne's genealogical approach treats assertion as the output of a practice that shapes producers. Taken together, the question is where the shaping happens. In humans, sanction operates online (reproach, loss of trust) and offline (reputation). In RLHF models, sanction operates almost entirely offline, through aggregated human ratings that modify dispositions of later versions, and in-conversation sanction has only in-context effect. The relevant contrast is therefore between a sanction loop closed within a conversation and one closed across model generations, which is how the practice shapes a lineage or species. The key premise is that norm-governance of a kind is constituted by selection on the producers' dispositions, not by the producer's real-time responsiveness. If so, the 'can it be sanctioned' question is not a question about the chatbot's capacities. It is a question about whether the relevant unit of sanction is the individual conversation partner or the lineage, and the existing positions disagree because they fix this unit differently without saying so.

[17] The question 'does the model perform a speech act, or does it merely produce text humans interpret as one?' rests on a false dichotomy. On an Austinian uptake-constitutive view, the apparent act is performed jointly by the exchange, so the dispute is about where the act is located, not whether it occurs.
    sketch: All four groups, including Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion, assume the act is a product of the speaker's properties: intentions, norms, sanctionability, agency. The 'only interpreted' alternative is the deflationary foil. But if uptake is partly constitutive of illocutionary acts (Austin, Hornsby, Langton), then a user who takes up an output as advice, and who relies on and can challenge it within a stable practice, is thereby a co-constituent of an advising. This is not mere interpretation, because uptake can fail. A user can misfire by treating a hallucination as testimony, in the way one can misfire in trying to bet with someone who doesn't accept. The key premise is that illocutionary force is a two-place achievement and that at least some speech act types (advising, warning, perhaps assertion in its testimonial role) can be secured with an impoverished speaker contribution. This explains why proxy and fiction accounts both feel half-right: each captures one component of a jointly constituted act. It also relocates the real philosophical question to what entitles the hearer's uptake, which is an epistemological and ethical issue and not one in the philosophy of mind.

[18] The assertion debate is individuated at the wrong grain. Speech acts are token acts, but a chatbot's reply is a draw from a policy. The live question is whether assertion can attach to the policy (what the model reliably would say) rather than to the sampled token, and on that question the cases for denial and for proto-assertion come apart from where they are now placed.
    sketch: Williams and Bayne ask whether particular outputs are assertions or proto-assertions, and the denial literature (Butlin and Viebahn on descriptive function, Gubelmann on malfunction versus deliberate error) likewise evaluates individual responses. But each response is one sample from a distribution, and the regenerate button shows the speaker 'would have said' otherwise at the same state. Assertion involves commitment to a content, and one sample commits to nothing, since the same prompt yields contradictory outputs. A model's dispositional profile (high-probability answers across resamples, calibrated confidence) is the closest analogue of a commitment. The key premise is that the commitment-bearing unit for an LLM is the policy or distribution and not the token. Two consequences follow. First, many chatbot outputs fail to be assertions not because the model lacks intentions or sanctionability but because the individuating unit is wrong, which is a different diagnosis from any in the literature. Second, outputs where the policy is sharply peaked (stable facts) can qualify as assertions with respect to the policy while low-entropy-failing outputs (confabulations) are mere samples. This shows that a genuine 'edge of assertion' runs through the same system and not between system types.

[19] 'Proto-assertion' conflates a genealogical category (a precursor that belongs to a lineage leading toward assertion) with a structural category (an output that meets only some of assertion's conditions). Chatbot outputs fit the structural reading, which does no explanatory work, and fit the genealogical reading only if a further condition holds that current deployments fail.
    sketch: Williams and Bayne motivate proto-assertion by looking at how assertion emerges. On the genealogical reading, proto-assertion is a stage in a process where a practice of informing acquires commitment and sanction through feedback among participants. On the structural reading, it is whatever partially satisfies assertion's profile (descriptive function, some responsiveness to evidence, uptake as testimony). Partial satisfaction is cheap: a weather display, a signpost and a thermometer all meet it, so the label would not mark chatbots out or settle the dilemma. The genealogical reading is substantive but has an extra requirement. For something to be a stage in a lineage, the practice must be one in which the added norms can stabilise, which needs the speaker-side entity to be a continuing participant whose conduct is shaped by the community's responses. The premise the argument turns on is that stage-hood is a relational fact about a practice's dynamics, not an intrinsic profile of the output. Whether chatbot outputs are proto-assertions then depends on whether the loop of user uptake, correction and developer updating is in fact driving the system toward answerability. That is an empirical and institutional question, not a classificatory one, and it may be answered differently for different deployments.
