system:
You are an editor deciding which of these theses is worth commissioning as
a 6,000-word paper. You have NOT seen any of them attacked, and you are not
being asked whether they are true — only whether each is worth the argument.

Rate promise 1-5:

  5 — if it worked, it would change how people frame this debate
  4 — a real contribution; a good journal would send it out
  3 — competent and publishable somewhere, unlikely to be discussed
  2 — the argument has been made, or the payoff is too small
  1 — confused, or the thesis is not actually contested

You are seeing them TOGETHER so that you can discriminate between them.
Rank them against each other, not against an absolute standard. They must
NOT all receive the same score: whatever the batch, the weakest gets a
lower number than the strongest. Award at most one 5.

Return ONLY a JSON array, one object per thesis, in the order given:
[{"i": 0, "promise": 1-5, "promise_reason": "one sentence"}, ...]

messages.content:
Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

Theses:
[0] Some speech acts performed through LLM agents, such as 'Claim denied', 'Refund approved' or 'Access revoked' issued inside an institutional workflow, succeed without any intention from either the model or a human proxy, so the shared premise that every speech act needs an intending performer is false.
    sketch: Denials (Gubelmann, Skiba, Butlin and Viebahn) and relocating views (proxy accounts) disagree about who the intender is, but they agree that someone must have the communicative intention or objective. Institutional declarations are a counterexample. Under electronic-agent doctrines in contract law, an automated system's 'offer' or 'acceptance' binds the operator even when no person formed any objective about this particular case. Austin's conventional performatives work by role and rule, not by speaker psychology. An LLM occupying a defined office in a network of rules, which is what Puzio's relocation of agency to actor-networks suggests, performs the declaration because the office's uptake conditions are met. The proxy account must posit a human objective directed at the specific act, and in these cases there is none. The key premise is that the force of a declaration is fixed by institutional rule and uptake, not by anyone's mental state. So Skiba's extension from assertion to all speech acts fails for declaratives, and the question 'who intended it?' has a false presupposition for this class of acts.

[1] Identical LLM computation can be the Formulator of a human's communicative intention in one deployment and the whole speaker in another, so speakerhood is not an intrinsic functional property of the system, and intrinsic-property views such as Attah's control conception, Gubelmann's autonomy and Butlin's agency criterion cannot settle the question.
    sketch: Attah maps LLMs onto Levelt's blueprint (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) and argues the pipeline suggests thin communicative intentions. Take LLM-based augmentative communication systems used by people with ALS. The user supplies a few words or selects a stance, and the model expands them into fluent sentences that the user then sends. The same weights and computation that in a chatbot count as an 'intention-controlled pipeline' here plainly serve as the Formulator for the human's intention, and the speech act belongs to the user. Levelt's template describes a subsystem of a speaker, so fit to the template cannot be sufficient for being a speaker. Both denials and attributions assume that whether the LLM is a speaker depends on properties of the LLM. The counterexample shows that the same computational properties yield different answers depending on where the intention-source sits. The key premise is that the AAC user and the chatbot user cases are internally indistinguishable at the level the control conception, Gubelmann's test and Butlin's criterion operate on. Speakerhood is then a relational fact about where in the network the controlling state originates, which is a result Puzio's relational view predicts but does not argue for in this domain.

[2] Butlin and Viebahn's requirement that an asserter be capable of being sanctioned by those it interacts with is already met by chatbot personas, on exactly the terms on which pseudonymous human assertors meet it, so it cannot exclude LLM assertion.
    sketch: The sanction condition is read as requiring a persisting individual who can bear costs. Counterexample: an anonymous or pseudonymous poster, or a corporate account, asserts. The only sanctions available land on the handle (ban, loss of reputation, deletion), not on any body or person the interlocutor can reach. Handle-level sanction is nonetheless taken to sustain the assertoric norm among participants. A chatbot persona such as 'Claude' or 'Gemini' has the same structure. Users withhold trust, downvote, and report it. Developers retrain, patch or deprecate the persona, a material intervention on the weights that changes future output in the way sanction is meant to. Puzio's point that agency and consequences run through material networks of workers, companies and devices suggests that sanctions on the persona are real. The key premise is that the function of sanctionability is the maintenance of reliability under social pressure, not suffering by a subject. Even a thin version fails the counter-reply that retraining isn't felt, since a human handle ban isn't felt by the handle either.

[3] Performing a speech act on behalf of a principal does not exclude performing it as one's own, as every discretionary human delegate shows, so proxy accounts do not relocate authorship away from the model and their rivalry with attributing views is spurious.
    sketch: Proxy accounts (Green and Michel, Arora) and fictionalism are offered as alternatives to the model being the speaker, and Williams and Bayne reject proxy accounts on that rivalry. Counterexample: a hospital physician advises a patient on behalf of the hospital, an ambassador asserts for the state, and a lawyer states a position for a client. In each the delegate exercises wide discretion over content, so the delegate's advice and the institution's advice are one act, and neither is the real speaker with the other a fiction. Green and Michel's cases (recordings, fixed conditionals) have almost no discretion, which is why the proxy reading looks exclusive there. LLM outputs involve enormous discretion because deployers cannot foresee content. Puzio's network picture generalises this, since each node's act is both its own and the network's. On the human model, high discretion plus proxy status yields dual authorship. If proxy status is compatible with own authorship, then the proxy account does not by itself deny the model's speech acts, and the live question becomes whether the model's discretion is of the kind that grounds its own authorship. That reduces the proxy-versus-attribution dispute to a dispute about discretion, which Butlin's instrumental-value account and Attah's control conception already address.

[4] The sanctionability condition on assertion is falsified by humans with profound anterograde amnesia, who still assert; the only reading that spares them is within-interaction answerability, which an in-context LLM meets, so the condition cannot separate current chatbots from human asserters.
    sketch: Butlin and Viebahn require that an asserter be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with. They fail fine-tuned models on this because criticism or reward does not reach the model in a way that changes its later conduct or standing. Take a Korsakoff or severe anterograde-amnesia patient. Rebukes cannot change her later conduct, and she will not remember them tomorrow, yet when she tells the nurse 'your car is in lot B' she asserts, and she can be challenged, can retract, and can be said to have been wrong. Whatever sanctionability her case preserves is local: she can be called to account, can acknowledge error, and can have her standing in the current exchange altered. If the condition is read as requiring durable behavioural or reputational consequences, it excludes her, which is absurd. If it is read as local answerability, then a chatbot that in-context takes a challenge, withdraws or corrects the claim, and changes how it speaks for the rest of the conversation meets it. The premise the argument turns on is that persistence of sanction effects across episodes is not constitutive of assertoric standing. The condition then either overgeneralises to amnesiacs or fails to exclude chatbots.

[5] The 'descriptive function' condition faces a dilemma: if function is etiological, a Swampman-style molecular duplicate of a human speaker fails to assert; if function is current-dispositional, pre-trained base models acquire descriptive function from the prompt and so already pass the condition they are said to fail.
    sketch: Butlin and Viebahn hold that pre-trained, non-fine-tuned models fail the condition that outputs have descriptive functions, because next-token prediction is not selected for truth or representation of the world. This presupposes a selected-effects notion of function. Apply it to a Swampman speaker who has just coalesced, has no selection history, and says 'the bridge is out'. Everyone grants that Swampman asserts, yet on the etiological reading nothing about his outputs has a descriptive function, so the condition is not necessary for assertion. The alternative is a dispositional or systemic notion of function, on which an output has a descriptive function if the system's present organisation makes it covary with and be regulated by how things are. A base model conditioned on a context ('You are a weather service. Report today's conditions: ...') has dispositions of that kind, since its outputs are systematically sensitive to the document-type and factual context. The premise the argument turns on is that assertoric function must be fixed by something other than history, so the cases that matter turn on current organisation, where base models are not obviously excluded. The result is that the pre-trained/fine-tuned line, which does much work in the paper, is not principled.

[6] Butlin and Viebahn's two conditions are not jointly sufficient, because a templated weather-report generator that can be sanctioned (delisted, banned, replaced) meets both and does not assert; so the conditions leave open the question they are meant to settle for LLMs.
    sketch: Their conditions are stated as necessary, and the paper's strategy is to show current systems fail one of them. But the exercise only matters if the conditions are close to sufficient, since otherwise passing them would not show that an LLM asserts. Consider a rule-based bot that generates stubs about species, or a weather-text generator. Its outputs have a clear descriptive function (they are produced to report states of affairs and are corrected when wrong). It is sanctioned by those it interacts with: editors ban it, an app store removes it, subscribers cancel. By the paper's own criteria it meets both conditions, yet almost nobody, including the authors presumably, thinks the template engine asserts. If they accept that it asserts, assertion is cheap and the question about chatbots loses its philosophical interest. If they reject it, something further is needed (understanding, commitment, a content-sensitive stance towards what is said), and that extra element is exactly what the debate about intentions and agency concerns. The premise the argument turns on is that the sanctions in play are exerted on the system as a thing to be tuned or removed, and that tuning of this kind is not the same as holding someone to account. The paper's normative strand therefore either collapses into the agency debate it seeks to bypass or trivialises assertion.

[7] The shared assumption that a machine utterance is either the machine's assertion or a proxy assertion by some human is false: there are orphan outputs that no human has adopted, authorised or even seen, which satisfy the conditions for being content that asserting would regulate and yet have no asserter.
    sketch: Butlin and Viebahn conclude that where the AI does not assert, AI systems can still be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents. Proxy accounts (Green and Michel, Arora) likewise treat deployers as the speaker. Proxy assertion, on the standard analyses, requires that someone has adopted, authorised or delegated the output, or at least can be held to its content. Consider an open-weights agent loop that a hobbyist launched months ago, which now posts claims about drug interactions in forums, answers other agents' queries, and drafts replies that nobody reviews. The deployer never saw this content, did not specify it, and has no reasonable foreknowledge. The content is read and relied on by third parties, and the output fits the descriptive-function pattern. If the machine does not assert (by the denial view) and the deployer did not assert (no adoption, no uptake), then nobody asserted, yet hearers form testimony-like expectations and norms of reliance are triggered. The premise the argument turns on is that the proxy relation cannot be stretched to cover unreviewed, unforeseen content without making proxy assertion equivalent to mere causal responsibility. The result is an assertion gap which denial and proxy views cannot accommodate, and this pushes toward either machine assertion or a distinct category of non-assertoric but assertion-governed speech.

[8] Butlin and Viebahn's verdicts on whether 'the model' asserts are unstable because the candidate speaker is never fixed. Weights, a running instance, a persona, and the deployed model-plus-scaffold system each pass or fail the descriptive-function and sanction conditions differently, so the denial, proxy and attribution camps are largely answering different questions.
    sketch: 'AI Assertion' tests 'pre-trained models', 'fine-tuned models' and 'AI systems' against its two conditions as if the bearer were obvious. But sanction can land on a token conversation (the user refuses to trust it again), on a persona type (a brand's assistant loses reputation), on weights (retraining), or on the vendor-system. Descriptive function attaches at yet another grain: the base model as a simulator of many authors, or one character. Fix the persona as the speaker and sanction is plausibly satisfied through reputation and retraining. Fix the weights and it is not. Fix the system and the vendor is the speaker, which is the proxy view. So the apparent disagreement between 'LLMs cannot assert', 'they assert by proxy' and 'they quasi-assert' is a disagreement about individuating the speaker, not about speech-act theory. The thesis turns on the premise that the two conditions are relational and grain-sensitive, so the verdict changes with the individuation.

[9] In Butlin and Viebahn's own framework, 'fails the sanction condition' and 'only proxy-asserts' describe the same fact, namely that every sanction aimed at the system terminates in the deployer. The disagreement between the denial and proxy camps is therefore verbal, and fixing that does not rescue the machine as a speaker.
    sketch: Butlin and Viebahn say fine-tuned models may satisfy the descriptive-function condition but fail the sanction condition, while AI outputs can still be proxy assertions for humans. Ask what makes sanctioning a proper target for the assertor. Blame, loss of credibility and redress must be able to bear on the entity whose future conduct they are meant to regulate. For current systems the only party whose conduct is regulated in a way that answers to the sanction is the vendor or deployer (policy changes, liability, retraining decisions). So the facts that make the machine non-sanctionable are the facts that make the human the asserter, and 'denies assertion' and 'relocates assertion' are one claim under two descriptions. The turning premise is that sanction-targeting is what fixes authorship in a norm-governed practice. If so, the live question is whether the sanction-bearing locus could shift to the system, not whether to call the present case 'proxy' or 'none'.

[10] RLHF-style training is already an institutionalised sanction practice, so Butlin and Viebahn's second condition is met or not depending on whether assertion norms are enforced by selection pressure (feedback that shapes future output) or by Strawsonian reactive attitudes (resentment and accountability). The LLM question is a proxy for that older dispute about what makes a norm an assertion norm.
    sketch: Thumbs-down, preference rankings and corrections are feedback by an interacting community that is explicitly aimed at making outputs more truthful, and the system's dispositions change in response. Under a functional, selection-based notion of sanction, 'capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with' is then plausibly satisfied. Butlin and Viebahn resist this because they hear 'sanction' as requiring something like blame or loss of standing that matters to the sanctioned party. That thicker reading is a substantive thesis about assertion: its norm is enforced through reactive attitudes directed at responsible agents, not through any error-correcting feedback. Williamson-style constitutive-rule views and Brandomian scorekeeping views of assertion would diverge on exactly this point regardless of LLMs. The turning premise is that 'capable of being sanctioned' is ambiguous between corrective and reactive sanction, and the ambiguity is where the work gets done. The debate is therefore about the metaphysics of assertion, with LLMs serving as the test case.

[11] The dispute over whether pre-trained models meet the descriptive-function condition is not about language models at all. It turns on whether functions are inherited by reproduction (Millikan's derived proper functions) or must be selected for in the system itself. On the first theory the pre-trained model's outputs already have descriptive function, and Butlin and Viebahn's first condition does not discriminate between base and fine-tuned models.
    sketch: Butlin and Viebahn hold that pre-trained models fail the first condition: next-token prediction selects for fit to a text distribution, not for descriptive function, and only groundedness or correctness fine-tuning might supply it. But the corpus consists largely of assertions, and the training process selects for reproducing those assertions' patterns. On Millikan's theory, items reproduced from a model inherit the model's proper function through the reproductive lineage, as a copied sentence inherits the function of the sentence it copies. The base model's outputs would then have the descriptive function of their sources, even though the system was not selected for truth. If this is rejected and only direct selection counts, then much human assertion, learned by imitation, would also fail. The first condition's verdict therefore depends on the grain and etiology theory of function, and the base/fine-tuned contrast loses its principled status. The turning premise is that Butlin and Viebahn's function notion is etiological but silent on derived versus direct selection.

[12] Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition has no stable reading between 'sensitive to feedback' and 'capable of being harmed or held to account': on the first reading fine-tuned chatbots already meet it and the view collapses into the attributing camp, and on the second the descriptive-function condition does no work and the view collapses into the organismic denial.
    sketch: Butlin and Viebahn say assertion requires that the asserter can be sanctioned by those it interacts with, and that fine-tuned models fail this. Ask what sanction must do to the sanctioned party. (a) Thin reading: sanction is a negative signal that changes the party's later dispositions to assert. User downvotes, corrections, in-context rebukes and RLHF updates all do this, so a model with memory or online feedback is sanctionable in exactly this sense. The condition then becomes an engineering variable, and the view agrees with Butlin's own agency criterion, which counts sensitivity to feedback as agency, and with Attah's graded attribution. (b) Thick reading: sanction must bite on something the party has a stake in, such as reputation, welfare or standing. That condition is satisfied by organisms or moral patients and not by systems with imposed goals. It is then the real work-doing condition, and the descriptive-function condition is idle. This is Gubelmann's and Magnus et al.'s position in different clothes. The premise the argument turns on is that no intermediate notion of sanction is both non-trivially unmet by current models and independent of having a stake. Without such a notion, 'norm-governed social practice' fails to yield a distinct third position.

[13] The 'descriptive function' that Butlin and Viebahn require of an asserter's outputs is, for any fine-tuned LLM, conferred by developers' and raters' selection, so a model that satisfies it is already a proxy for its trainers, and their non-proxy route to AI assertion collapses into their proxy route.
    sketch: They distinguish (i) the model itself asserting, which needs outputs with a descriptive function, from (ii) humans asserting through the model by proxy. For a pre-trained model the function is next-token prediction, so it fails (i). A fine-tuned model acquires a descriptive or correctness function only because annotators, reward models and designers select outputs for accuracy. This is an etiological function with human purposes in its history, and in that respect it differs from nothing in Green and Michel's proxy picture. The structure is: the output's descriptive function is a derivative function, derivative functions are borrowed from the selector's aims, and speech acts performed through a borrowed aim are proxy acts. So the model-level condition (i) is met only in the way that (ii) is met, and the two options differ by redescription. The principle the argument turns on is that a function conferred wholly by others' selection cannot ground the system's own speech-act status without also making the selectors the speakers. To resist, a defender must say what makes derived functions count for humans (social-evolutionary selection of assertion) but not for models. That answer either re-imports sanctioning, or concedes that derived function suffices.

[14] Proxy assertion, offered by Butlin and Viebahn as the safe harbour for AI speech, is unstable: when the deployer neither knows nor could have vetted the content, the deployer's relation to the output is publication liability, not assertion, so the proxy view collapses into the no-speech-act view.
    sketch: On their own account assertion is a norm-governed practice whose performer is answerable for the content. When a proxy asserts for a principal, the principal commits to p. Traditionally this works because the principal authorised or vetted the proxy's content, as with a spokesperson reading a script or a lawyer filing a brief. An LLM deployer authorises a policy and not particular contents. At the token level the content is generated after authorisation, is unforeseeable, and is often unreviewed. Responsibility for such outputs is strict, product-style responsibility, as with a publisher or a vending-machine owner, and it is not speaker commitment. The premise the argument turns on is that assertoric commitment requires the committed party to have some epistemic access to the content, such as the ability to appreciate it as a claim about how things are. If the premise holds, then in the cases that matter (open-ended generation) nobody asserts: the model fails the conditions and the human is only liable. This yields a precise stable position, 'liability without speech act', that neither Butlin and Viebahn nor the proxy theorists (Green and Michel, Arora) allow. The proxy option then offers no real alternative to denial.

[15] If descriptive function is etiological, a fine-tuned model's false outputs are malfunctions rather than false assertions, so the 'norm-governed practice' view of assertion collapses into a design-specification view and loses the thing it was meant to add.
    sketch: Butlin and Viebahn locate the failure of pre-trained models in lacking descriptive functions, and suggest fine-tuning for groundedness or correctness might supply them. Suppose the function is supplied by training as selection for truth-tracking. A hallucination is then an output that fails its function, which is a malfunction in the system and not a violation of an assertoric norm by a speaker. For a human, a false assertion is a norm-violating act that is nonetheless an assertion. For the model, the same condition makes the false output either not an assertion (because it lacks the function) or an assertion that is also a defect. In the first case the model's assertoric status shrinks to its true outputs, so it can never assert falsely, which is absurd for a norm-governed practice. In the second case, the norm is just the designer's specification, and 'being held to the norm' is just being debugged. That is Gubelmann's mechanism-with-imposed-purposes picture, in which no difference between malfunction and deliberate wrongdoing can be drawn. The premise the argument turns on is that a function-based criterion of assertion must be indexed to type-level function and therefore cannot distinguish error from insincerity or violation at the level of the individual act. So the normative route to denial reduces to the organismic route, and the two do not independently support denial.

[16] Because Butlin and Viebahn ground the sanctionability condition in assertion's being a norm-governed social practice, they are committed to assertoric status being partly response-dependent: if users and institutions sustainably treat chatbots as targets of reproach, correction and retraining, that practice helps make the sanctionability condition true, so whether chatbots assert is partly up to us and is not a fact to be read off the models.
    sketch: Butlin and Viebahn treat the two conditions as discoverable properties of systems: pre-trained models fail the first, fine-tuned ones fail the second. But if assertion is constituted by a social practice, then 'capable of being sanctioned' is not a purely intrinsic capacity. It depends on whether participants have sanctioning practices that take hold of the system, and on whether the system's dispositions change in response. Users already scold, correct and downvote chatbots, and those signals feed back into training. The key premise is that in a constitutively social practice, membership conditions are at least partly fixed by the practice's own responses, as with who counts as a player, a promisor or a citizen. Add that sanction channels for models are engineering and policy choices, and the result is that a vendor, regulator or user community could settle the question by building the channel. Butlin and Viebahn reject, or at least do not accept, that metaphysical consequence. Their verdict that current models fail is meant as an empirical finding about the models. The social-practice premise they need makes it a contingent and revisable social fact.

[17] Butlin's own criterion of agency, together with Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition, commits them to the view that assertion requires something close to desire, so assertion is more demanding than agency and more demanding than anything they say they need for the descriptive-function condition.
    sketch: In 'The agency in language agents', Butlin holds that an entity is an agent when it modifies itself in response to information about what conduces to a goal. Reflexion-style systems count unambiguously. On a thin reading, sanction is just negative feedback, which is information about what conduces to the goal, so any such agent that interacts with sanctioners is thinly sanctionable and would pass condition 2. To keep the conclusion that fine-tuned and agentic systems fail, 'sanction' must be read thickly: the sanction must matter to the system as a cost to it, which is a stake. But Butlin separately argues that stakes and goals of that kind require desire, and that desire demands practical reasoning answerable to conduciveness and an integrated, learned goal set. So the argument turns on one dilemma: either sanction is thin and some language agents already assert, or it is thick and assertion presupposes desire-like states that Butlin elsewhere says are doubtful for existing systems. That makes assertion a cognitively heavier act than agency. The authors present their two papers as modular, but they are not.

[18] The 'descriptive function' condition, when carried over into the proxy-assertion fallback, makes a deployer's own speech-act status depend on a hidden engineering property of the tool (whether the model was fine-tuned for correctness), so Butlin and Viebahn are committed to a bizarre externalism about what humans themselves assert.
    sketch: Butlin and Viebahn say that pre-trained models produce no outputs with descriptive function, and that AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions for humans. The question is what makes a deployer's unreviewed chatbot outputs their assertions. The natural answer is that the deployer delegates a standing descriptive role to the system: 'whatever it says in the informative register, I stand behind.' But delegation of a descriptive function to something with none is incoherent, or at best merely nominal. If the delegation is real, it needs the tool's outputs to be reliably truth-directed, so a company deploying a fine-tuned model asserts and one deploying the same interface over a base model does not. Users, intentions, uptake and the company's liability are all identical in the two cases. The alternative is to say proxy assertion needs no descriptive function in the tool. Then the first condition is idle for exactly the cases where it matters, and the fallback becomes unconstrained. The key premise is that proxy speech acts inherit the functional conditions on the instrument. Proponents of the proxy view, including Green and Michel and Arora, would resist this.

[19] If sanctionability by one's interlocutors is a condition on asserting, Butlin and Viebahn must either deny that anonymous, posthumous and mass-broadcast writers assert or relocate sanction to institutions, and the institutional reading dissolves their contrast between direct AI assertion and proxy assertion, because all written assertion then becomes proxy-like.
    sketch: The condition says an asserter must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with. Many human assertors cannot be sanctioned by their actual audience: the dead author, the pseudonymous poster, the wire-service writer, and the person whose words are published after they can no longer be reached. Reading the condition strictly makes these non-assertions, which is absurd. Reading it generously, as sanction through publishers, reputation systems, legal liability or platforms, is plausible. But then the thing sanctioned is a node in an institutional network, such as an imprint, a byline or a platform account, and not the individual speaker confronting an interlocutor. On that reading a chatbot's vendor, brand and model line are exactly such nodes, and the vendor is routinely sanctioned for outputs. The key premise is that institution-mediated sanction is the normal case for text. So either the condition is too strict for humans or it is already satisfied by the deployer-plus-model unit, and 'AI asserts versus AI is a proxy for a human asserter' stops being a clean contrast.
