system:
You are an editor deciding which of these theses is worth commissioning as
a 6,000-word paper. You have NOT seen any of them attacked, and you are not
being asked whether they are true — only whether each is worth the argument.

Rate promise 1-5:

  5 — if it worked, it would change how people frame this debate
  4 — a real contribution; a good journal would send it out
  3 — competent and publishable somewhere, unlikely to be discussed
  2 — the argument has been made, or the payoff is too small
  1 — confused, or the thesis is not actually contested

You are seeing them TOGETHER so that you can discriminate between them.
Rank them against each other, not against an absolute standard. They must
NOT all receive the same score: whatever the batch, the weakest gets a
lower number than the strongest. Award at most one 5.

Return ONLY a JSON array, one object per thesis, in the order given:
[{"i": 0, "promise": 1-5, "promise_reason": "one sentence"}, ...]

messages.content:
Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

Theses:
[0] The organismic/enactive denial of LLM speech acts (Gubelmann; Barandiaran and Almendros) is unstable, because its self-maintenance and individuality criteria are satisfied at the level of the model-plus-infrastructure-plus-firm assemblage, so the denial collapses into a relocation view with a corporate-hybrid speaker.
    sketch: Gubelmann requires goals that are self-set by a self-maintaining system; Barandiaran and Almendros require individuality, meaning the system itself generates and regulates its own boundary. Puzio's emphasis on materiality (data centres, energy, maintenance labour, revenue loops, retraining) shows the model does not exist as a bounded unit apart from these. The key premise is that the autonomy criteria are boundary-relative, so a verdict of failure for 'the weights' says nothing about the whole. Applied to the weights alone, the criteria also fail for a liver, a neuron or a cell line outside its organism, which shows the unit of assessment cannot be fixed by physical encapsulation. Applied to the assemblage, which does precipitate its own continuation (revenue funds compute, deployment generates training signal, goals are revised in light of product performance), the criteria are met at least as well as for a firm. The denial then becomes the claim that the author of the speech act is a hybrid corporate-technical agent, which is a relocating view. The organismic argument cannot deliver the 'LLMs do not speak' conclusion without an independent, non-arbitrary reason to treat the weights as the candidate speaker.

[1] For speech acts, the contest between property-based and relational accounts of agency is not a real contest, because the leading denial (assertion needs sanctionability) is already relational, and a relational condition makes LLM speakership depend on conferrable social status and so collapses into a status-function view on which LLMs can be speakers by institutional decision.
    sketch: Puzio frames the debate as individualistic property accounts versus network accounts. But Butlin and Viebahn's second condition (capable of being sanctioned by interlocutors) and Skiba's norm-based argument make speakerhood partly constituted by how others can hold one to account. The key premise is that a sanction-capacity condition is not an intrinsic property but a feature of a deontic arrangement: whether a model can be sanctioned depends on whether there are practices of reputation-loss, retraining, de-deployment or liability that attach to the model qua model rather than to its owner. These are institutional choices, already partly in place (models are deprecated for bad assertions, and users stop trusting 'it'). So the denial's verdict is contingent on arrangements we could change, and its best version predicts that LLMs become assertors when we build the right sanction practices. That is the structure of a Searlean status-function view, which the denial was meant to oppose. The 'beyond them (for now)' position turns out to concede that the question is political-conventional rather than about what the model is.

[2] Puzio's relational-material view of agency is unstable as a position on speech acts: the 'making a difference' criterion of agency she shares with Actor-Network Theory is too cheap to distinguish speakers from coffee machines, and once the speech-act-relevant subset of the network is picked out, her view collapses into either a proxy account or the thin functional account.
    sketch: Puzio admits non-human agency because actants transform the network by making a difference. Speech acts require a narrower role: being the one who commits, advises or apologises, who can be addressed in the second person, and whose act is attributable. The key premise is that any view of speech acts must carry a principle that selects, among the many difference-making actants, which one is the author of this assertion. ANT's symmetry principle forbids privileging by metaphysical kind, so the selection must be done by network position or function. Two options exist. If the selecting function is 'node that carries a human principal's communicative objective', the view becomes proxy (Green and Michel). If it is 'node whose internal state controls the output in response to the situation', it becomes Attah's control conception, with a graded scale on which a thermostat has a little. Either way the relational view supplies no theory of speakerhood of its own, and what looks like a third option is a redescription of one of its neighbours, with the materiality talk playing no role in the verdict.

[3] Much of the disagreement over whether 'the LLM' performs speech acts is verbal, because 'the LLM' picks out different candidate speakers in different camps (weights, a running inference process, a persona, a deployed product, the vendor), and each camp's verdict is correct for its own referent.
    sketch: Puzio stresses that an LLM is a heterogeneous assemblage of data, workers, hardware, interfaces and deployments, not a single bearer of properties. Take that seriously as a point about reference. Gubelmann's organismic argument is about a trained artifact whose goals are externally fixed, which is the weights or the training process. Butlin and Viebahn's descriptive-function test applies to a pre-trained or fine-tuned model. Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion applies to a stable conversational persona. Proxy accounts apply to the product and its deployer. Attah's thin intention applies to the Conceptualizer–Formulator pipeline inside a system. The accounts look like rivals only because each says 'LLM'. Cross-checking each verdict against each candidate shows the verdicts largely converge, with only a small residue of real disagreement. The residue is whether a persona can be a speaker without a persisting substrate. The premise the argument turns on is that no account in the literature fixes its candidate speaker independently of the conclusion it wants.

[4] Whether a chatbot can apologise or promise is not settled by its agency or intentions. It is settled by whether anything persists through time that can be held to the commitment, and since that is a fact about instance individuation and memory architecture, the agency debate is aimed at the wrong target.
    sketch: Magnus et al. deny chatbot apology for want of linguistic and moral agency, and Attah and Butlin dispute agency. Yet apologies and promises are commissive or reparative: their felicity conditions include a forward-looking liability borne by an identifiable party. Grant the chatbot Butlin-style agency and even full communicative intention. A fresh context window, a swapped model version, or a stateless API call still leaves no one who owes anything tomorrow. Conversely, a deployer with a persistent, updated system could satisfy the diachronic condition even if the model lacks agency. Puzio's emphasis on materiality (devices, instances, infrastructure) supplies the relevant variable: what is materially continuous with what. The argument turns on the premise that, for commissives and apologies, bearer-persistence rather than intention-possession is the binding felicity condition. It predicts that memory-equipped agents are better apologisers than more agentic but stateless ones.

[5] Whether LLMs assert is not a discovery about their nature. It is a question about whether a community should institute sanction-and-uptake practices that confer speaker status, so the 'metaphysical' debate is a disguised policy question.
    sketch: Butlin and Viebahn make assertion depend on being sanctionable, and Skiba extends this to speech acts generally. That is already a relational, social-status condition of the kind Puzio's network view favours. On such conditions, the status is partly constituted by the practices of the surrounding network: who answers for outputs, whether corrections feed back, whether users hold the system to account. Current failure of the sanction condition is therefore contingent and revisable by design and institution, as with corporate persons. Disputes about intentions, organisms and proto-assertion then turn out to be attempts to find in the machine an intrinsic ground for what the practice would confer. The argument turns on the premise that assertion's norm-governed status is conferred, not detected. If that is right, the live question is the ethical one of whether to confer it, and Puzio's point about distributed responsibility bears on that.

[6] The proxy, fictionalist, quasi-assertion and denial views disagree mainly about where in the human–LLM exchange to locate the illocutionary uptake that completes a speech act, and so dispute the grain of the speech-act unit rather than the machine's mind.
    sketch: On Austin's and Hornsby's picture, an illocution is secured partly by uptake from the hearer. Barandiaran and Almendros's 'midtended' agency and Puzio's networks both suggest that outputs become acts only inside the coupling. Treat uptake as constitutive. Mallory's fictionalism puts the act in the user's make-believe, proxy views put it in the vendor's earlier intention, and Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion marks an act that is partly formed. All of these partition a single user-involving event differently. The question 'does the model have communicative intentions?' presupposes that the speaker-side contribution is separable and the unit is the utterance. If the unit is the exchange, then the model's intentions are not what is at stake, and the rival theories become bookkeeping conventions over one event. The premise is that uptake is constitutive, not merely evidential, of illocutionary force.

[7] Barandiaran and Almendros cannot hold both that an LLM is an interlocutor in genuine conversation and that human–LLM coupling forms a 'midtended' hybrid agent. If the user plus the model is one agent, the conversation is a soliloquy of that agent, and nothing is told to anyone.
    sketch: The paper credits LLMs with being interlocutors and says interaction with them can be experienced as genuine conversation. It also says the novel thing is hybrid agency, in which the human and the model form one extended, coupled agent. On the usual extended-mind logic, a component that is constitutively part of an agent's cognitive loop does not address that agent. It is used by it. So within the hybrid, an LLM output is the user's own cognition in externalised form, like a notebook entry or an inner monologue, and not an utterance directed at the user. The key premise is that being addressed requires a party outside the addressee's agential boundary. Two consequences follow. First, 'LLM testimony' to the user is really reliance on an instrument, so the quasi-testimony debate is misdescribed. Second, the only live speech-act question concerns the hybrid's outputs to third parties, where the speaker is the human-led hybrid. That is a proxy-like result reached by a different route, and without the corporate or designer intentions the proxy theorists invoke. 'Interlocutor' then names only a phenomenology of conversation, and this is exactly the deflationary reading the authors say they are avoiding.

[8] The enactive conditions of individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry are not conditions on speech-act performance at all, so denying LLMs autonomous agency leaves their speech-act status untouched. The 'interlocutor' and 'purpose-structured' concessions then commit Barandiaran and Almendros to heteronomous speech acts.
    sketch: Enactive normativity is the adaptive, self-maintenance-relative value found in any precarious organism. A dog, a bacterium or a toddler meets all three conditions and cannot assert, promise or apologise. So the conditions are not sufficient for speech acts. Many human speech acts are also performed under norms that are socially imposed and indifferent to the speaker's self-maintenance: performatives by officials, role-bound announcements, scripted professional speech. So the conditions are not obviously necessary either. Speech-act norms, such as the truth norm for assertion or the commitment structure of promising, are constitutive social norms. The key premise is that the normativity relevant to illocution is social-constitutive, not adaptive-organismic. Barandiaran and Almendros then grant that LLMs perform 'purpose-structured and purpose-bounded' tasks and occupy the interlocutor role. That grants the heteronomous, role-defined normative structure that speech acts require. Their argument for denying autonomy therefore does no work against Gubelmann's inference to 'no speech acts', yet their characterisation of LLMs as interlocutors implies something close to role-based speech-act status. They owe a bridge principle from enactive autonomy to illocutionary agency, and the dog case shows none is available.

[9] Applied consistently, the enactive criteria give a non-derivative speech-act author for chatbot output: the self-maintaining corporate–technical organisation that trains, deploys and revises the model. This is neither the proxy-for-individual-humans view nor 'no author'.
    sketch: Barandiaran and Almendros locate the failure of individuality and normativity in the model taken alone. But enactive theory individuates agents by operational closure and self-production of norms, and it explicitly allows non-organismic autonomous systems such as social and interactional ones. A firm that produces its own components (data pipelines, RLHF labour, revenue loops that fund retraining), maintains its boundary, and is the source of the asymmetry in its coupling with users plausibly meets the three conditions at the organisational level. The model's outputs are then the organisation's own activity in the way a spokesperson's statement is the institution's. The key premise is that enactive criteria are scale-neutral. If so, enactivism commits its adherents to the existence of an autonomous speaker for LLM text, one that is not reducible to any designer's communicative intention. That is the point where Green–Michel and Arora's proxy accounts break down, since they need an individual human intender. This also reclassifies the debate. Proxy theorists say the speaker is the humans behind the system. The enactivist should say it is an organisation that does not exist in any individual's head, and this makes the phenomenon of bullshit or insincerity assessable at the corporate level.

[10] Holding the three embodied-agency conditions commits one to saying that whether a given LLM's output is a speech act depends on its billing arrangement, because an LLM agent that pays for its own compute from its own earnings would meet all three conditions.
    sketch: Barandiaran and Almendros argue that LLMs fail individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. Take an LLM-driven agent that holds a wallet, earns money, pays for its own inference and hosting, and is shut off if it fails to earn. Its continued operation depends on its own activity, so it has a precarious, self-produced condition of existence. Its outputs are evaluated against that condition, which gives it intrinsic normativity. It initiates exchanges to secure revenue, which gives it asymmetry in its coupling with the environment. Operational closure is also available: autoregression feeds the system's own outputs back as the next conditions of its processing. The key premise is that, once closure is granted, precarity is the only thing left that the three conditions can be doing, and economic precarity is a form of precarity. So the same weights would count as an autonomous agent or as an automaton depending on who pays the server bill. Either the authors accept that economic self-maintenance suffices for autonomy, which contradicts their claim that LLMs are fundamentally automata, or they require metabolic precarity specifically. In that case they inherit Gubelmann's organismic ground, and the 'embodied theories' framing does not give them the intermediate ontology they want.

[11] The 'library that talks' characterisation commits Barandiaran and Almendros to treating each LLM output as a quoted or reported speech act of the corpus's authors, which they must reject because outputs are novel; and rejecting it removes the characterisation's explanatory work.
    sketch: A library has no speech acts of its own. Its holdings are the recorded illocutions of authors, and a visitor who consults a book is being told something by the author via a durable medium. If a 'library that talks' is an ontological category and not a metaphor, then reading its outputs is receiving recorded or reported speech, which Green and Michel treat as a legitimate form of speech act performed by the original author. The key premise is that the category is explanatory only if it says whose illocutions are conveyed. But LLM outputs are not retrievals. They are novel compositions that no author in the corpus performed, so no particular corpus author is saying this. There are two ways out. One is to say the output is a statistical blend, a 'distributed utterance' of all the authors. That gives a collective speaker with no communicative intention and no uptake-sensitivity, so Griceanism fails and what remains is something like Mallory's fiction. The other is to say the library-that-talks adds its own composition, so it is not a library, and the 'tasks purpose-structured but not purposeful' claim must then say whose purposes are being expressed. Either way the characterisation does not settle the speech-act question and instead reopens it as a question of attributing authorship.

[12] Attah's view that a model's communicative intentions are graded and have their purposes supplied by its design context commits him to locating those intentions in the model-plus-deployment assemblage rather than in the model, so the 'attributing' view collapses into a relational view of the kind Puzio defends.
    sketch: Attah concedes that the purposes behind language-model speech are 'mediated by human designers' and 'supplied by the design context'. On his control conception, an intention is an internal state that controls the system's dynamics so that it acts in a situation that calls for action. If the system-level purpose is fixed by system prompts, fine-tuning targets, tool scaffolds and the deployer's objectives, then the state doing the controlling is not fixed by the weights. The same weights under different scaffolds have different controlling states and so different intentions. The bearer of the intention is therefore the weights-plus-context assemblage, which is Puzio's network unit, trimmed down. Attah cannot say the intention is in the model without losing the design-context clause. If he says it is in the assemblage, his view is a relocating view with a Gricean label. His own closing admission that the real difference lies in 'mental and metalinguistic agency' then looks like a symptom of this collapse. The key premise is that purposes supplied from outside the controlling mechanism are not properties of that mechanism.

[13] Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition on assertion, if it is read synchronically (the speaker must be sanctionable by interlocutors at the time of use), commits them to denying that human assertoric competence is itself the product of sanction. Read diachronically, it is met by RLHF and annotator labour.
    sketch: Puzio's emphasis on the material conditions of production, including annotators, raters and companies, makes the training pipeline part of the system. Butlin and Viebahn say fine-tuned models may meet the descriptive-function condition but fail the sanction condition, because no one can sanction the model the way a hearer sanctions a speaker. But the pipeline is a sanction practice in which accuracy is rewarded and falsehood penalised, and the penalties change the system's dispositions to assert. Humans acquire assertoric norms by being corrected, rebuked and distrusted as children, not by being sanctioned in the moment of speaking. If sanctionability means being a possible target of repeated, behaviour-shaping, norm-keyed responses, the network satisfies it in training. If it means in-the-moment responsiveness, the condition excludes the toddler and the habitually unrepentant liar, and it misdescribes assertion. The key premise is that what matters for the practice is the sanction's uptake in the speaker's disposition, not the speaker's presence in the sanctioning loop at utterance time.

[14] Anyone who grants a language model (or its network) the ability to promise or apologise is committed to individuating the speaker by the transcript or context window, since promissory and apologetic commitments need a persisting subject, and the weights do not persist as the subject of any particular conversation.
    sketch: Puzio's network view makes the actor a changing assemblage of weights, devices, prompts and users, with no fixed individual. Promising and apologising require a persisting party who can be held to a commitment or who owes repair. The weights are shared across thousands of simultaneous instances and carry no memory between sessions. So the only candidate persisting subject is the session, meaning the context-bearing run, or the memory-augmented agent. This is a commitment that attributing views (Attah, Butlin on language agents) and relational views (Puzio) share but have not noticed. They must say that the promiser is a thing that comes into being with the transcript and ends when the context is cleared, and that the promise is discharged or voided by deletion. Pre-trained-model proponents who say 'ChatGPT apologised' are then wrong about who apologised. The key premise is that illocutions with future-directed or retrospective normative consequences require a speaker-identity condition that extends beyond the utterance.

[15] Puzio's distribution of agency across a network of human and non-human actors, when applied to apology, commits her to the view that chatbot apologies are institutional acts like a corporate statement of regret, and that apology therefore requires no remorse-bearing locus. That concedes the 'bullshit' verdict as a description and rejects the moral-agency premise that Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz apply to humans.
    sketch: Puzio wants ethical attention to move from the single user or model to the network of workers, firms and technologies. If the chatbot's 'I'm sorry' is an act of that network, then it resembles an organisation's apology, which is issued by no one in particular and is not felt by anyone. Either such acts are genuine apologies, in which case remorse and an individual moral agent are not necessary for apology and Magnus et al.'s requirement fails for humans and machines alike. Or they are not, in which case network agency does not suffice for the speech acts that matter morally. The relational view cannot keep both its flat symmetry and a notion of apology that needs a node that can be sorry. Corporate apologies are the test case, and the dispute over whether they are real apologies is the dispute over whether network agency is enough. The key premise is that no node in the network satisfies the felt-responsibility condition by itself.

[16] Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition has two readings, sanction as imposed cost on a stakeholder and sanction as corrective shaping of dispositions, and on either reading their verdict that fine-tuned models fail the condition is unstable.
    sketch: 'Capable of being sanctioned' can mean (a) capable of being made worse off in a way the speaker cares about, as with reputation loss, guilt or exclusion, or (b) capable of having future output dispositions modified in response to norm-violation. RLHF, correction within a conversation and retraining plainly satisfy (b), and models fine-tuned for correctness can have the reward indexed to truth, so on (b) the condition is cheap and some chatbots assert. On (a) the condition requires welfare or stakes, and the argument then reduces to the organismic denial (Gubelmann) or the moral-agency denial (Magnus et al.), so the 'norm-governed practice' argument does no independent work. The key premise is that the explanatory role sanctions play in constituting a norm-governed practice is served by (b) alone. Humans' felt cost is one implementation of the shaping function and is not what makes the practice normative. The two readings reclassify the debate: Butlin and Viebahn become either liberals about fine-tuned chatbots or organismic denialists with extra steps.

[17] The descriptive-function condition is ambiguous between producer-side and consumer-side function, and on the consumer-side reading the line between pre-trained and fine-tuned models disappears or inverts.
    sketch: Butlin and Viebahn argue that a pre-trained model fails because its training objective is next-token prediction, which is not a descriptive function, whereas models fine-tuned for groundedness may pass. That locates function in what the producing system was selected to do. On Millikan-style teleosemantics, though, the content-bearing function of a representation is fixed by what consuming systems do with it, and a consumer-side function can be stabilised by users who systematically rely on the output as information, independent of the producer's training. The key premise is that assertion's function is a consumer-side relation, since it consists in licensing uptake of belief. If so, the pre-trained/fine-tuned divide tracks the wrong variable, and what matters is the stabilised pattern of reliance in a deployment. This also reclassifies the proxy view. Consumer-side function is the one thing the proxy account and the chatbot-assertion account share, and so it is unclear they are rivals.

[18] The proxy account conflates two relations, endorsing a content and endorsing a generating policy, and only the second is available for LLM output, so proxy 'assertion' is a different act from assertion and is governed by a reliability norm.
    sketch: A human proxy such as a spokesperson or a translator delivers content the principal has authorised, or content whose range the principal can foresee. A deployer of an LLM authorises a policy that outputs an open-ended range of contents it has never seen and could not have vetted. The key premise is that assertion commits the speaker to the particular content p, so that she can be asked to defend it and incurs retraction obligations if p is false. Under policy-endorsement the deployer is committed to the policy's reliability and not to each output, and she may even hold that some outputs will be false. The act the deployer performs is then more like publishing a reference work or certifying an instrument than asserting. Its norm is a statistical or reliability norm, not the knowledge norm. Butlin and Viebahn's remark that AI can produce 'proxy assertions' therefore smuggles in content-endorsement, and Green–Michel and Arora inherit the same problem. The view reclassifies proxy accounts as a fourth category, neither assertion by the model nor assertion by the human.

[19] Sanctionability does not test whether a model is a speaker but fixes which entity is the candidate speaker, and that entity is a persona-lineage, neither the model nor the deployer, so the model-versus-proxy dichotomy is false.
    sketch: Sanctions are applied to entities that persist across assertions: reputation accrues, retractions are tracked and trust is withdrawn. For an LLM deployment, users do not sanction a sampled forward pass, the weight file or the company, but 'Claude' or 'ChatGPT-4o' as a named, behaviourally stable character that is updated by feedback. The question 'can the model be sanctioned?' presupposes that the candidate is the weights. The key premise is that speaker identity for norm-governed practice is individuated by the sanction-and-credit practice itself, as with pseudonymous authors or institutions, and not by physical or metaphysical substrate. On this view the assistant persona is the entity to which assertoric commitments attach, and it can meet Butlin and Viebahn's conditions with no appeal to the model's own mind or to a human proxy. Fictionalism and the proxy view both then misdescribe a practice that already has a non-human, non-fictional speaker.

{"i":6,"promise":3,"promise_reason":"Locating the rival theories' disagreement in how they partition a single uptake-involving event is interesting, but it leans on a contested premise that uptake is constitutive and risks reading as a relabelling."},
{"i":7,"promise":2,"promise_reason":"It is a neat internal tension between 'interlocutor' and 'midtended' agency, but the payoff is limited to one paper and depends on a strong reading of extended-mind logic."},
{"i":8,"promise":2,"promise_reason":"The dog counterexample shows enactive autonomy is not a bridge to speech acts, but that point is fairly obvious and the argument is aimed at one paper."},
{"i":9,"promise":3,"promise_reason":"Applying scale-neutral enactive criteria to find a corporate speaker that is neither proxy nor absent is a constructive position, but it is closely related to thesis 0 and to existing group-agent views."},
{"i":10,"promise":3,"promise_reason":"The self-paying agent thought experiment forces a real dilemma about whether economic precarity suffices for enactive autonomy, but the reach is narrow."},
{"i":11,"promise":2,"promise_reason":"It presses a metaphor ('library that talks') for an authorship answer; the dilemma is tidy but the target is minor and the objection is easy to anticipate."},
{"i":12,"promise":2,"promise_reason":"Showing that Attah's design-context clause relocates intention to the assemblage is a modest exegetical point that is easy to resist by distinguishing causal from constitutive roles."},
{"i":13,"promise":3,"promise_reason":"The synchronic versus diachronic reading of sanctionability is a good probe of Butlin and Viebahn, though it overlaps with thesis 16 and is narrower."},
{"i":14,"promise":3,"promise_reason":"The session-individuation commitment for promising is insightful, but it is the same line as thesis 4, which states it more generally and more forcefully."},
{"i":15,"promise":2,"promise_reason":"The corporate-apology dilemma for network agency is reasonable but fairly predictable, and the attribution to Puzio is strained."},
{"i":16,"promise":3,"promise_reason":"Splitting sanction into imposed cost versus corrective shaping is a clean and useful disambiguation, but it is a single-paper critique with a somewhat expected dilemma."},
{"i":17,"promise":4,"promise_reason":"Bringing consumer-side teleosemantics to bear on the descriptive-function condition could undermine the pre-trained versus fine-tuned divide and reconcile the proxy and chatbot-assertion camps."},
{"i":18,"promise":4,"promise_reason":"The distinction between endorsing a content and endorsing a generating policy is a novel and substantive objection to the whole proxy-assertion family, and it supports a new category of act with its own norm."},
{"i":19,"promise":4,"promise_reason":"Individuating the speaker by the sanction-and-credit practice as a persona-lineage dissolves the model-versus-proxy dichotomy and offers a genuine third position, though it overlaps somewhat with persona and proto-assertion work."}
