system:
You are an editor deciding which of these theses is worth commissioning as
a 6,000-word paper. You have NOT seen any of them attacked, and you are not
being asked whether they are true — only whether each is worth the argument.

Rate promise 1-5:

  5 — if it worked, it would change how people frame this debate
  4 — a real contribution; a good journal would send it out
  3 — competent and publishable somewhere, unlikely to be discussed
  2 — the argument has been made, or the payoff is too small
  1 — confused, or the thesis is not actually contested

You are seeing them TOGETHER so that you can discriminate between them.
Rank them against each other, not against an absolute standard. They must
NOT all receive the same score: whatever the batch, the weakest gets a
lower number than the strongest. Award at most one 5.

Return ONLY a JSON array, one object per thesis, in the order given:
[{"i": 0, "promise": 1-5, "promise_reason": "one sentence"}, ...]

messages.content:
Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

Theses:
[0] If intentions are the internal states that control output, then at standard sampling temperatures the control state of an LLM fixes only a probability distribution over speech acts, so Attah must either count the stochastic sampler as part of the speaker's will or accept that LLMs have only disjunctive intentions that never settle which illocutionary act was performed.
    sketch: A speech act is individuated by what the speaker does, such as asserting versus conjecturing versus joking, and the control conception ties intention to the state that brings about that action. In an autoregressive model the state at each step is a logit vector, and which token follows is settled by a sampling procedure outside the network, often by a pseudo-random number. The same internal state therefore yields "I promise" on one run and "I'll try" on another, and the same prompt yields confident or hedged assertion. Attah has three options. (a) The intention is the distribution, which gives an intention to perform some act from a set but not to perform any particular act, and Gricean communicative intentions are specific. (b) The sampler is part of the controller, so the temperature setting, which is a user or API parameter, partly sets the system's will. (c) Greedy decoding is the canonical case, so sampled outputs are not really the model's acts. Each option costs him something: (a) undermines the fit with the Gricean basic intention he retains, (b) is bizarre and pushes agency outward again, and (c) excludes most actual use. The premise it turns on is that intention must individuate the act type, not merely cause the output.

[1] Attah's thin, non-mind-reading conception of intention cannot support his own Levelt/POMDP argument, which makes the case for LLM intention depend on a hearer-modelling component, so his view is either a graded Gricean view or unable to rank ELIZA below ChatGPT.
    sketch: Attah rejects the strong Gricean requirement of higher-order representation of other minds as empirically untenable, citing children, animals and hominins. Yet his positive case relies on the dialogue-system architecture, in which belief-state tracking estimates the user's intention and the Conceptualizer selects messages in light of that estimate. That is a functional analogue of modelling the hearer's mind. The same component is what he uses to rank systems on the gradient from coffee machine to ELIZA to ChatGPT. This yields a dilemma. If the hearer model is not needed for communicative intention, the Levelt and POMDP machinery does no work, and nothing in the control conception distinguishes a speech-intending system from any goal-directed controller, so a thermostat-style regulator ranks as high as ELIZA. If the hearer model is what earns the higher grade, then the gradient measures depth of hearer-modelling, and the view is a Gricean view in degrees. The anti-Gricean empirical citations then show only that the threshold is low, not that the structure is different. The premise it turns on is that what grades the gradient must be what the thin conception counts as essential to the intention.

[2] Attah's closing concession that the real human–LLM difference is the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency commits him to the normative denial of speech acts, because it makes the capacity to own, monitor and answer for an utterance, rather than communicative intention, the condition for speech-act performance, so winning on intentions concedes the question.
    sketch: Attah argues that LLMs have communicative intentions in a graded, limited form and that intention is therefore not what separates them from humans. But he also says the genuine difference lies in mental and metalinguistic agency, meaning representing one's own states and one's utterances as utterances. Speech acts are standardly taken to be acts whose performer can be held to what was said, can retract, correct or clarify, and can recognise the act as the kind it is. Apologising, promising and asserting each require this. That is the substance of Butlin and Viebahn's sanction condition and of Magnus et al.'s agency condition. If the missing capacities are exactly the ones needed for being the author of a speech act, then the intention-based argument, even if sound, establishes at most that LLMs have an ingredient of speech acts and not that they perform any. Attah must either deny that metalinguistic agency matters for speech acts, which makes his own diagnosis of the difference idle, or accept that the normative views have the correct verdict and the intentions debate is orthogonal to it. The premise it turns on is that speech-act performance requires the ability to take the act as one's own, and that this is not supplied by having a control state aimed at an effect.

[3] The dispute over whether 'the LLM' performs speech acts is partly verbal, because the rival camps are predicating of different subjects (weights, running instance, simulated persona, deployed product), and Barandiaran and Almendros's failed 'individuality' condition is satisfied at one of these levels and not at others.
    sketch: Barandiaran and Almendros deny individuality because an LLM is a statistical artefact with no self-produced boundary: one set of weights is instantiated in many parallel conversations. But they evaluate the weights-plus-architecture. Gubelmann's organismic argument also evaluates the system as such. Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion and the proxy views each tacitly pick another bearer (the persona or the deployer). The thread-level process is a different case: within a conversation, a context window bounds a self-referentially constrained process that maintains its own coherence (persona, commitments, consistency) against perturbation. That is a thin but real operational closure of the kind enactivists use for individuality. The key premise is that the enactive individuality criterion is level-relative and does not fix a unique referent for 'the LLM'. Once the referent is fixed, most of the denial/attribution disagreement splits into compatible verdicts (no for the weights, perhaps partial for the thread, yes for the deployer-proxy). What remains is a dispute about which level 'the speaker' in speech-act theory should pick out, and that is a question about the role and not about agency.

[4] Barandiaran and Almendros's own category of tasks that are 'purpose-structured and purpose-bounded' but not purposeful gives illocutionary force everything it needs, so the whole intention-and-autonomy debate is aimed at the wrong determinant of speech-act identity.
    sketch: Gubelmann, Attah and the enactivists all argue about whether LLM purposes are the system's own, and so about whether the speaker has intentions. But what makes an utterance an advising, a warning or an answer is largely fixed by the frame (genre, institutional role, the exchange so far), not by the speaker's private goal hierarchy. A scripted clerk or a witness reading a prepared statement performs acts whose force is set by the frame, with the speaker's own purposes playing little part. Barandiaran and Almendros concede that LLM outputs are purpose-bounded by the interaction frame. If force is frame-determined, this concession already gives the output a determinate force, and the self-set-goals question concerns only who is answerable for the act, not what act it is. The key premise is that force-identity and authorship/answerability can come apart, and that the autonomy literature runs them together. The result is a reframing: the argument is about answerability, not about speech-act performance.

[5] If LLMs are 'libraries that talk', the question 'does the model assert?' presupposes a production-side individuation of speech acts that fits spoken conversation but not texts, and on the uptake-completed model that suits stored-and-retrieved language the dispute dissolves into a question about when, and by whom, the act is completed.
    sketch: Barandiaran and Almendros's best image is that an LLM is a library rendered conversational. Nobody asks whether a library asserts. We ask who asserted what is in the books, and a reader consulting a book is not asserted to in the same sense. Written and recorded speech already shows that illocutionary acts need not be located at the moment of production. Austin's insistence on uptake offers a model in which an LLM output is an act-potential completed by the user's prompt-and-reading, much as a lawyer's template becomes a contract only when invoked. Under this model, 'Did the LLM assert?', 'Did the proxy assert?' and 'Did the user assert to themselves?' are answers to different temporal questions. The key premise is that the participants all treat the speech act as a production-time event with an agent. Giving it up removes the pressure behind the proxy and quasi-assertion proposals, because the act has no single performer at all and is a joint, distributed completion.

[6] The 'interactional asymmetry' condition that Barandiaran and Almendros use to deny LLM agency measures initiative, not agency; the acts at issue (answering, advising, apologising, asserting-in-reply) are responsive, so the denial concerns a different class of speech acts than the one the debate is about.
    sketch: The enactivist asymmetry condition says the system must be the source of its own coupling to the environment, whereas an LLM is activated, turn by turn, by the user. But in human speech the same pattern holds for a large class of acts: an expert answering a question, a clerk confirming a booking, a person apologising when told they have offended. These acts are structurally triggered by the interlocutor and take their content from the prompt. The asymmetry condition would deprive the responder of agency in just these exchanges, which is absurd, so it must be tracking something else, namely the capacity to initiate. Initiating acts (promising unprompted, volunteering a warning, changing the topic) are where the denial is really strong. The paper's own examples of ordinary 'genuine conversation' sit on the responsive side. The key premise is that the structure of speech acts allows a principled initiating/responsive divide, and that the arguments about agency in this literature are driven by the initiating case while the cited cases are responsive. The dispute then turns out to be partly about two different explananda.

[7] Speech acts need no intender of their content at the moment of production: sortition and oracle cases show that an output can be a valid assertion, verdict or directive when no one intended that content and an institution simply adopts it. If so, the proxy account (a human intended it, by proxy) and the denial account (nobody intended it, so no act) both rest on a false shared premise.
    sketch: Barandiaran and Almendros call LLM tasks 'purpose-structured and purpose-bounded' without being purposeful, and call the LLM a 'library-that-talks'. Proxy theorists (Green and Michel, Arora) and deniers (Gubelmann, Skiba) agree that a speech act needs a content-level intention, either the machine's or a human's by proxy. Counterexample: verdicts by lot, drawing a name for office, a coin toss that settles who must testify, and a jury's quotient verdict. In each the content is generated by a process nobody intended, and the act is nonetheless performed, and attributable to someone, because a competent party adopts the output under a convention. Here the act is constituted by ratification or uptake, not by an antecedent intention; the proxy relation (a human intended it on someone's behalf) is not what makes it an act. The premise the argument turns on is that these cases are speech acts and not mere decisions. That is supported by their having felicity conditions and being open to challenge as invalid. If so, an LLM output ratified by a deployer or user can be an assertion or advice with no content-intender, and the 'midtended' hybrid is a ratification structure, not a blend of agencies.

[8] Organismic individuality is not a necessary condition on speakers: the individuation that speech acts require is of a commitment-and-sanction locus, as with a pseudonymous collective author or a rotating-staff institutional account. The relevant individual for LLM speech acts is therefore the persona-thread, not the model, so Barandiaran and Almendros's failed individuality test is aimed at the wrong entity.
    sketch: Barandiaran and Almendros argue that LLMs lack individuality, in the enactive sense of self-produced and self-maintained boundaries. Gubelmann and Butlin-Viebahn assume the candidate speaker is 'the model' or 'the chatbot'. Counterexample: Nicolas Bourbaki, a long-lived pseudonymous account run by a rotating team, or an anonymous editorial board. These have no organism, no self-maintaining boundary and no single body, yet they make assertions, retract them, are corrected and are held to them. The speaker is individuated by a stable pattern of commitments and by uptake of sanctions. A conversation thread with a persisting persona, in which each output conditions later outputs and so constrains what the persona can consistently say, is a candidate locus of this kind, even though the weights are not. The individuality condition then splits into organismic individuality, which LLMs lack, and discursive individuality, which is the one speech acts need. The argument turns on the premise that Bourbaki-type cases are speaker-individuation cases and not proxy cases for the members. That premise can be defended because the team members cannot be held to Bourbaki's claims.

[9] The assumption that a speech-act intention exists prior to or alongside output, which underlies both Gubelmann's malfunction-versus-deliberate test and Attah's Levelt-style planning template, is false even of human speakers. Much human illocution is incremental, with the force of the act settled by retrospective ownership, so the human-versus-LLM difference cannot be located in the presence of an intention.
    sketch: Both denials and attributions treat the speaker as having something like a conceptualised message and a communicative intention that the Formulator then realises (Attah) or whose failure can be told apart from malfunction (Gubelmann). Barandiaran and Almendros likewise contrast the LLM's purpose-structured but not purposeful operation with human purposefulness. Counterexample: ordinary improvised talk. Speakers begin sentences without having settled what they will assert, discover the force of the utterance from where it goes ('I was going to say it was a warning, but I suppose it was an accusation'), and become committed by endorsing or disowning it in the next turn. Splitting such acts from their reflective ownership makes the intention post hoc and constituted by follow-up conduct, not causal. Speech acts are therefore constituted by a diachronic pattern of owning and retracting. This reframes the dispute: the question is whether LLM threads show the right pattern of taking up, owning and being held to earlier outputs. This is an empirical question about interaction structure, not an issue about internal mental states. The premise it turns on is that retrospective force-fixing is not a marginal case.

[10] Barandiaran and Almendros's 'interactional asymmetry' condition, on which the system does not originate or set the terms of its own coupling, overgenerates. It excludes human communicators whose speech acts are uncontroversial, such as locked-in patients using a gaze speller, or people with advanced dementia whose conversational frame is wholly scaffolded by carers, so it cannot be a necessary condition on agency or on speech-act performance.
    sketch: Barandiaran and Almendros argue that LLMs fail interactional asymmetry because the human initiates, sustains and defines the interaction, and the model cannot modulate its own coupling. They treat this as a necessary condition for autonomous agency, and the speech-act literature takes autonomy as the target contrast. Counterexample: a locked-in patient whose only channel is an eye-tracked speller. The speller's language model predicts words, the carer starts the session, sets the topic and frames the options, and the patient's contribution is a series of binary selections. A person with advanced dementia in a carer-scaffolded exchange likewise neither starts the interaction nor controls its terms. Yet 'yes, I forgive you', 'I want to go home' and 'no' are paradigm assertions, promises, apologies and requests. If asymmetry of coupling does not defeat the speech act there, it cannot defeat it for LLMs. What does matter is whether the asymmetry is total, or whether the system has some residual veto and norm-bearing capacity, which is a graded and different condition. The argument turns on the premise that the enactive 'autonomy' condition is meant to ground speech-act performance and not only full autonomous agency. Barandiaran and Almendros can concede the counterexample only by splitting the two, which concedes the speech-act question.

[11] Barandiaran and Almendros's category of 'interlocutor without agency' is unstable: if interlocutorhood is the thick status of a participant in a normative discourse practice, it requires the normativity they deny LLMs, and if it is a thin role assigned by the human participant, their view becomes a form of fictionalism.
    sketch: They present the LLM as a 'linguistic automaton' or 'library-that-talks' that is nonetheless an interlocutor, one that can be experienced as a genuine conversational partner. The question is what interlocutor status consists in. On a Brandom- or Clark-style reading, an interlocutor undertakes commitments, can be held to them, and keeps score. That is a normative standing, so it conflicts with their claim that LLMs lack enactive normativity. On a thin reading, 'interlocutor' names a slot in the interaction that the human fills by treating the system as someone who answers. Then what makes the system an interlocutor is the human's stance and the shared pretence in the exchange, and that is Mallory's fictionalism under another description. The 'library' metaphor cannot hold the middle. A library has authors behind it, so if the system generates novel text the metaphor fails, and if it only conveys the authors' content the view is a proxy view. The key premise is that the interlocutor role cannot be filled by something that is neither a normative participant nor a fictional character.

[12] The enactivist denial of LLM speech acts, which rests on individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry, collapses into the sanction-based normative denial of Butlin and Viebahn, because only the social-normative reading of its conditions bears on speech acts at all.
    sketch: Enactive normativity is viability-relative: it concerns what is good or bad for a precarious, self-producing system. The norms of assertion, promising or apology are social and deontic: commitment, entitlement, answerability. These come apart, since people routinely assert, promise and apologise at cost to their own viability. So the enactivist has two options. One is to say the social norms are derived from viability norms, which is implausible given that these speech acts regularly override viability. The other is to concede that the individuality and normativity conditions do no work on speech acts, leaving 'interactional asymmetry' and the question of being a party to sanctionable exchange. That leaves the Butlin–Viebahn question of whether the system can be sanctioned and answer for its outputs. That question is contingent, and it can be answered differently for RLHF-tuned, memory-bearing deployed systems, where users reprimand, models revise, and training is updated in response. The enactive verdict then stops being a principled 'no' grounded in life and becomes an empirical verdict about current deployment. The key premise is that the biological and social senses of 'norm' are independent in speech-act contexts.

[13] If the enactivist grants, as Di Paolo and colleagues do, that human linguistic agency is largely constituted by socially imposed, self-sustaining norms of language, then the line between 'purpose-structured' and 'purposeful' cannot do the work Barandiaran and Almendros need, and the dispute reduces to a question about the metabolic substrate, which is irrelevant to illocutionary content.
    sketch: They say LLM tasks are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded but not purposeful, because the purposes are imposed from outside. Enactivism's own account of language ('linguistic bodies', participatory sense-making) says that most of a human speaker's communicative purposes, and the norms of what counts as asserting or apologising, are acquired through enculturation. They are inherited, imposed and sustained by a community before any individual endorses them. What is distinctively the human's own is not the content or even the origin of those purposes. It is that the human has a precarious metabolic substrate in which they matter. So purposefulness is a property of a substrate that adopts purposes, not of the purposes. The denial of speech acts then needs a further premise connecting substrate-precariousness to illocutionary performance, and nothing in the account of speech acts supplies it. Without that premise the position becomes either Gubelmann's material-autonomy view, with its odd consequence that a precarious but linguistically incompetent organism has a better claim to speak, or Attah's graded functional view, which it set out to reject. The key premise is that imposed origin of purposes cannot be what separates human from LLM purposiveness.

[14] Barandiaran and Almendros's 'midtended' hybrid agency is not a new third kind of agent. It is the author–ghostwriter relation that proxy accounts already model, so it either collapses into a proxy view or must treat the LLM as a co-speaker, which contradicts their denial of its agency.
    sketch: The novelty claim is that the human–LLM coupling yields forms of agency that earlier tool-extensions did not. For speech acts this must mean the following. Either some entity (the hybrid or the human) is the speaker, or the LLM's contribution is part of what makes the act that of its speaker. Take speechwriting, ghostwriting and spokespersons, which are well-studied cases of proxy and conditional speech acts (Green and Michel). The person who endorses the output is the speaker, and the drafter's contribution creatively shapes what is said without making the drafter a speaker. A human who adopts an LLM's draft stands in the same relation. What is new is only a change in degree: how much of the content is authored by the drafting part, and how little endorsement the human gives. If the hybrid is the speaker, its individuality and precariousness are exactly the human's, so the hybrid is the human plus an instrument, and the denial of LLM agency is preserved but nothing is new. If instead the LLM's non-endorsed contributions make speech acts that no human performs, then the LLM is in effect a co-author, and that needs an agency they explicitly deny. The key premise is that endorsement by a human is what makes the hybrid's speech acts someone's.

[15] The question 'can an LLM perform speech acts?' is under-specified because the candidate speaker can be individuated at four different grains (the weight file, the running inference instance, the deployed persona, the human–model network), and the main positions in the debate differ largely because each silently picks a different grain.
    sketch: Puzio treats 'the LLM' as a node whose boundaries are an open question, and she dissolves it into a network. The speech-act literature never asks this. Gubelmann's organismic argument targets the trained artifact, whose goals are externally fixed. Attah's graded intention is assigned to a pipeline instance with belief-state tracking. Butlin's agency criterion applies to the system plus memory and reflection scaffolding, i.e. a language agent. Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion fits a persona in a conversation. Proxy views make the 'machine' a mere conduit. Once the grains are separated, many apparent disagreements go away. The weight file is a policy-type that cannot assert, just as a grammar cannot. A persona can be a fictional character whose assertions are real only inside the fiction, which brings fictionalism and attribution close together. The instance is the only grain with a single context and a single stream of 'commitments'. The key premise is that each speech-act condition (intention, sanctionability, descriptive function) is satisfied or failed at different grains, so no single grain passes them all. The denials then win only by mixing grains, for example assessing intention at the instance and sanction at the weights.

[16] Proxy accounts conflate two relations, authorization (a principal licenses the speech) and norm-sourcing (someone's standards fix what counts as a correct output), and in LLMs these come apart: designers and deployers authorize outputs, while the dispositions that determine each output's content and tone are shaped by annotators and raters who never authorize anything.
    sketch: Green and Michel and Arora model machine speech on proxy or recorded speech, where the principal's objectives fix what is meant. For a thermostat-like or scripted device this works, because the designer's objectives settle the content. For a model whose outputs come from RLHF-shaped dispositions, the designer's objective is typically only 'be helpful and harmless', and the particular content is the aggregate residue of thousands of raters' judgments. Puzio's attention to the labour conditions of LLM production makes these workers visible as contributors to the network. The distinction shows that the proxy relation has two candidate principals. The authorizing principal is answerable but does not fix the content. The norm-sourcing crowd fixes content but has not licensed any utterance. If a proxy speech act needs a principal whose objectives are expressed in the utterance, then for much LLM output nobody satisfies both roles. Proxy accounts then split into a 'responsibility-assignment' view, which survives but is not a theory of what was said, and a 'ghostwriting' view, which is implausible. The key premise is Armstrong-style speaker meaning in terms of the principal's objectives, which requires that the objective bear on the specific content.

[17] The debate is about production-constitution (a speech act exists in virtue of facts about the speaker), whereas the relational picture suggests uptake-constitution (illocutionary force is fixed in the hearer's securing of uptake). These two give opposite classifications of fictionalism and of the 'text that humans interpret as speech acts' deflationary option.
    sketch: Every denial and attributing view asks whether the machine has the intentions, norms or agency to produce the act. The fallback 'it only produces text that humans interpret as such' treats interpretation as epistemically downstream of a fact about production. Puzio's relational view and the Austin-Hornsby-Langton tradition on uptake suggest another structure. Some illocutions, such as promising, advising, apologising and warning, are completed or constituted in an interaction in which a hearer takes them up and so incurs entitlements. On a strict uptake-constitutive reading, a human interpreting a chatbot's text as advice does not merely misdescribe a non-act. It may help bring about an act of advice whose speaker slot is filled by the network, with the 'interpretation' being part of the act. This makes the standard denial 'merely interpreted' ill-formed for uptake-dependent acts, while leaving it fine for acts like assertion that may be production-constituted. Fictionalism then becomes the view that users deliberately withhold uptake. The key premise is that the speech acts differ in whether their constitutive conditions are speaker-side or hearer-side, so that no uniform answer across assertion, promise and apology is available.

[18] Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition is ambiguous between being a target of sanction (being the kind of thing that can be held to account) and being a conduit of sanction (being a node through which sanction alters future outputs), and current models plausibly meet the second but not the first, so their argument establishes less than a denial.
    sketch: The norm-based denials say assertion requires openness to sanction, and models cannot be blamed, penalised or made to lose standing. But consider a user complaint, a downvote or a red-team report entering a training loop that shifts the dispositions generating later outputs. Sanction is then literally routed through the model's behaviour, as when a human speaker's reputational losses change what they later say. Puzio's network view makes this routing visible, since the sanctioning, the company, the raters and the retraining are part of one agentive network. The condition can be read in two ways. On the first, sanction must land on a bearer who suffers or is answerable. On the second, sanction must be functionally efficacious in regulating the producer's outputs. Read the first way, the condition is a moral-agency requirement that does the same work as Magnus et al.'s apology argument and is not specific to assertion. Read the second way, it is satisfied by models with online or periodic learning from feedback. Butlin's own agency criterion, sensitivity to instrumental value through learning, seems to give the second reading. So his two papers pull in opposite directions unless he adopts the stronger reading, which then has to be justified for assertion specifically. The key premise is that the practice-internal function of sanction in assertion is regulation of the speaker's reliability, not retribution.

[19] Proxy accounts of LLM speech acts are unstable: they presuppose a determinate principal whose objectives the machine's utterance carries, but for RLHF-trained models no such principal exists, so the view collapses into attributing the speech act to the trained system itself.
    sketch: Green and Michel and Arora model proxy speech acts on a spokesperson or recorded message, where an identifiable principal has the relevant objective (Armstrong-style) and the device transmits it. Puzio's actor-network point is that an LLM's dispositions are shaped by annotators, preference-aggregation procedures, scraped authors, policy teams and optimisation dynamics that no one fully specified. The key premise is that proxy-hood requires the output to be answerable to some agent's communicative objective, and that this objective must be fixed prior to and independently of the particular output. For a deployed model, the only objective that reliably and specifically covers a particular novel utterance is the one encoded in the model's learned policy. If the principal is the company, the company has no objective about this sentence (a conditional proxy about all outputs is too thin to ground a particular assertion or promise). If the principal is the distributed network, no one is the speaker. So either the proxy view is true only of scripted systems, or its explanatory work is done by the policy's own objective-tracking, which is the attributing view (Attah, Butlin) under another name.
