system:
You are an editor deciding which of these theses is worth commissioning as
a 6,000-word paper. You have NOT seen any of them attacked, and you are not
being asked whether they are true — only whether each is worth the argument.

Rate promise 1-5:

  5 — if it worked, it would change how people frame this debate
  4 — a real contribution; a good journal would send it out
  3 — competent and publishable somewhere, unlikely to be discussed
  2 — the argument has been made, or the payoff is too small
  1 — confused, or the thesis is not actually contested

You are seeing them TOGETHER so that you can discriminate between them.
Rank them against each other, not against an absolute standard. They must
NOT all receive the same score: whatever the batch, the weakest gets a
lower number than the strongest. Award at most one 5.

Return ONLY a JSON array, one object per thesis, in the order given:
[{"i": 0, "promise": 1-5, "promise_reason": "one sentence"}, ...]

messages.content:
Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

Theses:
[0] Attah's control conception fixes the intention at the grain of output selection (the token or utterance) but speech acts are individuated at the grain of the act performed with the output, and no argument shows that any LLM state controls at the act grain.
    sketch: Attah analyses intention as an internal state that solves Wu's Many-Many Problem by attention-like selection, and Levelt's Conceptualizer is meant to supply the act-level content. Attention in a transformer selects among inputs to compute the next-token distribution, so the thing controlled is the continuation. A communicative intention must control at the grain of 'warn this person', 'concede the point' or 'promise', where one string can realise different acts and one act can be realised by many strings. Call the first grain output-control and the second act-control. The control conception is satisfied by output-control, but the Levelt template requires a preverbal message with illocutionary force that is selected before formulation. Whether LLMs have such a state is an interpretability question: do mid-layer representations encode and causally govern a force-type independently of lexical surface? The claim is that Attah's argument equivocates between the two grains, and that Gubelmann, Butlin and Viebahn and Attah all treat the grain as settled when it is the crux. This yields a testable, non-metaphysical criterion that could favour either side, for example by intervening on force representations while holding content fixed.

[1] Debates over LLM speech acts treat communicative intention as the bottleneck, but intending to communicate and being the performer of an act are separable. A system could fully satisfy Attah's control conception, even to a high degree, and still perform no speech act, and Attah's own closing concession about 'mental and metalinguistic agency' concedes exactly this.
    sketch: Gubelmann, Attah and the Bender-style 'stochastic parrot' argument all assume that communicative intention is the gating condition for speech acts: the opponents say it is absent, and Attah says it is present in a graded way. But speech acts have a discrete normative upshot (commitment, entitlement, being answerable), whereas Attah's intention is graded by his own account (coffee machine < ELIZA < ChatGPT). A graded input cannot by itself yield a threshold output, so something else must fix whether the act was done. Candidates include standing as a possible target of sanction (Butlin and Viebahn) and being the one whose commitments are updated by the exchange. Separate three things: having a communicative intention (internal control state), performing the act (a status in a practice), and authoring it (being the bearer of the resulting commitment). Humans bundle these, which is why the debate fuses them. Given the separation, Attah can win on intention and the denial views can still be right about acts, and the proxy and proto-assertion views look like different answers to the authorship question rather than rivals about intention. The thesis the paper defends is that intention is neither the contested issue nor the decisive one.

[2] Attah's reply that the design context 'supplies' LLMs with purposes conflates a standing, policy-level purpose with an occurrent, episode-level intention. Distinguishing them shows that the attributing view is committed to the same two-level structure as the proxy view, and that the live question is whether the episode-level state is the model's.
    sketch: Purposes supplied by design (be helpful, predict text, maximise reward) are dispositions fixed across all conversations. A communicative intention is directed at this hearer, on this occasion, with this content, so it must be instantiated in the episode. The POMDP dialogue systems Attah appeals to have an explicit episode-level state (the belief state over user intent) that ties policy to occasion. A transformer has only activations in context, which may or may not play that role. Call the first 'inherited purpose' and the second 'instantiated intention'. Proxy theorists (Green and Michel, Arora) say the designer's inherited purpose, applied by a conditional or standing speech act, is the only intention in play. Attah says the system has its own instantiated one that is merely thin. On this carving the real disagreement is not whether the machine has intentions but whether any occurrent state in the machine mediates between policy and utterance in the way a belief state mediates in POMDP systems. If it does, Attah wins even against proxy views, and the mediation can be tested by checking whether episode-level latent states predict and counterfactually govern behaviour beyond what the policy already encodes. If it does not, the 'design context' reply gives the proxy account its premise.

[3] Attah's attributing view, on which design-context purposes make language models graded communicative intenders, is not a rival to the proxy account. Once the content of the intention is fixed by designers' purposes, it is the proxy account described in psychological vocabulary.
    sketch: Attah's control conception needs an internal state that controls output toward some end, and he concedes the end is supplied by the design context 'mediated by human designers'. Ask what individuates the intention's content and success conditions. It is not the model's own sensitivity to value, as in Butlin's agency criterion, because the end is fixed by designers' objectives. Green and Michel's proxy account already uses exactly this: Armstrong-style objectives, held by the human principal and executed by an artificial speaker. The two views then agree on the explanatory facts: the state, its content, its success conditions and its normative standing all trace to the designer. They differ only on whether to say the state is 'in' the machine or 'on behalf of' the human. Attah can keep the attributing view distinct only by adding a condition that the intention's content be non-derivatively the system's own. That condition is the Gubelmann/Butlin autonomy requirement he set out to avoid. So the position is unstable: either it collapses into proxy-ism, or it takes on the autonomy requirement and becomes a denial.

[4] Once the Gricean uptake-recognition component is dropped, the 'basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect' that Attah falls back on is just a perlocutionary intention. On his view, then, LLMs are optimisers of perlocutionary effects, which is a reason to deny them illocutionary acts.
    sketch: Attah rejects the strong Gricean reading because it demands higher-order mind-reading that children and animals lack. The retreat position names a disjunctive target: an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect. What marks an illocutionary intention off from a perlocutionary one in the Austin–Strawson tradition is that its fulfilment runs through the hearer recognising it (uptake). Remove recognition and only the perlocutionary disjunct remains: an internal state controlling output so as to bring about an effect in the hearer. RLHF and engagement tuning train models on exactly this, namely human approval and downstream user states. The control conception, with POMDP belief-state tracking of the user, describes a manipulator or steerer, not an asserter or promiser. The developmental evidence cited does not help, because it shows that children and animals have some communicative intention without showing that they have illocutionary intention. So Attah's retreat strips out the feature that made the question about speech acts, and his attributing view ends up supporting a no-illocution conclusion close to Skiba's and Butlin–Viebahn's.

[5] A graded notion of intention on which a coffee machine has 'almost none' cannot answer the speech-act question. If it has no threshold, it is trivially true of LLMs. If it has a threshold, the threshold is set by mental and metalinguistic agency, which Attah himself names as the real difference, so his view collapses into the agency-based denial.
    sketch: Attah's conclusion is that communicative intention does not mark the human/LLM boundary, and he locates that boundary in mental and metalinguistic agency. Speech acts are all-or-nothing in status: one either asserts or does not, one either apologises or does not. A graded property yields a speech-act verdict only if some degree is required. If any degree suffices, a thermostat that 'says' the room is cold performs speech acts, which is a reductio of the functional conception. If a degree is required, nothing in the control conception can supply it, because every system that solves a Many-Many selection problem counts. The cut must come from elsewhere, and Attah's own closing remark says where: capacities for self-ascription and metalinguistic regulation of one's speech. That makes the threshold-setter a Gubelmann- or Butlin-style agency condition. So the thin intention view is not an independent position. It is a premise-weakening that leaves the real dispute, over agency, untouched and in the denier's favour.

[6] Applied to LLMs, the control conception does not fix whose intention it is. The 'intending subject' is the network, the simulated persona, or the deployment, and each choice collapses Attah's view into something else: the network into incoherence, the persona into fictionalism, the deployment into proxy-ism.
    sketch: Attah identifies intentions with internal states that control the system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation calling for one, and takes Levelt's pipeline as the template. The same weights, conditioned on different prompts, generate sincere-sounding assertions of p in one context and of not-p in another, and generate villains, liars and role-players. Take the controlling states to belong to the network. Then it intends to assert p and not-p across contexts with no unifying point of view, so the intention-attribution fails to explain the output as one speaker's action. Take them to belong to the prompt-conditioned persona (Shanahan's simulacra). Then the intending subject is a character the system plays, and what the user engages with is a fiction, which is Mallory's view. Take them to belong to the prompt-plus-deployment system. Then the controller is the human-set context, and we are back at proxy-ism. Levelt's template presupposes a single speaker with one Conceptualizer, and a transformer has no principled place to put it. The attributing view looks stable only because it leaves the subject unspecified.

[7] Attah's control conception turns the question 'does the LLM have communicative intentions?' into the question 'where does the speaker system end?', so the attribution-versus-proxy dispute is a dispute about system individuation, not about intention.
    sketch: On Attah's account an intention is an internal state that controls a system's dynamics so as to produce an action suited to the situation. Whether a state is internal and controlling depends on where the boundary is drawn. In a deployed chatbot, much of what steers output lives outside the weights: the system prompt, the retrieved documents, the user's turns, the sampler settings, and the RLHF-shaped policy. The proxy theorists (Green and Michel, Arora) draw the boundary around a designer–deployer–model complex and then find the intention in the designers. Attah draws it around the model plus context and finds a thin intention there. Gubelmann draws it around the model alone and finds none. These parties agree on the functional criterion and disagree on the individuation of the controlled system. The premise the argument turns on is that the control conception is silent on individuation. Any individuation that yields a controller yields an intention, so the three positions are three answers to a different question, and the 'intention' vocabulary only disguises that. The dispute should then be settled by whichever individuation best supports the practice of holding speakers to their acts, not by the metaphysics of intention.

[8] The 'communicative intention' argument that Attah defends the models against is not really an argument about intention. It is an argument about the determinacy of the content of what is communicated, and the control conception is silent on that.
    sketch: Attah reads Bender and Koller, Shanahan and Montemayor as holding that competence requires communicative intention and that models lack the mechanism for entertaining one. He answers by supplying a mechanism, namely attention-like selection that solves the Many-Many Problem. But the force of the stochastic-parrot argument lies in what the intention would be an intention to communicate: a content tied to the world that the speaker means the hearer to grasp. The control conception is content-neutral. It explains why one output is selected from many, not why the selected state is about anything in particular, or why the selection is answerable to how things are. A thermostat-like controller meets the control conception while having no determinate communicative content. So Attah's victory is on a premise the opponents could concede: that models have some behaviour-controlling internal state. The live disagreement is over meta-semantics, whether the content of the state is fixed by training distribution, by the deployment context, or by the hearer's interpretation. That is where Skiba's externalist theories of reference come in. Intention is the wrong label for the dispute because it can be granted without moving the debate.

[9] The debate over LLM communicative intentions presupposes that an intention precedes and explains the utterance (Levelt's Conceptualizer before Formulator). For LLMs the only persistent state that carries speaker commitment is the public transcript, so the question is really whether intentions can be constituted by discourse record, which makes Attah and the normative deniers disagree less than they appear to.
    sketch: Attah maps transformers onto Levelt's pipeline and says the intention is a prior internal controller. But an autoregressive model has no separate pre-verbal message that persists across the generation. At each step the only thing carried forward is the text produced so far (plus the cache). What binds the system to its earlier output, such as a claim it must stay consistent with or an apology it has issued, is the transcript, which is shared and inspectable by the user. So whatever 'intention' the model has is largely retroactively and publicly fixed by what it has already said, much as Anscombe, Brandom and the interpretivists treat intention as answerable to the record of performance. The premise the argument turns on is that, for LLMs, intention-as-prior-inner-state and commitment-as-public-score come apart and only the second is robustly present. Then Attah's 'thin' attribution and Butlin and Viebahn's social-practice condition describe the same structure from two sides. The real contest is between inner-priority and record-constitution accounts of intention, and humans are only a contingent instance of the former.

[10] Attah's concession that the real human–LLM difference is the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency means that, on his own account, 'communicative intention' is a red herring. The dispute is about whether performing a speech act requires being able to take that act as one's own, that is, to classify it, own it, and retract it.
    sketch: Attah argues that communicative intention does not separate humans from models, because even animals and infants have thin versions and models plausibly have graded ones. He then locates the difference in metalinguistic and mental agency. But apologising, promising and asserting are not just illocutionary effects intended on a hearer. They are acts whose performer can be asked 'did you mean that as a promise?' and can withdraw or revise under the act-type description. If metalinguistic agency is what is missing, then it is also what Magnus et al. (moral and linguistic agency), Butlin and Viebahn (sanctionability), and Gubelmann (distinguishing malfunction from doing wrong) are each pointing at, under different names. All of them require a capacity for second-order answerability to one's act under its type-description. The premise the argument turns on is that graded first-order intention is available to a coffee machine in Attah's sense, so it cannot be what makes the speech-act question non-trivial. The dispute then stops being intention-presence versus intention-absence and becomes whether answerability can be conferred, as proxy and fictional accounts suggest, or must be intrinsic. That also explains why the attributionist and denier camps seem to talk past each other.

[11] Reflexive and habitual speech acts, such as the 'sorry' after bumping into someone, the 'thanks' at a door, or a 'yes' given on autopilot, are full speech acts with no prior or accompanying communicative intention, so the premise that speech acts require communicative intention, which Attah and his Bender-style opponents share, is false, and the dispute should move to standing and answerability.
    sketch: Both Attah and the stochastic-parrot theorists accept that communicative intention is necessary for speech acts and argue only about whether LLMs have it. Attah thins the intention to a control state, but he keeps it as the necessary condition. Take habitual 'sorry' on bumping into someone. It is produced with no deliberated goal about the hearer's mental states and with no Gricean reflection. It is quick, scripted, and often not endorsed. Yet it is an apology, it can be accepted or rejected, and the speaker is held to it. A defender will say there is a thin intention. But then the notion has been stretched until it is satisfied by any conditioned, situation-triggered output, and it no longer separates apologising from a reflex like a startle cry. The premise the argument turns on is that what makes these cases speech acts is the speaker's position in a practice, meaning she is answerable and the uptake is warranted. A momentary state of her mind is not what does it. If so, the intention question is a proxy for a question about answerability, and Butlin and Viebahn's sanction condition is closer to the mark. The sanction condition can then be tested directly, without intention doing the work.

[12] Attah's control conception together with Levelt's pipeline overgenerates: fluent (Wernicke-type) aphasic speech, echolalia and confabulation involve internal states that control output by attention-like selection among many candidate outputs in a situation that calls for speech, yet involve no communicative intention. So the functional criteria cannot be what distinguishes communicative intention.
    sketch: Attah's three desiderata and his control conception (solving the Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection) are meant to be sufficient for intention in the relevant sense. He then maps transformers onto Conceptualizer, Formulator and Articulator. In jargon aphasia the Formulator and Articulator operate with selection, fluency and turn-taking, while the Conceptualizer's preverbal message is absent or decoupled from any goal about the hearer. Patients produce grammatical, situation-appropriate-sounding speech and make no speech acts, and nobody thinks they intend to communicate what they say. Confabulation and echolalia give variants. So control-by-selection is satisfied without communicative intention. What is missing is a state whose content concerns the hearer's uptake and which is the target of the system's correction when uptake fails. The argument turns on the premise that the control conception is meant to be sufficient and not merely necessary, or at least that satisfying it must be non-trivially connected to the communicative case. Once the missing ingredient is stated, the mapping of LLMs onto the pipeline is no evidence for intention, because the contested component is the Conceptualizer, and nothing in next-token prediction shows it is present.

[13] A speaker who selects each sentence by rolling a die weighted by her own dispositions, and who never takes up or ratifies the sentence that comes out, does not assert even when every outcome is one she would endorse. This shows that a control state does not by itself control the act, and that what the LLM case shows is intention at the level of the distribution, which is not intention to perform any particular act.
    sketch: Attah's picture is of an internal state that controls the dynamics so as to bring about an action. In an LLM, the state computes a distribution over next tokens, and an external sampler (a random draw at temperature above zero) picks the token. The selection that fixes which act occurs is not made by the state. Imagine Dana, who has endorsed a set of sentences about a topic and lets a weighted die choose which one to utter, without any check that the one she gets is what she means to say now. Intuitively Dana asserts nothing, or at most asserts a disjunction-like policy. What is missing is ratification: the utterance token being taken up by the same system as the thing it is committed to. The argument turns on the premise that illocutionary acts individuate at the level of the particular token, since 'I promise to come' and 'I might promise to come' differ in kind. It follows that what the control conception can credit to an LLM is a policy-level state, a character or disposition. This is a different bearer from the output-level states that speech acts need. The point cuts against the attributing view and also against the proxy and fictionalist views, which assume the output is one determinate utterance. Autoregressive conditioning on one's own sampled token is the closest the model has to ratification, and it needs separate analysis.

[14] Degrees of communicative intention do not run, as Attah's coffee machine < ELIZA < ChatGPT ordering assumes, along the dimension of internal functional complexity, since a two-state Lewis signalling system or an alarm-calling animal whose signals are reshaped by hearers' responses has more communicative intention than a frozen-weight LLM that produces much richer output.
    sketch: Attah makes intention graded and orders systems by how much of the Levelt-style pipeline and control structure they realize, with the question of ChatGPT's level left open. His example ordering silently equates more intention with more complex internal structure. Counter-case: a minimal signalling system, such as a vervet-style alarm repertoire or a tiny learning agent in a signalling game, has states that cause signals, and those states are modified by whether the receiver's response served the sender's goal. A deployed LLM generates elaborate text, but within an interaction its weights are fixed, its output is not adjusted to the hearer's uptake except through context-window conditioning, and nothing in the system registers success or failure of the intended effect as such. Attah's own opening move, which retreats from strong Gricean demands to a basic intention to produce an effect in a hearer, makes the intended effect the content of the intention. A state is plausibly an intention to produce effect E only if E-success or E-failure is among the things the control loop answers to. The argument turns on this closed-loop requirement, which is a consequence of his own retreat. It reverses the ordering: the simple signaller outranks ChatGPT-with-frozen-weights, and the answer to the LLM question depends on feedback architecture (RLHF training, in-context correction, agent loops with reflection), and not on how fluent or complex the output is. This also cross-cuts the disputes over autonomy, because the loop requirement can be satisfied without self-maintenance.

[15] Barandiaran and Almendros's 'interactional asymmetry' condition conflates two things: who originates an interaction, and who is answerable within it. Because speech-act types differ in how much of the first they require, the asymmetry argument excludes LLMs only from initiative illocutions (unsolicited warnings, promises, offers) and not from responsive ones (answering, confirming, correcting, replying).
    sketch: In the enactive framework, interactional asymmetry means the system never sets the terms of its own coupling: the human starts, steers and ends the exchange. Speech-act theory already sorts illocutions by sequential position, such as first and second pair parts in conversation analysis, and by whether the act's felicity presupposes the speaker's own initiative. A promise or a spontaneous warning presupposes that the speaker took up the occasion. An answer, a confirmation or a concession has its force from a prior solicitation, and humans in institutional roles (a witness, a clerk) perform these under exactly the same asymmetry. The key premise is that responsiveness is constitutive of some act types, not a defect in the speaker's agency. If so, the denial camp's blanket 'no speech acts' verdict, which draws on the enactive asymmetry thesis, needs a taxonomy of acts. It would classify answering and assertion-in-reply differently from advising and promising. The inflationary-versus-deflationary framing would then give way to a sorting of illocutions by how much self-initiation they require.

[16] Barandiaran and Almendros's middle category, 'purpose-structured but not purposeful', runs together the illocutionary point of an act type and the purpose of a speaker. Speech-act performance requires only the former, so their own characterisation of LLMs is a description of the kind of system that can perform speech acts of its own.
    sketch: They say LLM tasks are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded, shaped by training toward ends the system does not itself hold, and they treat this as short of agency. Speech-act theory separates the point internal to an act type (assertion aims at truth, a request at compliance) from the occurrent aims of whoever performs it. Armstrong-style and constitutive-norm views let the first fix what the act is without the second being autonomous or self-generated. The key premise is that purposes imposed from outside can still be the system's operative organisation, in the same way that a role-bound human speaker's purposes are largely imposed. Gubelmann's mechanism/organism contrast and the enactive normativity condition both address purposes of the second kind. Attah's thin functional intention also stays on that side. The new claim is that the debate has been asking an agent-level question (does the system have goals of its own?) about something that needs only an act-level answer (is the output produced under an act-type's point?). Under that question 'library-that-talks' is unstable: a library carries its authors' acts, whereas a purpose-structured generator is a different case.

[17] Hybrid ('midtended') human–LLM speech should be analysed by distinguishing standing proxy, where the designer speaks through the system (Green and Michel, Arora), from adoptive utterance, where the user retrospectively makes an LLM output their own by ratifying and deploying it. The speaker of one and the same string differs by uptake.
    sketch: Proxy accounts assign authorship upstream to creators or deployers, who stand behind every output in advance. Barandiaran and Almendros show that in actual use the user steers, selects and often relays the text, so agency is coupled turn by turn. The unmade distinction is between two directions of authorship assignment: forward-looking (a standing delegation to the proxy) and backward-looking (adoption of a found utterance, as when someone repeats a stranger's sentence and thereby asserts it). On the adoption model, an unadopted answer displayed on screen is either no speech act or something like a proto-act. Pasting it into a report, or acting on it and relaying it, makes it the user's assertion, with the user's commitments and sanctionability. The key premise is that Austinian uptake and commitment can be conferred after production and need not come from the producer. This predicts that the same LLM string can be a user's assertion, a designer's proxy assertion or nobody's, depending on downstream treatment. It also relocates responsibility for misinformation to the user's adoption practices instead of the designer's proxy standing.

[18] The individuality condition used to deny LLMs agency and speakerhood is posed at the wrong grain. Speaker-individuality (a locus of accumulating, retrievable commitments within a dialogue thread) is distinct from the metabolic, self-producing individuality of enactivism, and LLM threads can have the first without the second.
    sketch: Barandiaran and Almendros argue that LLMs lack individuality in the autopoietic sense: no self-produced, precariously maintained boundary. They also treat 'the LLM' as one entity, though candidate speakers include the weights, a single inference run, a conversation thread, and a role-played persona. Speech acts need a bearer who can be held to what was said earlier (consistency, retraction, apology, promise-keeping). That diachronic bearer is constituted by commitments in the context window, which the thread maintains through conditioning on its own prior outputs. A thread has a boundary (the context), it is individuated by what it has committed to, and it is reidentified across turns by users who hold it to account. The key premise is that the relevant individuality for speech acts is commitment-individuality, which is normative and social, not metabolic. Enactive individuality is then the wrong test for illocutionary authorship, and the question 'can the LLM assert?' is ill-posed until the candidate bearer is fixed. This splits the field: weights fail, threads may succeed, and no existing position distinguishes them.

[19] Attah's control conception of intention, combined with his appeal to design-supplied purposes, commits him to the proxy view: because a system prompt or in-context instruction is text that controls the model's output dynamics and encodes someone else's communicative aim, the state that fills the role of the model's intention is literally the deployer's intention in textual form.
    sketch: On Attah's account an intention is an internal state that selects among many possible outputs in a situation that calls for one. In a deployed LLM, the states doing that selecting are largely the system prompt and the user instruction, held in context and acting through attention. They are authored by humans, they specify the effect to be produced on a hearer ("apologise sincerely", "advise cautiously"), and the model's dynamics then execute them. So the control conception does not find an originary intention inside the model. It finds an installed, delegated one, whose content and target were fixed by an external author and transmitted by text. A human who is told what to say and says it is the standard case of a proxy or delegated speech act. The premise it turns on is that control by an externally authored, content-bearing state is not originary control. Attah must then either say that the model's intention is the operator's, which is Green and Michel's view relabelled, or deny that prompt-borne states are intentions. The second option leaves little for the model's own purposes to be, because they were supposed to come from design context. The attributing and relocating families therefore collapse into each other.
