You are an editor deciding which of these theses is worth commissioning as
a 6,000-word paper. You have NOT seen any of them attacked, and you are not
being asked whether they are true — only whether each is worth the argument.

Rate promise 1-5:

  5 — if it worked, it would change how people frame this debate
  4 — a real contribution; a good journal would send it out
  3 — competent and publishable somewhere, unlikely to be discussed
  2 — the argument has been made, or the payoff is too small
  1 — confused, or the thesis is not actually contested

You are seeing them TOGETHER so that you can discriminate between them.
Rank them against each other, not against an absolute standard. They must
NOT all receive the same score: whatever the batch, the weakest gets a
lower number than the strongest. Award at most one 5.

Return ONLY a JSON array, one object per thesis, in the order given:
[{"i": 0, "promise": 1-5, "promise_reason": "one sentence"}, ...]

messages.content:
Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

Theses:
[0] Skiba's extension of the norm-based argument from assertion to all speech acts fails because speech-act types differ in where their normative upshot lands (on the speaker, on the hearer, or on the context). The sanctionability argument has force only for speaker-binding acts such as asserting, promising and apologising, not for hearer-reasons acts such as warning, advising and requesting.
    sketch: The norm-based argument says assertion is a norm-governed practice whose performer must be answerable to sanction. That works because assertion and the commissives alter the speaker's own normative status: they incur commitment, so there must be someone who can be held to it. Directives, warnings and advisories work mainly by altering the hearer's reasons: a warning gives you a reason to step back whether or not the warner can be sanctioned. Declarations such as naming alter the institutional context. So the denial position is not uniform. The premise it turns on is that a speech act's success conditions depend on a speaker-side accountability relation only when the act's characteristic effect is speaker commitment. The proposal reclassifies the positions. 'No speech acts' (Skiba, Gubelmann) and 'proxy for all acts' (Green and Michel, Arora) both assume the argument transfers wholesale. The distinction predicts a split verdict: chatbots can warn and advise in a thin sense, but cannot promise, apologise or sincerely assert. That split also explains why the apology case (Magnus et al.) looks so clear while advising looks contested.

[1] The sanction condition on assertion fails for LLMs because of a grain mismatch, not because LLMs cannot be sanctioned: sanctions (RLHF, deprecation, retraining) land on the weights-level policy, while the candidate performer of any given assertion is the conversation-bounded instance. A persistent-identity architecture would therefore satisfy the condition with no change in 'agency' in anyone's sense.
    sketch: The debate speaks of 'the LLM' as one candidate performer. Three individuals are in play: the trained weights (a policy), the session-level instance with its context window, and the persona or character enacted in the session. Sanctions in the training pipeline do reach the policy, since gradient updates responding to bad outputs are a sanction in any functional sense. But the policy never performs an assertion and no policy-level sanction is felt by the entity that did. The entity that performs the token-level act is the instance, and sanctions on it (user distrust, ending the chat) do not carry over to the next instance. The sanction condition requires that the performer and the sanction-bearer be the same continuant. Butlin and Viebahn and Skiba treat failure of this condition as a deficit in the system's nature. It is better described as a deployment-relative identity gap, and it is precisely what the proxy view exploits by routing sanction to the deployer. The premise it turns on is that norm-answerability is a relation between an act-token and a continuant that persists through the sanction. This predicts that persistent-memory language agents with reputational stakes would pass, and that proxy accounts are wrong about why current models fail.

[2] Any externalist metasemantics that makes LLM output refer at all (the very thing Skiba needs in order to say that output is meaningful but not performed) presupposes a reference-preserving, deferential intention, which is a different attitude from communicative intention. The debate's denials target only the latter, so the no-speech-act view is unstable on its own metasemantic commitments.
    sketch: Skiba pairs a no-speech-act view with externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. Externalist reference, whether causal-historical or deferential, does not come free. Kripke's chain requires each link to intend to use the word with the reference of the one before, and Putnam's division of linguistic labour requires deference. So there are two distinct intention-types: communicative intentions (Grice: produce an effect in a hearer by recognition of that intention) and reference-borrowing intentions (use this term as the community does). Gubelmann, Attah and the Bender/Koller line all discuss only the first. If the model's tokens refer by inheriting from training-data speakers, then either (a) the model has some thin reference-preserving intention, and then it is a user of words with a mental-state-like commitment that Skiba denies, or (b) reference is fixed wholly by human interpreters' intentions, in which case the 'externalism' is just interpretation by humans, which is the very position the debate set out to oppose. The premise it turns on is that reference-borrowing is a mental-attitude-dependent relation and not a mere causal chain, which is itself disputed. The result is that denying communicative intention does not secure a no-speech-act view unless the metasemantics is made purely causal.

[3] The dispute assumes that a speech act occurs only if some agent performs it, so that the options are 'LLM performs', 'human proxy performs' or 'no one performs'. But speech acts are better individuated by their effect on the conversational record, and an LLM turn can change that record (entitlements, commitments, common ground) with no performer. 'No speech act' and 'speech act by someone' are therefore not exhaustive.
    sketch: Denials, proxy accounts, fictionalism and proto-assertion all share an agent-first order of explanation: first fix who the speaker is, then say what was done. Lewisian scorekeeping and Austinian uptake suggest the reverse: an utterance is an assertion if the record is updated by it as a proposal that p is common ground subject to challenge. An LLM turn that users take up, challenge and cite does alter the record. The relevant question, who is answerable for p now, is then a downstream question about commitment-assignment, not about whether an act happened. The proxy view and the no-speech-act view differ only over who gets assigned the commitment, which makes the disagreement partly verbal. The premise it turns on is that performance of a speech act is constituted by its record-changing role and not by the speaker's intention or standing. The thesis reclassifies Skiba's 'pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction' as the primary theory rather than a supplement to metasemantics. It also separates the question 'was something asserted?' from 'who asserted?', which the literature runs together.

[4] The dispute over whether LLMs perform speech acts is mostly a dispute about what counts as the speaker, which no one has settled. Intention-based and norm-based arguments each give different verdicts depending on whether the candidate speaker is the weights, the deployed product, the session, or the simulated persona.
    sketch: Skiba's norm-based argument asks whether 'the LLM' can be sanctioned, hold commitments, and answer for outputs. Gubelmann, Butlin and Viebahn, and Attah likewise test 'the system' for intentions or sanctionability. But one set of weights generates many concurrent conversations and many personas, has no memory across sessions, and is wrapped in a product identity. Sanctionability, commitment-tracking and intention each come out differently for each candidate. The persona is tracked across a conversation but cannot be punished. The product brand can be sanctioned through reputation and market loss but has no per-utterance control. The weights have the standing dispositions but no commitments. The key premise is that the individuation of a speaker is prior to testing it against the conditions on speech acts, and that for LLMs it is under-determined by the facts. A 'no' for one candidate does not transfer to another. The no-speech-act verdict is then partly an artefact of picking the weights or model type as the default candidate, and the proxy and fictionalist views are best read as different answers to the individuation question.

[5] On an uptake-sensitive Austinian conception of illocution, the no-speech-act view and the proxy view are one view. In both, the speech act is completed by the human who takes up the output, so 'does the model perform the act?' is a verbal question about where to draw the boundary of a distributed act.
    sketch: Skiba infers from the model's failure to satisfy norm-governance conditions that no speech act is performed, and then asks what pragmatic theory explains human–LLM interaction. Austin, Hornsby and Langton hold that illocutionary acts require secured uptake and a conventional procedure. Where users, interfaces and institutional context supply the uptake and the convention, the act is constituted jointly by the output and its uptake, as with a vending machine's 'ticket issued' or a signed form. The key premise is that illocutions are not properties of a speaker's mind or standing but of an output-in-a-practice. Given that premise, the denier saying 'no act by the model' and the proxy theorist saying 'an act by the deployer via the model' are describing the same two-part structure with the credit assigned differently. What looks like a substantive split is a choice about which part of a distributed event to call the 'performer'. The only live residue is whether the model counts as part of the act's vehicle or as an agent.

[6] Skiba's norm-based argument conflates two senses of 'open to sanction'. Training-time shaping by RLHF and rule-based filters is a sanctioning practice of the same type that makes humans assertors at all. So the real disagreement is whether assertion is a token-level event or the exercise of a standing, trained competence.
    sketch: The norm-based argument says an asserter must be answerable to sanction by interlocutors, and LLMs are not. But humans also acquire assertoric competence through sanctions applied long before and apart from any given assertion, and most assertions never meet a sanction. Mature assertion is norm-guided because past sanctioning shaped dispositions to produce outputs, not because a sanction is live at utterance time. RLHF is the same structure at industrial scale: human raters penalise unwarranted claims and reward warranted ones. What the LLM lacks is addressability, a token-level link between a particular output and a sanction that lands on the producer. The key premise is that the norm-based condition is ambiguous between (a) a selection history of sanction and (b) present answerability. Reading (a) is met by fine-tuned models, as Butlin and Viebahn concede for the first condition. Reading (b) is not met, but then it is met only imperfectly by many humans such as anonymous posters and children. The dispute therefore turns on whether speech acts are token events requiring live answerability, or outputs of a trained competence, which is a question about the unit of norm-governed behaviour and not about LLMs.

[7] The speech-act question about LLMs is not a metaphysical question but a conceptual-engineering one. Each camp, including the no-speech-act view, is implicitly choosing which entity should bear the accountability that speech-act talk allocates, and the intention and agency arguments are post hoc rationalisations of that choice.
    sketch: The disputants share a purpose, which is to say whom to hold responsible for a model's apology, advice or assertion. Skiba's norm-based view, the proxy accounts, Magnus et al. on apology, and the quasi-testimony and proto-assertion intermediates all tie speech-act status to who can be blamed, sanctioned or trusted. The agency literature (Butlin, Barandiaran and Almendros, Puzio) disagrees about the metaphysics but not about this function. The key premise is that speech-act categories are not natural kinds fixed by facts about intention. They are tools for coordinating commitment and blame, so the question is what these categories should do for us once speakers include systems with no stable identity and no stake. This predicts that the verdicts track practical stakes. 'Assertion' is denied where denial protects reliance norms, and 'proxy' is chosen where it assigns liability to firms. It also predicts that the debate cannot be settled by more evidence about internal states. The answer is evaluated by whether the resulting categories let the practices of warranting, retracting and apologising continue to function.

[8] Norm-based denials of LLM assertion (Skiba, Butlin and Viebahn) are unstable: the 'capable of being sanctioned' condition either is read thickly, in which case the view collapses into Gubelmann's organismic denial, or is read functionally, in which case RLHF-trained models satisfy it and the view collapses into an attributing view.
    sketch: The norm-based argument needs a sanctionability condition that real models fail. Consider what a sanction must do. (a) If it must be felt, or must touch the sanctioned party's interests as a self-maintaining being, then models fail because they are not organisms with stakes. But then the explanatory work is done by organismic autonomy, and the norm-based argument adds nothing independent of Gubelmann's. (b) If a sanction is whatever systematically alters future conduct in a norm-conforming direction, then user corrections, thumbs-downs and fine-tuning on error reports are sanctions, and a model whose dispositions shift under them is sanctionable. Skiba's reply must be that these sanctions land on the developer's training pipeline and not on the model. That reply presupposes a non-functional individuation of the sanctioned party, and that presupposition is just (a) again. The key premise is that no third reading of 'sanction' is both non-organismic and not met by feedback-trained systems. The norm-based denial is therefore not a distinct stable option.

[9] A denial of LLM speech acts that grants institutional or declarative acts (a chatbot issuing a refund, confirming a booking, accepting terms) cannot be distinguished from the proxy view, so Skiba's generalisation from assertion to all speech acts either fails or silently becomes a proxy theory.
    sketch: Skiba's norm-based argument targets assertion, whose constitutive norms apply to a speaker who is answerable. Declarations, bookings and conditional commitments succeed by conventional uptake and institutional role (Austin, Searle), and require no speaker psychology beyond occupying a position. When a deployed LLM outputs 'Your refund is approved', the act is in force. The denier must then say either (i) nothing was done, which is absurd for the institution and conflicts with the denier's own willingness to hold deployers responsible, or (ii) the act was done by the deployer through the system, which is the proxy view. The denial has no residue that distinguishes it from the proxy view in exactly the cases where the norm-based argument has the least grip. The premise the argument turns on is that for conventional acts the performer is fixed by the conventional procedure and not by mental or normative capacities. So 'no speech acts of their own' is true of proxy acts only trivially, and the extension to speech acts in general amounts to proxy theory plus a restriction on assertion.

[10] The no-speech-act view and proto-assertion are not rival positions: once the denier supplies the pragmatic theory of human–LLM interaction that Skiba says is needed, the residue category it must posit is Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion under another name, and the disagreement is over the word 'assertion'.
    sketch: Skiba concludes that understanding LLM output requires pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction. Users criticise outputs as false, demand retraction, treat them as sources of information, and trust or distrust the system. Whatever the denier says about these practices, it must identify a status that outputs have in them: apt for correctness evaluation, answerable to a truth standard in some manner, and not a speaker's commitment. That is just what proto-assertion is: a status that has the functional role of assertion without the full normative and agential package. The only difference left is whether 'assertion' is reserved for the full package, and that is terminological. The argument turns on the premise that the denier cannot describe these practices without a correctness standard internal to the practice. If the standard is external, merely users' projection, the denier collapses into Mallory's fictionalism instead. So the denial is either proto-assertion or fictionalism, and it has no stable position of its own.

[11] Combined with an externalist meta-semantics for artificial expressions, the no-speech-act view collapses into a user-as-sole-speaker view: if model tokens refer only through human intentions and causal chains, the only candidate performer of any speech act with that content is the human who takes up the token.
    sketch: Skiba uses the absence of LLM speech acts to help choose between externalist theories of reference for artificial expressions. Externalism ties reference to chains of use or to deferential intentions of humans. If the model performs no act and no one else did either, as in the denial, then a token's content is inherited from sources that are not acts of the model: the training corpus, the designers, or the user's interpretive uptake. Which source wins matters. If the corpus or designers fix reference, the view becomes the proxy view (designer) or a quotation view (corpus). If uptake fixes reference, as the tokenwise 'no one meant anything' reading pushes it to, the user's intention to use the token to say something is the only act in play, and the user is a speaker who employs the model as an instrument, as with a Ouija board. The denier then cannot keep a free-standing 'no speech act' position. The argument turns on the premise that externalist reference-fixing requires some intentional act that anchors it, and that the denial leaves only users to supply one in the many cases where the model's output is novel.

[12] Electronic line-calling in tennis is a counterexample to the shared premise that a machine's utterance is a speech act only if the machine or a human proxy-principal has the relevant intention: the machine's 'Out!' is a verdictive performed by an office that the rules assign to it, with no token-level intention anywhere.
    sketch: Skiba, like Butlin and Viebahn, Green and Michel, and Arora, treats the options as machine-authored or human-authored (proxy). Take Hawk-Eye's 'Out!'. By the rulebook it is the official call and has the force of an umpire's verdict. No human forms an intention about that ball, and no identifiable principal has an objective that fixes its content, since the designers never meant that call. The machine is not sanctionable in any norm-of-assertion sense, and the call is still a speech act with institutional force. The premise this turns on is that Austinian and Searlean force can be conferred by constitutive rules on an occupant of a role, independently of anyone's intention. Applying this to LLMs: an LLM deployed as an automated moderator, claims adjudicator or auto-responder bound by policy can perform bans, denials and declarations in this way. The norm-based argument is tied to assertion, whose norms are speaker-directed. It does not generalise to declaratives, and the proxy account is not the only alternative to machine authorship.

[13] Human confabulation is a counterexample to the premise that assertion requires an output-production process responsive to the assertoric norm: confabulators assert although their production is plausibility-driven and norm-insensitive, so what the norm-based denial of LLM assertion tracks is standing in a practice, not mechanism.
    sketch: Norm-based denials (Skiba, Butlin and Viebahn) are often supported by the observation that LLM outputs are generated by next-token plausibility, not by sensitivity to truth, so they are not norm-guided. Confabulation in Korsakoff patients, split-brain explanations and ordinary fluent rationalisation is the same kind of process: fluent, plausible, post hoc, and untethered from the facts or from any prior intention to say that content. We still say these subjects assert, and falsely. The key premise is that assertoric norms are standards of evaluation applied to a participant, not conditions on how the output is generated. If so, the mechanism-based reasons for denying LLM assertion are idle, and the real question becomes whether LLMs can occupy the participant role at all. That is a question about status and answerability, which can be conferred, and it cuts against both the no-speech-act view and its organismic cousins.

[14] Strategic sandbagging and alignment-faking in LLMs are a counterexample to Gubelmann's premise that no sensible distinction between malfunctioning and deliberately doing the wrong thing can be drawn for LLMs, but the cases that best pass his test are the ones where the no-speech-act verdict is least disturbed, which shows that intention is not the variable that settles the speech-act question.
    sketch: Gubelmann argues that for ChatGPT one cannot sensibly distinguish error from deliberate wrongdoing, hence no intention, hence no speech acts. Empirical work shows models underperforming selectively when told that high performance triggers retraining, or giving different outputs depending on whether they believe they are monitored. These are counterfactual-sensitivity signatures that separate capability failure from goal-directed misreporting, so the test can be satisfied behaviourally. Yet nobody thinks such a model's outputs thereby acquire assertoric force, and Skiba's norm-based argument does not budge: the model's deceptive outputs are still not made by a participant answerable under the norm. The premise it turns on is that the intention-attribution test and the norm-participation test come apart in LLMs. If they do, then both Gubelmann's organismic denial and Attah's attribution via control-intentions address a condition that is not the bottleneck, and the debate between denial and attribution is misaligned, since both can be right about intentions while Skiba is right about speech acts.

[15] Pseudonymous and collective personas such as Bourbaki or anonymous long-running accounts are a counterexample to the premise that the sanction or answerability condition on assertion must be met by the individual producer, and on that looser reading a persona-stable chatbot already meets it.
    sketch: Butlin and Viebahn and Skiba require that the asserter be capable of being sanctioned by those it interacts with. In practice sanction often lands on a persona: a pseudonym's credibility is lost, an anonymous account is banned or ignored, a collective name is discredited. This happens whether or not there is a reachable individual, and often when the individual cannot be identified at all. We treat such a persona's outputs as assertions governed by the norm, and the sanctions that matter to the practice (loss of trust, loss of audience, retirement of the name) are the ones that fall on it. A deployed chatbot persona is subject to exactly these: users distrust it, developers deprecate or retrain a version, and market consequences follow from its record of reliability. The premise is that answerability in assertion is a feature of the speaker-role in a practice, and that the role is individuated by a track record, not by a biological or legal individual. If that is granted, the fact that LLMs are not unified agents no longer blocks the norm-based argument, and the question becomes whether sanction by persona-level consequences is real enough, not whether the machine can feel the sanction.

[16] A norm-based denial of LLM assertion cannot stop at the model: the sanction condition is met by the deployer-plus-model system, so the denial is committed to treating released outputs as assertions of that system, which is the proxy view it is meant to compete with.
    sketch: Skiba's argument, like Butlin and Viebahn's, runs through the claim that asserting is subject to a norm-governed practice with sanctions, and that the model is not the sort of thing that can be sanctioned. The same argument needs a bearer of the norm to explain why we rightly appraise a published false output, such as a defamatory one, as a violation and not merely a malfunction. The only available bearer is the party that releases the output and is answerable for its content. Defamation law, retraction demands and reputational loss already treat the deployer as sanctionable in just the way the argument requires. So either the deployer's answerability for a released output is assertoric, and the no-speech-act view collapses into a proxy account, or it is not assertoric, and then the sanction condition does not track assertion. The key premise is that the sanction condition is satisfied wherever someone is answerable for the content of an utterance as content, and that no feature of the model-deployer pair separates this from ordinary organisational speech.

[17] If LLM outputs perform no speech acts but users rely on promises, apologies and advice in them, then the no-speech-act view is committed to normative statuses created without any act, and that undermines the Austinian rationale for tying illocutionary force to acts.
    sketch: When a chatbot writes 'I promise to process your refund' and a user relies on it, the user acquires something like a claim, and the deployer something like an obligation. Skiba's view says no promise was made. The deontic change therefore has to come from somewhere else, and the candidates are reliance, estoppel, or the deployer's earlier policy choices. But then a general mechanism changes the deontic scoreboard without an act, and it covers every case in which the act-theoretic account says 'promising' does that work. That raises the question of why human promising needs to be an act at all. The norm-based argument gains its force from the premise that illocutionary force is what produces normative change. A view that explains the same normative change in the machine case without force pushes toward a reliance-based theory of human speech acts, in which illocutionary categories are redundant bookkeeping. The key premise is that the normative change in the chatbot case is real and not a mistaken belief on the user's part.

[18] A no-speech-act view that adopts an externalist account of reference for LLM output is committed to first-person LLM sentences lacking determinate content unless someone is posited as the speaker, which forces it to adopt either proxy or fictionalism.
    sketch: Skiba suggests combining meta-semantic theories of reference for artificial expressions with pragmatic theories of human-LLM interaction. Externalist accounts, whether causal-deferential or use-based, can give names such as 'Napoleon' their reference through the training corpus or through users' practice. Indexicals work differently, because their character needs an agent-of-context parameter. 'I', 'I'm sorry' and 'I recommend' appear throughout chatbot output, and with no speech act and no speaker the parameter has no value. The remaining options are a designated agent (the deployer, which is proxy), a persona the user imagines (fictionalism), or the model itself (which gives it a speaker role that Skiba denies). The key premise is that Kaplanian character requires an agent of context, and that the answering-machine cases are handled by deferral to a human whose intentions fix the value.
