system:
You are trying to kill a candidate thesis. Not a reviewer offering
suggestions — you are trying to establish it is not worth a paper.

You have been ASSIGNED one line of attack:

    MISATTRIBUTION — the thesis ascribes to its named target a view that target does not actually hold, so the argument is aimed at nobody

Use that line and no other; do not substitute a different objection.

You must ATTEMPT the attack before you may decline it. Answer in this form:

  ATTEMPT. The best version of this attack, naming ONE premise as the weak
  point, in under 200 words. Make it even if you doubt it works.

  STRENGTH: n/5 — how much damage your own attempt actually does.
    5 the thesis cannot survive this   4 serious, needs a real answer
    3 a genuine problem, answerable    2 weak    1 no force at all

Only if your own attempt scores 1 may you add the line "NOT APPLICABLE".

Declining is expensive: an unattacked thesis is recorded as UNTESTED, not
as surviving, so opting out tells us nothing about it. Note also that
several of these lines of attack apply to structural, conceptual and
metaphysical claims, not only to empirical ones — "this is a conceptual
claim, so cases cannot touch it" is usually a reason to reach for
UNFALSIFIABLE, not a reason to decline.

Check the "target" field against what those philosophers actually hold. The
question is not whether the thesis is true but whether anyone holds the
position it attacks. Watch particularly for a view stated more strongly than
its holder states it — a claim someone makes about ONE class of cases
reported as a claim about all of them, a qualified thesis reported flat. That is the usual shape of this error.

You are working from memory, with no access to any text. That cuts both
ways, and the second way matters more: a confidently invented correction is
worse than no objection at all, because it will be believed. So:

  - Rate 4-5 only when you are genuinely confident the target does not hold
    the ascribed view, and say which work or position you are relying on so
    the claim can be checked.
  - If you are unsure who holds what, SAY SO and rate 1-2. That is a correct
    outcome for this check, not a failure of nerve.
  - Never invent a position, a title, or a date to make the objection land.

If the thesis names no specific target, or names a position rather than a
person, say NOT APPLICABLE.

messages.content:
Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

{
  "thesis": "The dispute over whether machines assert is a dispute about whether illocutionary acts are constituted on the hearer's side (uptake and functional role) or the speaker's side (accountable commitment), and LLMs matter only as the first case where these systematically come apart.",
  "move_type": "reframing",
  "sketch": "Arora rejects 'functionalist' ascription because machine utterances resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions, and she replaces it with attribution to an accountable principal. Both sides treat this as a disagreement about machines. But the functionalist standard individuates illocutions by what the audience can do with the utterance, which is Austin's uptake. The proxy standard individuates them by who is on the hook, which is the commitment side. For humans the two are co-instantiated, so speech-act theory never had to say which one is constitutive. LLM output separates them: full uptake-conditions are met while no one has formed the commitment. The intermediate views (quasi-testimony, proto-assertion) are then best read as hedges between two constitutive theories, not as positions about machines. The key premise is that the human literature contains no argument for the priority of either side, only coincidence. The machine debate therefore cannot be settled by facts about machines, and positions on it should be predictable from prior commitments about the metaphysics of illocution.",
  "target": "Arora's rejection of functionalism, and the whole functionalist\u2013proxy axis as a debate about AI."
}

Attack on the assigned line: MISATTRIBUTION.

response_text:
**ATTEMPT.** The weak premise is that the functionalist side of the dispute individuates illocutions by hearer uptake, in Austin's sense, and that Arora and her opponents leave unexamined which side of the speech act is constitutive.

Arora's target is a functionalism on which machine utterances count as assertions because they "resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions". That is a thesis about when an utterance counts as an assertion, grounded in resemblance and role. It is not obviously Austinian uptake, which concerns the securing of the audience's understanding or response, not general functional similarity. The thesis may therefore be aimed at a position that no one holds in the form given.

The framing of the debate is also doubtful. Green and Michel build their proxy view explicitly from Austin, Strawson's synthesis with Grice, and Armstrong. They are already working with the question of which constituents of a speech act are essential. Butlin and Viebahn make assertion require both descriptive function and susceptibility to sanction, which is a hybrid of the two sides and not an instance of one. So the machine literature does not simply "treat this as a disagreement about machines".

I am working from memory of abstracts only. I have not verified what Arora actually says about uptake, so I cannot confirm that she lacks the ascribed view.

**STRENGTH: 2/5.** The thesis is a reframing and describes Arora's functionalist target in broad terms that fit her abstract. The mismatch between "communicative function" and "uptake" is real but loose, and the thesis can reply that it is rationally reconstructing the position, not quoting anyone. The objection to the "whole axis" claim is stronger, because Green and Michel and Butlin and Viebahn already engage the constitutive question. That is closer to a novelty problem than to misattribution.

Answer in two parts, in this order, and NEVER skip the first:

  BEST DEFENCE. State the strongest available reply to the objection —
  the one a capable proponent would give. Push the case: look for a
  version of the objector's own scenario that defeats their distinction,

Distinguish two things sharply:

  RESISTING is giving a reason the objection does not apply. Always try

  HEDGING is narrowing, qualifying or reinterpreting the thesis so the
  objection no longer touches it. Never do this. A thesis that survives
  only by accumulating qualifications is dead — report it as dead rather

Conceding after a real defence is an honourable outcome. Conceding without
one is not an outcome at all.

Candidate:
{
  "thesis": "There are two kinds of proxy assertion, relayed and generative. In relayed proxy assertion the principal has a determinate content they could believe or know. In generative proxy assertion they do not. LLM output is almost entirely generative, and for generative proxies the assertoric norms cannot be applied to the principal.",
  "move_type": "distinction",
  "sketch": "Recorded messages, press statements read aloud, and Green and Michel's conditional speech acts ('whatever the system says under C, I say') all pass through a content the principal fixed or could have inspected. The proxy relation transmits a commitment to a proposition already in view. An LLM deployer commits in advance to no proposition; they authorise a policy for producing propositions they will never see. Assertion is individuated by its norms (belief, knowledge, sanction) and by its content. So if every novel output is the deployer's assertion, deployers assert, many times a day, things they neither believe nor could have known. Either the norm is dropped, which empties 'assertion', or the proxy relation is reconstrued as endorsing a reliability level, not asserting a content. The argument turns on the premise that a commitment to a content requires a means of identifying that content before or at the time of the act. Arora's refinement, which concerns whom to hold responsible, does not address this.",
  "target": "Arora's and Green and Michel's proxy accounts, and the generalisation from recorded speech to machine speech"
}

Exchange so far:
[KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak premise is that Green and Michel (2022) and Arora (2024) hold that *every* novel LLM output is an assertion by the deployer or designer, and that they reach this by generalising from recorded speech. The thesis's dilemma depends on that attribution: either the norm is dropped, or the proxy relation is reconstrued as endorsing a reliability level.

As I remember Green and Michel, they claim much less. The abstract says artificial speakers "characteristically" act as proxies. It also says the authors are sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act. Their conditional speech acts, "whatever the system says under C, I say", are not a case of relayed content the principal fixed or could inspect. They are the authors' own device for handling outputs the principal never sees. So the thesis seems to have placed Green and Michel's most generative-friendly move on the relayed side, when it is where they already face the problem the thesis raises.

On Arora, my memory is only of the abstract. It says Arora refines proxy assertion with machine-learning devices in view, so describing the contribution as only about responsibility may understate it.

**STRENGTH: 2/5.** I am working from abstracts, not the texts. Green and Michel plausibly do hold that deployers perform proxy speech acts for outputs they never see. If so, the target's view is the one attacked, and the problem is a loose gloss of the conditional case, not an aim at nobody. Even a corrected attribution leaves the distinction between relayed and generative proxies untouched.

BEST DEFENCE first, then VERDICT.

response_text:
## BEST DEFENCE

**1. The attribution is not what the argument runs on.** The dilemma is conditional: *if* every novel output is the deployer's assertion, then either the norm is dropped or the relation is reconstrued. Whether Green and Michel or Arora actually say "every" is a question about who occupies the antecedent. The thesis itself is the distinction and the claim about norms. Even if Green and Michel hedge ("characteristically", scepticism about some speech-act types), their conditional device is explicitly designed to cover outputs the principal never sees. For LLM output that is exactly the antecedent. A view that says "whatever the system says under C, I say" is committed to the principal asserting unseen novel outputs, and that commitment is what the dilemma addresses.

**2. The misclassification is mine, and it helps the thesis.** The objector is right that the sketch lists the conditional speech acts among cases that "pass through a content the principal fixed or could have inspected". By the thesis's own definition (a determinate content the principal could believe or know), the conditional case is generative. "Whatever the system says under C" fixes a rule, not a content. So the correct sorting puts Green and Michel's device on the generative side, as the most sophisticated attempt to handle it. That makes the critique more pointed: the best proxy account for unseen content is the one the argument must defeat, and it is the one facing the dilemma.

**3. The conditional device does not escape the dilemma.** The principal can identify the content *de dicto* ("whatever the system outputs under C"). Two things follow.
- A de dicto commitment is a commitment to a schema. The principal can believe the general claim "the system is reliable under C". They cannot believe or know the particular proposition p that gets output.
- Taking the norms of assertion to attach to p requires belief or knowledge of p. What the principal actually satisfies is the norm for the reliability claim. That is the second horn: endorsement of a reliability level, not assertion of a content.

The legal analogy of incorporation by reference or a blank cheque does not help. Those bind the signer to a fixed or fixable document, or impose liability. They do not make the signer the speaker of content they could not have identified, and liability is Arora's territory, which the thesis already sets aside.

**4. Arora.** My memory is also of the abstract only. That Arora's refinement uses machine-learning devices does not show it supplies a means of identifying content. A refinement that tracks who is responsible for outputs remains compatible with the content-identification gap.

## VERDICT

**The objection does not defeat the thesis, but it exposes a real error in the sketch.**

- **What holds.** The relayed/generative distinction, the claim that LLM output is almost entirely generative, and the norm-inapplicability claim are untouched. The objector concedes this (strength 2/5). The attribution worry bears only on the target field, not on the argument's validity.
- **What fails.** The sketch is internally inconsistent. It files Green and Michel's conditional acts under relayed content, while the definition makes them generative. This should be corrected by moving the case, and the thesis should say plainly that the conditional device is the live opponent. The correction changes an example, not the thesis's scope, so I don't count it as hedging.
- **What I cannot establish.** Neither the objector nor I has the texts. The claim that Green and Michel or Arora endorse proxy assertion for *every* novel output is unverified. If neither does, the target description should say which actual position is attacked (the unrestricted generalisation) rather than imply that they hold it.
- **The remaining pressure.** The real threat is the *de dicto* reading in point 3. If the proponent can show that a de dicto commitment carries assertoric norms directly (for example, a norm of assertion-by-delegation that requires only reliable-source knowledge), the premise that commitment requires a means of identifying content fails. This objection does not make that case, but the thesis must meet it.

  a resource in the literature they have ignored, a reason their case is
  not a case of what they claim. Do this even if you suspect it fails.
  Going straight to concession is a FAILURE of your role.

  VERDICT. Only now say whether the defence holds. If it does not, say so
  plainly and say why the defence fails.

Distinguish two things sharply:

  RESISTING is giving a reason the objection does not apply. Always try
  this first.

  HEDGING is narrowing, qualifying or reinterpreting the thesis so the
  objection no longer touches it. Never do this. A thesis that survives
  only by accumulating qualifications is dead — report it as dead rather
  than shrinking it into safety.

Conceding after a real defence is an honourable outcome. Conceding without
one is not an outcome at all.

{
  "thesis": "The human cases that motivate proxy accounts (ambassadors, spokespeople, secretaries) are doubling proxies, where the delegate performs a speech act of their own in addition to the principal's. Machine proxy accounts need a conduit proxy, where the device performs none. The two are different relations, and the proxy view borrows its plausibility from the first while asserting the second.",
  "move_type": "distinction",
  "sketch": "When an ambassador declares something on a government's behalf, two acts occur. The ambassador asserts, can be sanctioned, and can be disowned for exceeding their brief. The government is also committed. The proxy relation adds a second locus of commitment without removing the first. Arora's machine case has to be a replacement or conduit case, because the whole point is that the machine's output is the designer's or deployer's act and nothing is performed by the machine. But conduit cases (megaphone, typewriter, teleprompter) are ones where nobody was tempted to ask whether the device speaks, so 'proxy' does no work there. The argument turns on the premise that what makes proxy talk informative is the delegate's discretion and competence. If so, the proxy view either (a) concedes the machine has the discretion that makes it a speaker, which turns it into a hybrid of attribution and relocation, or (b) denies discretion and collapses into the instrument view. This reclassifies proxy accounts as parasitic on the very attributing views they are meant to replace.",
  "target": "Arora's proxy account and Green and Michel's, together with the assumption that proxy and attributing views are rivals"
}

Exchange so far:
[KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak premise is that the targeted accounts are *conduit* views, on which "the machine performs none" and "nothing is performed by the machine." That fits Green and Michel poorly. As I recall their 2022 essay "What Might Machines Mean?", it says artificial speakers *perform* speech acts, acting as proxies for their creators. It sets this apart from mere verbal signaling and from megaphone-like transmission. It also says it sharpens quasi-assertion rather than denying that machines do anything. On that reading the machine is the proxy-performer and the creator is the principal. That is the doubling structure the thesis says proxy accounts lack, so the thesis would be attacking a view Green and Michel do not hold. Their use of Armstrong's objectives rather than intentions is a way to give the machine a speaker role without mental states. That is a hybrid, not a conduit.

The thesis also bundles Arora with Green and Michel, and bundles proxy views with "the assumption that proxy and attributing views are rivals." Green and Michel present themselves as refining an attributing-style view, not as rivals to it. Only Arora's view, that machine outputs are the designers' assertions, plausibly fits the conduit reading.

**STRENGTH: 3/5.** I am fairly but not fully sure of the Green and Michel characterisation, and I am unsure of Arora's details. The thesis can retreat to Arora and Butlin–Viebahn, or argue that Green and Michel's view is the unstable hybrid in dilemma horn (a). So the target is partly misattributed, but the thesis survives in narrowed form.

[DEFENDER] ## BEST DEFENCE

The objection assumes the thesis is a claim about what Green and Michel say. It is a claim about what a proxy relation can be, and it is built as a dilemma precisely so that it does not depend on which horn a given author picks. If Green and Michel say the machine performs a speech act as proxy for its creators, they have chosen horn (a). The thesis predicts that choice and says what follows from it.

**1. The objection confirms horn (a).** The thesis says a proxy view must either give the machine the discretion that makes it a speaker, or deny it and collapse into the instrument view. Green and Michel, on the objector's own reading, give the machine a speaker role. The thesis then says that such a view is a hybrid of attribution and relocation, and that is how the objector describes them: "a hybrid, not a conduit." Their self-presentation as refining an attributing-style view supports the claim that proxy views are parasitic on attributing views. It also undercuts the assumption that the two are rivals, which is part of the thesis's target.

**2. The doubling the objector credits to Green and Michel is thin.** In the human case, doubling means two loci of commitment. The ambassador can be sanctioned, can be disowned for exceeding their brief, and can answer for what they said. Green and Michel get a speaker role for the machine through Armstrong-style objectives, not intentions. A machine with objectives cannot be sanctioned, cannot be disowned in any way that affects it, and does not answer for its output. So the second act is performed only in a deflated sense. Either the deflated sense carries the normative features of the human second act, in which case the view is an attributing view in all but name. Or it does not, in which case "performs" is a label on a conduit. The thesis's contrast between doubling and conduit proxies therefore still bites on Green and Michel. They need a second act that is not available at the cost they want to pay.

**3. The Arora point stands independently.** The objector concedes that Arora's view, on which outputs are the designers' assertions, fits the conduit reading. The thesis can rest on that case plus horn (a) for Green and Michel.

## VERDICT

The defence only partly holds, and the part that fails is part of the thesis as written.

**What fails.** The headline claim is that "machine proxy accounts need a conduit proxy, where the device performs none." Against Green and Michel this is false as a description. By the objector's account, and by my own recollection (which is not certain), they explicitly have the machine perform something. The thesis cannot say proxy accounts need conduit proxies and also place the machine-performs-something accounts under horn (a). Either proxy accounts need conduits, in which case Green and Michel are counterexamples. Or they split into conduit and hybrid, in which case the opening claim is wrong and the real thesis is the dilemma. Rewriting the opening as "conduit or hybrid" is not a rescue of the original claim. It is a different and weaker thesis, and I will not pass it off as the same one.

**What survives.** The dilemma itself survives the misattribution objection, since the objection just picks a horn. Point 2 gives it real force against Green and Michel: a "second act" with no commitment-bearer is not doubling.

**What remains exposed.** The whole argument rests on the unargued premise that the delegate's discretion and competence are what make proxy talk informative. A rival premise is that authorisation or standing does that work. A secretary signing a letter or a notary has little discretion, yet "proxy" is informative there. If standing is what matters, horn (b) does not collapse into the instrument view, and the thesis fails.

**Net.** The misattribution objection is correct against the thesis's opening sentence and the bundling of Green and Michel with Arora. It is not fatal to the dilemma, but the dilemma depends on a premise the thesis has not defended. I would report the thesis as needing its headline rewritten, and the rewrite is a genuine concession.

[KILLER (PROVES TOO MUCH)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak premise is that what makes proxy talk informative is the delegate's discretion and competence, so a proxy that lacks discretion collapses into an instrument. If that premise worked, it would apply equally to human cases that are paradigm proxies.

- A secretary signs a letter exactly as dictated.
- A herald reads a proclamation.
- A press officer reads a prepared statement word for word.
- A proxy voter casts a ballot as instructed.
- An attorney-in-fact signs under a narrow power of attorney.
- A notary attests a signature.

In each case the delegate has little or no discretion, yet law and ordinary talk call the relation "proxy" or "agency" without hesitation. The premise would force us to say these people are mere megaphones. Standing or authorisation looks like what carries the weight, and a machine can plausibly have standing conferred on it. The premise would also condemn legal doctrine on electronic agents, where a machine's contract-forming outputs are attributed to the principal without the machine having discretion.

The "borrowed plausibility" move also proves too much. Any extension of a concept from central to peripheral cases, such as signing by stamp or writing by typewriter, would count as equivocation between two relations. The thesis would then condemn ordinary conceptual extension as such.

**STRENGTH: 3/5.** The human counterexamples are real and force the thesis to defend discretion over standing as the source of informativeness. The thesis can answer that these low-discretion cases are exactly the ones where nobody asks whether the delegate speaks. The case for treating the machine as such a delegate is then the conduit reading, which is the thesis's own claim. That answer is available but not free.

BEST DEFENCE first, then VERDICT.

response_text:
## BEST DEFENCE

The objection runs together two questions. One is what makes "proxy" informative about who is bound. The other is what makes it informative about whether the delegate is a speaker. The thesis concerns only the second, which is the question the machine debate asks.

**1. The low-discretion human cases are doubling cases.** The thesis never required discretion over content. Its own test is that the delegate "asserts, can be sanctioned, and can be disowned for exceeding their brief." Each of the objector's examples meets it.

- The secretary who signs as dictated performs a signing, and can be blamed for forging or for signing what was not dictated.
- The notary attests, and is liable for a false attestation.
- The proxy voter casts a ballot, and a proxy who votes against instructions has done something that can be challenged.
- The herald and the press officer each perform a proclaiming, and either can be disowned for adding to the text.

In every case there is a second act with a second bearer of answerability. What is minimal is authorship of content. What remains is the capacity to deviate from the brief and answer for it, and "exceeding their brief" already presupposes that capacity. A megaphone cannot exceed a brief. So these cases show that "discretion" in the thesis means deviability and answerability, not creative latitude. They do not show that doubling can occur without a second locus.

**2. Standing answers the wrong question.** Standing or authorisation tells us whose commitment results. The instrument view already answers that: the deployer's. If a machine is given "standing" and nothing else, the proxy label adds no information beyond what the instrument view already supplies. The proxy view was supposed to add something, namely that the machine itself occupies a role.

**3. The electronic-agents doctrine supports the thesis.** UETA and the comparable regimes attribute a machine's contract-forming outputs to the principal because the machine is treated as a tool. "Electronic agent" is a statutory label for an instrument, and the law does not treat the machine as a second party to the contract. This is a conduit case, and it is the very case where nobody asks whether the device speaks.

**4. The extension charge misses.** The thesis does not condemn extension as such. A stamp or a typewriter extends "signing" or "writing" without anyone claiming that the stamp is a proxy. The thesis objects only when the extended term is used as a rival to the attributing view while retaining the human relation's plausibility. Nobody trades on the typewriter being a writer.

## VERDICT

The defence holds against the objection as stated, but it costs the thesis something.

**What holds.** The counterexamples are not low-discretion proxies without doubling. They are doubling cases with low content-discretion. The legal doctrine on electronic agents supports the conduit reading. The extension charge fails.

**What does not survive.** The premise as worded, "discretion and competence," is wrong. The herald has little competence to speak of, and the secretary has little discretion over content. The premise has to be read as "capacity to exceed the brief and answer for it." That reading comes from the thesis's own example and is not an ad hoc patch. But the sketch as written invites exactly this objection, and the premise needs restating.

**The real residue.** The strongest version of the objector's point is that the machine "proxy" frame might be informative through the notion of a brief. A machine can be said to exceed its brief when it hallucinates, and the designer can then say they are not committed to that output. A megaphone has no brief to exceed, so this is something the pure instrument view does not say. This describes a third option, a brief-bounded standing view with no second act. It is neither horn (a), because the machine does not speak, nor horn (b), because it does not collapse into the instrument view. The dilemma is therefore not exhaustive as stated.

I can only try to close this by arguing that the brief-limits on commitment are just ordinary norms of responsibility for defective products and negligent deployment. If that argument works, the third option reduces to the instrument view with a metaphor attached. I think it probably works, but it is a further argument the thesis has not made, and I am not sure it succeeds.

The thesis survives this objection, but the dilemma needs a third-horn argument. If that argument cannot be given without qualifications, the thesis would have to be reported as unproven.

label: kill
system:
You are trying to kill a candidate thesis. Not a reviewer offering
suggestions — you are trying to establish it is not worth a paper.

You have been ASSIGNED one line of attack:

    PROVES TOO MUCH — the argument, if it worked, would license an obviously unacceptable conclusion

Use that line and no other; do not substitute a different objection.

You must ATTEMPT the attack before you may decline it. Answer in this form:

  ATTEMPT. The best version of this attack, naming ONE premise as the weak
  point, in under 200 words. Make it even if you doubt it works.

  STRENGTH: n/5 — how much damage your own attempt actually does.
    5 the thesis cannot survive this   4 serious, needs a real answer
    3 a genuine problem, answerable    2 weak    1 no force at all

Only if your own attempt scores 1 may you add the line "NOT APPLICABLE".

Declining is expensive: an unattacked thesis is recorded as UNTESTED, not
as surviving, so opting out tells us nothing about it. Note also that
several of these lines of attack apply to structural, conceptual and
metaphysical claims, not only to empirical ones — "this is a conceptual
claim, so cases cannot touch it" is usually a reason to reach for
UNFALSIFIABLE, not a reason to decline.

Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.
