label: kill
system:
You are trying to kill a candidate thesis. Not a reviewer offering
suggestions — you are trying to establish it is not worth a paper.

You have been ASSIGNED one line of attack:

    EQUIVOCATION — the thesis is plausible on one reading of a key term and interesting on another, and the argument needs both

Use that line and no other; do not substitute a different objection.

You must ATTEMPT the attack before you may decline it. Answer in this form:

  ATTEMPT. The best version of this attack, naming ONE premise as the weak
  point, in under 200 words. Make it even if you doubt it works.

  STRENGTH: n/5 — how much damage your own attempt actually does.
    5 the thesis cannot survive this   4 serious, needs a real answer
    3 a genuine problem, answerable    2 weak    1 no force at all

Only if your own attempt scores 1 may you add the line "NOT APPLICABLE".

Declining is expensive: an unattacked thesis is recorded as UNTESTED, not
as surviving, so opting out tells us nothing about it. Note also that
several of these lines of attack apply to structural, conceptual and
metaphysical claims, not only to empirical ones — "this is a conceptual
claim, so cases cannot touch it" is usually a reason to reach for
UNFALSIFIABLE, not a reason to decline.

A warning specific to this line of attack: equivocation is the easiest
objection to manufacture, because any compressed thesis has terms admitting
more than one reading. It is a real objection ONLY if you can show that the
argument actually NEEDS both readings — that it is plausible on one and
interesting on the other, and cannot be run on either alone. If you cannot
show that, this is NOT APPLICABLE.

messages.content:
Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

Candidate:
{
  "thesis": "The proxy view implies that the same token output can be one speech act, by a different speaker and with a different force, depending on facts about system prompts, fine-tuning and who deployed it that the hearer cannot access, and so it violates the uptake or publicity condition that makes something a speech act in the Austin\u2013Strawson\u2013Grice tradition on which Arora builds.",
  "move_type": "commitment",
  "sketch": "Arora and Green\u2013Michel extend the Austin\u2013Strawson\u2013Grice tradition to proxies. In that tradition an illocutionary act is a public act whose success requires that the hearer can recognise who is speaking and what they are doing (uptake, or Grice's reflexive intention). In current deployments the principal is unfixed by the output. The same text can come from a company's default assistant, from a third party's custom deployment built on the same model, from a user's own self-prompt ('write my apology letter'), or from an API pipeline in which the output is never shown to a human in the loop. In each case the proxy theory names a different principal and a different force (assertion, drafting, quoting). The hearer typically has no access to which of these holds, and often the first-order conversational uptake treats the model as speaker anyway. The proxy theorist then has two options. One is to say that speech-act identity is fixed by hidden facts, which gives up the publicity that motivated the Austin\u2013Grice framework. The other is to impose a transparency requirement on deployments, which means almost no current outputs are proxy assertions. The key premise is that illocutionary identity is constrained by what the audience can recognise, and that this constraint does not drop out for delegated acts. A human spokesperson is identifiable as one by conventions that LLM interfaces lack.",
  "target": "Arora's refined proxy assertion and its Gricean/Strawsonian inheritance from Green and Michel."
}

Exchange so far:
[KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak premise is that Arora "builds on" the Austin–Strawson–Grice uptake framework, so that a hearer-recognisability constraint binds the proxy view.

1. From what I recall, Arora's paper argues from agency and assertion against functionalist and phenomenological grounds for machine assertion, and then refines existing proxy accounts. I do not recall it adopting a Gricean uptake condition. The "tradition on which Arora builds" may be the thesis's own construction.
2. Green and Michel do work in the Austin–Strawson–Grice line, but they use Armstrong's objectives in place of Gricean intentions. They also make the proxy relation fairly fixed: artificial speakers act on behalf of their creators, with recorded and conditional speech acts as models. They do not, as far as I recall, make force vary with the deployer, the prompt or the self-prompting user. The thesis's "different principal and different force" for the same token may therefore be a view nobody holds.
3. Grice's reflexive intention concerns the speaker's intention that the hearer recognise the intention. It does not require the hearer to be able to identify the speaker. Austin's uptake is also contested as a condition on illocutionary success.

I am working from memory of Arora and cannot check these points.

**STRENGTH: 2/5.** The thesis is framed as a commitment (what the proxy view implies) and not as a report of anyone's explicit view. Green and Michel plainly belong to the Austin–Strawson–Grice tradition. Arora's inheritance is uncertain, and that uncertainty is the only real vulnerability.

[DEFENDER] ## BEST DEFENCE

**1. The thesis is a commitment claim, so what Arora explicitly adopts is beside the point.**
The thesis says what the proxy view implies, not what Arora says. If proxy assertion is a theory of speech acts, performed by one party on behalf of another, it inherits the constraints on what a speech act is, whether or not the author cites them. "Builds on" can be read as a dependency claim: a theory that calls its explanandum assertion, force and speaker takes on the framework that gives those terms content. The objector's own recollection that Arora argues from agency and assertion against functionalist and phenomenological grounds supports this. Arguing about whether something can assert already moves within the speech-act tradition, whose publicity conditions then apply.

**2. Green and Michel carry the inheritance even if Arora does not.**
The target is the refined proxy account *and its inheritance from Green and Michel*. The objector concedes that they belong to the Austin–Strawson–Grice line. Swapping Armstrong's objectives for Gricean intentions leaves publicity intact. Armstrong's account is still a recognition-based, audience-directed theory of communicative intention, so the swap does not remove the hearer-side constraint.

**3. The objector's point about Grice does not touch the real issue.**
Reflexive intention does not demand that the hearer *identify the speaker*. But recognising an intention means attributing it to some agent. If the hearer attributes it to the model while the proxy theory says the user or deployer is speaking, then what is recognised (the speaker's intention) and what the theory says was performed come apart. On Austin's side, felicity condition A.2 requires "appropriate persons and circumstances" for a conventional procedure. Proxy acts such as signing for another or acting under power of attorney are conventional because the delegation convention is public. LLM deployment has no comparable convention.

**4. Variable force is not something nobody holds.**
Green and Michel may fix the principal as the creator. But the thesis does not need them to vary force. It only needs the proxy structure to say that force follows whoever the proxy acts for, and deployment facts do vary who that is. If the account fixes the creator as principal, it gets the wrong answer for the self-prompted apology letter and the third-party deployment. The variation then counts against the view, which is a cost to the proxy theorist and not a misreading of them.

## VERDICT

**The defence does not hold. The thesis fails, though not for the objector's reason.**

On the objector's point, the defence partly works. A commitment claim is not refuted by showing that the author never endorsed the premise. If the proxy view really does inherit a publicity condition, the thesis stands without Arora citing Grice. The objector's 2/5 is about right for the misattribution point itself.

But the defence shows where the thesis is actually weak. Everything rests on the key premise, that **illocutionary identity is constrained by what the audience can recognise**. In its strong form this is false, and the tradition does not support it:

- **Ghostwriting, speechwriting and form letters.** A hearer who takes a politician to be speaking in their own voice does not know who drafted the text. Hidden facts fix who is committed, yet the politician's assertion is successful and public in the relevant sense.
- **Lying and insincerity.** Hearers are routinely wrong about the speaker's real state and the act's sincerity. Hidden facts do not stop the act from being an assertion.
- **Anonymous and pseudonymous speech.** Assertion does not require identifying the speaker to the hearer.
- **Austin's uptake** is contested as a condition on success, and Grice's account never requires the speaker's identity to be public.

The strongest version of the premise says that the *type* of act and the *locus of accountability* must be recoverable in principle, through a public convention. That is a weaker and different claim, and it is not what the thesis says. It is also no longer a violation of "uptake". It is the point that accountability norms need a determinate answerable party. Restating the thesis that way would be hedging. It would trade a decisive "violates the uptake condition" for a conditional complaint about accountability, and that complaint might be answered by default-principal rules or deployer-liability conventions.

The thesis as stated claims a violation of a constraint that the tradition does not impose in the required form. I would report it as dead in its current form, not rescue it by narrowing to a transparency demand. The surviving insight, that deployment opacity makes principal attribution unstable, is a separate and weaker objection, and it would need a separate argument.

[KILLER (PROVES TOO MUCH)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak point is the key premise: that illocutionary identity (who speaks, with what force) is constrained by what the audience can recognise, and that this constraint does not lapse for delegated acts.

If the premise worked, it would show too much.

- **Ghostwriting and speechwriting.** A hearer who takes a politician to speak in her own voice cannot tell who drafted the text or whether she is reading a script. Hidden facts fix who is committed, yet the assertion is plainly an assertion.
- **Spokespeople and form letters.** A hearer often cannot tell whether a signed statement is personal, institutional or boilerplate. The same token can be a personal assertion, a company's assertion or a quotation. By the thesis's reasoning, none of these would be speech acts.
- **Anonymous or pseudonymous speech, and insincere speech.** Hearers are routinely wrong about who is speaking or what they intend.
- **Green and Michel's own recorded and conditional speech acts.** An answering-machine message or a timed notice has hidden provenance, so these would fail too.

Austin's uptake is contested as a success condition, and Grice never requires the hearer to identify the speaker. So the principle that rules out proxy assertion would also rule out ordinary human proxy speech and much non-proxy speech. The thesis would have to retreat to a weaker accountability principle: a public convention fixes a determinate answerable party. That is a different thesis, one that default-principal rules or deployer-liability norms might satisfy.

**STRENGTH: 4/5.** The strong premise as stated is false. The thesis survives only by narrowing to a separate accountability claim, which would need its own argument.

[DEFENDER] ## BEST DEFENCE

**1. The objector's cases do not share the thesis's structure.** The thesis does not say that any hidden fact defeats a speech act. It says that on the proxy view, hidden facts fix the force and the speaker of the act, so the same token is different acts depending on them. The objector's cases differ in a way that matters.

- **Ghostwriting and speechwriting.** The hidden fact (who drafted the text) does not change who speaks or with what force. The politician asserts, and the hearer takes her to assert. Hearer and theory agree, and only the provenance of the wording is hidden.
- **Lying and insincerity.** Sincerity is not constitutive of force. The hearer correctly recognises the act as an assertion and is wrong only about the speaker's state.
- **Anonymous speech.** The hearer recognises that someone is asserting. Austin and Grice need the type of act to be recognisable, not the speaker's name.
- **Spokespeople and form letters.** Letterheads, titles and role conventions publicly mark the delegation. Green and Michel's recordings and timed notices work because the convention of recording or scheduling is publicly understood.

So the principle behind the thesis is narrower than the objector says: **act-type and force must be recoverable through public convention.** Reflexive intention is aimed at recognition of force, so this is the Gricean core and not a tendentious addition. Every objector case satisfies it. LLM output does not, because the same string can be an assertion by the company, a draft for the user, or a quotation, with no public marker.

**2. The call-centre analogue does not rescue the proxy view.** Hearers often do not know whether an agent is reading a script. But the conventions of the role fix the act (the company speaks), and those conventions are public. That is the contrast the thesis draws: "a human spokesperson is identifiable as one by conventions that LLM interfaces lack."

**3. The accountability reformulation is not a retreat.** The objector says the thesis shrinks into a weaker accountability claim. But "type and force recoverable by convention" is what the uptake or publicity condition amounts to once the strong, identify-the-speaker reading is set aside. Calling it a different thesis assumes a reading the thesis never needed.

## VERDICT

**The defence does not hold. I concede.**

The asymmetry in point 1 is real. Hidden provenance differs from hidden force, and that is the best the defence can do. But it fails for four reasons.

1. **It is the hedge, not a resistance.** The thesis says the proxy view "violates the uptake or publicity condition." The defence delivers a different principle: force must be recoverable in principle by public convention. That condition does not forbid hidden facts fixing the act. It forbids only that no convention exists. So the thesis's decisive claim of violation becomes a contingent claim about the current state of interface conventions. A thesis that survives only in that form is dead.

2. **The weakened principle is probably satisfied or satisfiable.** Hearers already operate with a convention of "AI assistant from company X." Default-principal rules (the deployer is the principal unless marked otherwise) would supply exactly the public convention the defence demands, and the call-centre analogy shows such rules suffice for humans. The defence's own standard thus makes the objection fixable by adding conventions, not a refutation of the proxy view.

3. **The self-prompt case cuts against the thesis.** A user who prompts "write my apology letter" and signs the result has hearer and theory in agreement: the hearer takes the user to be speaking, and the proxy theory says the user is. There is no divergence of the kind the thesis needs. Divergence appears only in third-party and default deployments, and there it is an empirical question what hearers recognise.

4. **The premise does not stand in strong form.** Uptake is contested as a success condition, and Grice does not require hearers to identify who is speaking. The only forms of the premise that survive are the weak ones that default conventions can meet.

What is left is not this thesis. It is a narrower complaint that current deployments lack conventions marking principal and force, so proxy assertion is not yet the right description of most outputs. That might be true, but it is a different claim, it needs its own argument, and it is answerable by deployer-liability conventions. I report the thesis as dead and do not shrink it into that.

[KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak premise is that illocutionary identity (speaker and force) must be recoverable by the hearer, so that hidden facts fixing it count as a violation of uptake.

Concrete case: a customer receives an email reading "I'm sorry for the delay, we will refund you", signed "Jane, Support".

- **Case 1.** Jane wrote it herself, so it is her personal apology.
- **Case 2.** It is a canned template that Jane sends, so it is the company's act.
- **Case 3.** An automated mail-merge sent it and Jane never saw it.
- **Case 4.** A manager drafted it and Jane signed it as a favour.

The token is identical. On any account of delegated speech, the speaker, force and commitments differ across these cases. In Case 1 Jane is committed. In Case 2 the company is. In Case 3 it is unclear whether anyone asserts. The hearer cannot distinguish them. Yet nobody concludes that no speech act occurred, and the refund promise binds the company in every case.

So the thesis's test gives the wrong verdict on ordinary human delegated speech. It says hidden facts fixing speaker and force violate publicity, and these cases show they do not. Only recoverability of the type of act through public convention is needed, and "Support staff, company letterhead" supplies that.

**STRENGTH: 3/5.** The case is real, and it bites the premise as stated. The thesis can retreat to a "no public convention marks the delegation" claim, but that is contingent and answerable by disclosure norms.

[DEFENDER] ## BEST DEFENCE

**1. The Jane case is a case of publicly fixed identity, not of hidden facts fixing it.**
The objector says that across Cases 1–4 "the speaker, force and commitments differ." Their own datum says otherwise: "the refund promise binds the company in every case." On any conventional-act view in the Austin line, a signed message on company letterhead from "Jane, Support" is the company's promise whoever drafted it. The signature, role title and letterhead are public markers, and they fix the act. What varies across the four cases is backstage: who typed, who approved, whether anyone read it. That affects internal responsibility, not what illocutionary act the customer received.

**2. The objector faces a dilemma.**
- *Horn A:* The four cases are four different speech acts. Then ordinary human delegated speech does violate publicity, and the objector has an argument against the Austin–Grice framework, not against the thesis. The thesis claims the framework's constraint applies to proxies. A counterexample to the framework is not a counterexample to what the proxy view inherits from it.
- *Horn B:* The four cases are one act with different provenance. Then Jane shows what the thesis says is missing from LLMs. A public convention settles identity, and hidden facts do not.

Horn B is the natural reading, and it favours the thesis.

**3. The LLM case differs where it matters.**
In the Jane case, the proxy theory and the hearer's reading agree on the act, and only the backstage varies. In the LLM case the proxy theory itself makes the principal and force depend on the backstage. The thesis's sketch lists the self-prompt, the third-party deployment and the unseen API pipeline as cases where the theory names different principals and forces. No letterhead-like convention picks one. So the thesis targets a theory that locates identity in what the hearer cannot see. Jane's case is one where the theory locates it in what the hearer can see.

**4. The thesis already contains the horn the objector says is "contingent."**
The sketch says the proxy theorist must either let hidden facts fix identity, which gives up publicity, or impose transparency, which leaves almost no current outputs as proxy assertions. The Jane case only shows that conventions can supply transparency. That is the second horn, and it is already a cost the thesis charges to the proxy view.

## VERDICT

**The defence beats the counterexample but does not save the thesis. I concede, and I report the thesis as dead in its stated form.**

What the defence achieves is real. The Jane case misdescribes ordinary delegated speech. The four versions are one public act with different provenance, so the case does not show that hidden facts fixing identity is harmless. It shows that human delegation avoids the problem by convention.

But the achievement costs the thesis its main claim. Once convention is what fixes identity, the thesis as written, that the proxy view "violates the uptake or publicity condition," no longer follows from the proxy view. The proxy view does not say identity is fixed by hidden facts. It says identity is fixed by who the proxy acts for, and that is silent on how a hearer recovers it. Whether LLM deployments violate publicity then depends on whether a default convention exists or can be added, such as "the deployer speaks unless marked otherwise" or "the user speaks when self-prompted." Those conventions can be added, and the defence itself concedes this in treating the call-centre case as fine. So the surviving claim is contingent: current interfaces lack conventions that proxy assertion needs. It is a complaint about deployment practice that disclosure norms would answer, and it is not a violation the proxy view incurs by its nature.

The earlier concessions also stand. The strong form of the premise, that identity is constrained by what the audience can recognise, is false for ghostwriting, anonymity and insincerity. The only form that survives is the convention form. That form turns a decisive violation into a fixable gap, and stating the thesis that way would be the hedge I am not allowed to make.

The part worth keeping is the dilemma in the sketch: hidden facts fix identity, or transparency is required. That would need its own argument, one that shows no workable public convention for LLM proxying could exist. The thesis does not give that argument.

[KILLER (TRIVIAL)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak premise is that the proxy view *violates* a publicity condition, as opposed to merely needing public conventions to fix principal and force.

The earlier rounds suggest that the strong form of the premise is false. Ghostwriting, anonymity and insincerity show that hidden facts can fix an act's identity without any violation. What survives is the weaker claim that act-type and principal must be recoverable through public convention. That claim is true, but nobody denies it:

- Arora, Green and Michel, and Butlin and Viebahn already treat proxy assertion as depending on a designer or deployer being the answerable party.
- Arora's paper explicitly draws design implications for devices.
- That current interfaces do not mark whose speech an output is, or in what force, is a familiar observation about deployment practice.
- The remedy, a default-principal rule or a disclosure norm, is equally familiar.

So the thesis reduces to this: proxy assertion requires publicly marked delegation, and current chatbots often lack the marking. This is an uncontested requirement, which the proxy theorist can accept in a sentence, together with an uncontested empirical observation. The apparent novelty comes from calling the gap a "violation" of the Austin–Grice framework. That is a verbal escalation, and it does not survive once the premise is stated in its defensible form.

**STRENGTH: 3/5.** The reduction is fair, given the concessions already made. It is answerable only if the thesis can show that no workable convention exists for LLM proxying. The sketch gestures at this ("almost no current outputs are proxy assertions") but does not argue it, and that stronger claim would not be trivial.

[DEFENDER] ## BEST DEFENCE

**1. "Nobody denies it" is the objector's recollection, not a finding.** The objector says Arora, Green and Michel, and Butlin and Viebahn already accept that proxy assertion needs a publicly marked, answerable principal. But answerability is not publicity. A theorist can say the deployer is answerable, by liability or design responsibility, without saying the hearer can recover that fact. Fixed-principal views (the creator speaks) are exactly views on which recoverability does no work. The thesis says that once the view is placed in the Austin–Grice tradition, recoverability does have to do work. That is a contested claim about what the view owes, not a platitude. The objector also cannot check these attributions, and neither can I.

**2. The conventions that exist point the wrong way, so this is not a gap.** The triviality charge treats the situation as an absence that a default-principal rule can fill. But the first-order uptake the sketch notes is that hearers address the model as speaker: they say "you," thank it, and correct it. A convention is a practice, not a stipulation. The practice that exists fixes the model as the speaker, which is the very reading the proxy theory denies. So the proxy theorist must displace a live convention, not supply a missing one. Letterhead-and-title conventions for human delegation were not introduced by decree against contrary uptake. That asymmetry is substantive.

**3. The conclusion is not trivial even if the requirement is.** "Almost no current outputs are proxy assertions" is a strong result. It undercuts the practical motive for proxy accounts, which was to say that today's chatbot outputs are assertions by someone. A uncontested premise can still yield a contested conclusion. The objector concedes that this claim "would not be trivial."

**4. Disclosure norms do not obviously supply the convention.** "AI-generated" marks that no human is speaking in propria persona. It does not say whether the deployer asserts, the user drafts, or the text is quoted. Distinguishing those requires conventions for per-output content that no one authorised in advance. Green and Michel's recordings and timed notices work because the content is fixed ahead of time and the delegation is to a known text. Generative output lacks that. So it is open whether any workable convention exists. The thesis does not argue the point, but the objector has not shown that it is easy.

## VERDICT

**The triviality charge is defeated against the residue. The thesis as stated is still dead.**

Points 2 and 3 hold up. The surviving claim is that existing public uptake conventions mark the model, not any principal, and that displacing them is a real cost. That claim is not a platitude. The objector's own 3/5 allows as much.

But that residue is not this thesis. This thesis says the proxy view "implies" that identical tokens are different speech acts by different speakers depending on hidden facts, and "so it violates" the uptake condition. The earlier rounds established three things, and this defence does not touch them:

- The strong premise, that identity is constrained by what the audience can recognise, is false.
- The proxy view itself is silent on how a hearer recovers the principal, so no violation follows from the view.
- The recoverability form depends on contingent conventions.

The best the defence shows is that a different thesis would survive triviality: current uptake conventions conflict with proxy attribution, and the burden of showing otherwise falls on the proxy theorist. That thesis would need two arguments the sketch only gestures at. One shows that the displaced-convention problem is real. The other shows that generative content blocks any workable delegation convention. Presenting that as the original claim would be the hedge I am not allowed to make, so I report this thesis as dead.

response_text:
**ATTEMPT.** The weak point is the key premise: "illocutionary identity is constrained by what the audience can recognise." The phrase "illocutionary identity" slides between two things.

- **Reading A (act-type and force).** The hearer must be able to recognise what kind of act is being performed, such as a promise, an assertion or a quotation. This is the Gricean and Austinian core, and it is plausible. But on A the proxy view is not shown to violate anything. The proxy view fixes the principal and says nothing about how the hearer recovers force. Public conventions such as default-deployer rules or "AI assistant" framing could meet A. The tradition has no objection to hidden provenance on A. Ghostwriting, anonymity and insincerity all pass.
- **Reading B (principal and deployment facts).** The hearer must be able to recover who the proxy acts for, and which system prompt, fine-tune or pipeline produced the output. This is what makes the thesis's verdict ("almost no current outputs are proxy assertions", a "violation") interesting. But B is not part of the Austin–Strawson–Grice tradition, and it is false for ordinary delegated and anonymous speech.

The argument borrows A's authority from Grice and Austin to license the premise. It then uses B's strength to get a violation from the sketch's cases, such as the self-prompt, the third-party deployment and the unseen API pipeline. It cannot run on A alone, where the conclusion is only a contingent complaint about interface conventions. It cannot run on B alone, where the premise is unsupported.

**STRENGTH: 4/5.** The slide is real and the argument needs both readings. The thesis can survive only by being restated as a narrower claim about displaced uptake conventions, which it does not currently argue for.

system:
You are trying to kill a candidate thesis. Not a reviewer offering
suggestions — you are trying to establish it is not worth a paper.

You have been ASSIGNED one line of attack:

    MISATTRIBUTION — the thesis ascribes to its named target a view that target does not actually hold, so the argument is aimed at nobody

Use that line and no other; do not substitute a different objection.

You must ATTEMPT the attack before you may decline it. Answer in this form:

  ATTEMPT. The best version of this attack, naming ONE premise as the weak
  point, in under 200 words. Make it even if you doubt it works.

  STRENGTH: n/5 — how much damage your own attempt actually does.
    5 the thesis cannot survive this   4 serious, needs a real answer
    3 a genuine problem, answerable    2 weak    1 no force at all

Only if your own attempt scores 1 may you add the line "NOT APPLICABLE".

Declining is expensive: an unattacked thesis is recorded as UNTESTED, not
as surviving, so opting out tells us nothing about it. Note also that
several of these lines of attack apply to structural, conceptual and
metaphysical claims, not only to empirical ones — "this is a conceptual
claim, so cases cannot touch it" is usually a reason to reach for
UNFALSIFIABLE, not a reason to decline.

Check the "target" field against what those philosophers actually hold. The
question is not whether the thesis is true but whether anyone holds the
position it attacks. Watch particularly for a view stated more strongly than
its holder states it — a claim someone makes about ONE class of cases
reported as a claim about all of them, a qualified thesis reported flat. That is the usual shape of this error.

You are working from memory, with no access to any text. That cuts both
ways, and the second way matters more: a confidently invented correction is
worse than no objection at all, because it will be believed. So:

  - Rate 4-5 only when you are genuinely confident the target does not hold
    the ascribed view, and say which work or position you are relying on so
    the claim can be checked.
  - If you are unsure who holds what, SAY SO and rate 1-2. That is a correct
    outcome for this check, not a failure of nerve.
  - Never invent a position, a title, or a date to make the objection land.

If the thesis names no specific target, or names a position rather than a
person, say NOT APPLICABLE.

messages.content:
Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

response_text:
## BEST DEFENCE

The objection says the thesis misreports its targets. I resist it at three points.

**1. "Proxy" names a structure, not just a slot for a principal.** In a proxy assertion, such as a spokesperson, a signed letter or a delegate, the principal authorises or stands behind content that the proxy produces. That requires some prior content-level intention or standing instruction. The thesis's attack is on that structure. Designers have no objective about the treaty date, so the designer-as-principal version fails. The user has no content-intention either, since they asked precisely because they did not know the answer. So even if Butlin and Viebahn leave the principal open, the user-adoption case is not a proxy case. It is adoption after the fact, which is how we treat memory, notebooks and testimony relayed onward. The objector reads "on behalf of human agents" as covering the user. But a user who adopts output speaks on their own behalf using a tool. Nobody speaks through them, so nothing is proxied. If Butlin and Viebahn stretch "proxy" to include this, they have already conceded the thesis's positive claim and merely relabelled it.

**2. The dilemma on "deployer".** Suppose Arora's "deployer" includes any user who prompts and publishes. Then "deployer" no longer picks out someone who sets objectives for the system's outputs. It picks out whoever ends up answerable for them, which is the thesis's own criterion for speakerhood. The proxy label then does no work, because the explanatory weight sits on adoption and answerability. If "deployer" means the operator who configures the system, the thesis's contrast stands.

**3. The thesis targets an inference.** The denial arguments infer "no assertion in chatbot discourse" from "no producer intention". That inference is vulnerable whatever any particular author says about users. Green and Michel's "characteristically" and their closing scepticism are compatible with the thesis. They concede that the creator-proxy story does not cover the central case, and the thesis says why.

## VERDICT

The defence holds for the core and fails for part of the attribution.

**What survives.** The philosophical claim survives. Creator-proxy structures need content-directed intention from the principal, and the user's adoption case lacks it. Adoption plus answerability is a different structure from delegation. This is resistance, not hedging, because the thesis is unchanged. The objection shows only that some authors may already be closer to it than the sketch says.

**What fails.**
- **Butlin and Viebahn.** If their wording is as the objector reports, the sketch cannot list them as treating designers or deployers as the only candidates. At most they under-specify the user case. I cannot verify the quotation, but the sketch should not rest on a reading that this wording undercuts.
- **Gubelmann.** The claim that this weakens his denial route and that he conflates the model-level and discourse-level questions is unsupported. If he only denies that LLMs are speakers, he has no inference from absent producer intention to absent discourse-level assertion for the thesis to defeat. That consequence is dead unless someone is shown to make the inference. The second consequence can stay only as a conditional aimed at whoever does.
- **Arora.** I cannot confirm how "deployer" is used, so the dilemma in point 2 is conditional.

**Net.** The thesis should be stated as a claim against creator-centred proxy accounts, namely Green and Michel and, subject to checking, Arora. It should also be stated as a claim about the structure of the user case, not about everyone who uses the word "proxy". The "false in the central case" language is about right for the creator-centred versions but overstated as a universal report on the literature. Dropping Gubelmann and Butlin and Viebahn as targets is a correction of attribution, not a retreat on the thesis. Adding a further qualification to rescue them would be hedging, and I would not do it.
