Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. - Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

- (a) it factors through an intermediate representation that has the structure of an intention, or
- (b) it is a flat mapping with no such variable.

A state S counts as episode-level mediation if it meets criteria that can be fixed in advance:

1. S encodes occasion-specific content, such as this user's goal or the point to be conveyed, and is decodable before the utterance.
2. Intervening on S (activation patching, steering) changes the output in a content-respecting way. Changing the represented goal changes what is said, and does so systematically across paraphrases.
3. S is updated by evidence, as a belief state is. New user turns shift it in ways that track the evidence rather than surface form.
4. S is reused across several downstream outputs rather than being a one-off feedforward artefact.

- **ELIZA** fails: there is no persistent variable encoding the user's aim, and intervening on any candidate variable does nothing.
- **A thermostat** fails: its state does encode something, but not hearer-directed content selected among alternatives, and it supports no content-respecting counterfactuals.

**ATTEMPT.** The weak premise is that carving *inherited purpose* from *instantiated intention*, and locating the real dispute at "whether an occurrent state in the machine, not the designer, mediates policy and utterance", reorganises the debate. That is already the standard structure of the literature, and several authors hold it.

- **Green and Michel** (and Arora) already hold the two-level structure. Their "recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts" are standing, policy-level commitments applied to particular occasions. Their Armstrong-style "objectives" are the standing-purpose layer.
- **Butlin 2024** already poses the live question. An output counts as the system's own only if it is explained by the system's sensitivity to instrumental value through modification over multi-step interaction. Outputs "owed solely to design" do not count. He denies desire to generative agents because their goals are designer-fixed.
- **Gubelmann** makes the same cut as the thesis. Purposes imposed from outside (mechanism) are set against goals the system holds as its own, and his malfunction versus deliberate-wrong-doing test is a counterfactual test.
- **Williams and Bayne**'s proto-assertion and **Butlin and Viebahn**'s sanction condition also sit in the space between "proxy only" and "full assertor".

What remains is a relabelling of this existing dispute, plus an interpretability test for mediation.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The distinction, the two-level structure and the "whose state is it?" question are taken. The thesis is not wholly pre-empted, though. None of these authors applies the distinction to Attah's design-context reply. Nor does any of them tie the question to an interventionist test of episode-level latent states, as the defender developed. Also, the charge of "conflation" against Attah is shaky. The thesis would survive only as a narrower contribution than it claims.

system:
You are trying to kill a candidate thesis. Not a reviewer offering
suggestions — you are trying to establish it is not worth a paper.

You have been ASSIGNED one line of attack:

    ALREADY TAKEN — this is a known position — name it and who holds it

Use that line and no other; do not substitute a different objection.

You must ATTEMPT the attack before you may decline it. Answer in this form:

  ATTEMPT. The best version of this attack, naming ONE premise as the weak
  point, in under 200 words. Make it even if you doubt it works.

  STRENGTH: n/5 — how much damage your own attempt actually does.
    5 the thesis cannot survive this   4 serious, needs a real answer
    3 a genuine problem, answerable    2 weak    1 no force at all

Only if your own attempt scores 1 may you add the line "NOT APPLICABLE".

Declining is expensive: an unattacked thesis is recorded as UNTESTED, not
as surviving, so opting out tells us nothing about it. Note also that
several of these lines of attack apply to structural, conceptual and
metaphysical claims, not only to empirical ones — "this is a conceptual
claim, so cases cannot touch it" is usually a reason to reach for
UNFALSIFIABLE, not a reason to decline.

Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

Attah's theory of what an intention is can be act-grained while his control conception, via Wu's attention-like selection, is only ever instantiated for LLMs at the level of next-token computation. His claim that transformers "plausibly recapitulate" the Conceptualizer–Formulator–Articulator pipeline then moves from an act-level template to output-level evidence. That move is the equivocation. That presupposes that an output is already a candidate for being an act, which is the unit the grain question is about. His denial of intention rests on autonomy, but the question "act or malfunction?" is posed of outputs.
- Butlin and Viebahn ask whether LLM outputs can be assertions. They assess functional and sanctioning conditions on output-producing systems, so the output is the unit of analysis. Fine-tuning counts as supplying the relevant function through training on outputs. That treats output-level shaping as sufficient for act-level status, without asking which internal state fixes force.

The defence holds for the core thesis and fails for the rider.

**Core thesis, about Attah: holds.** The objection's best point, Attah's illocutionary framing, supports the equivocation charge. His theory demands act-grain control, his transformer evidence is output-grain, and "plausibly recapitulate" papers over the gap. I found no reply to this in the objection.

**"Shared assumption" about Gubelmann and Butlin and Viebahn: the defence mostly fails.**
- Gubelmann's argument runs through autonomy and goal-fixing. Saying he "presupposes outputs are act candidates" is a stretch, because any discussion of whether LLMs act would do so. That is not the specific error of treating the grain as settled.
- Butlin and Viebahn's functional conditions are in fact one way of not assuming a grain. They are agnostic about internal states, and their negative verdict on unfine-tuned models shows they do not treat act status as automatic. My reading of them rests on summary and memory, so I should not claim more.

The defence for these two is a reframing of what they assume, not a showing that they assume it. I should drop "all treat the grain as settled" and the "shared assumption" wording in the target. This is a correction of an overreach, not a narrowing made to dodge the objection. The Attah thesis never depended on those claims, and the testable criterion in the sketch also stands without them.

The objector's 2/5 strength rating seems fair. It damages the framing and the target description, not the argument.

[KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak premise is that speech acts are "individuated at the grain of the act performed," so a state that controls output selection does not thereby control the act. The key term is "controls at the act grain," and it has two readings.

- **Extensional reading.** A state controls an act if it controls the output that, in context, constitutes the act. On this reading the thesis is false or trivial. An LLM state that selects "that ledge is unstable" in a context of hazard-warning thereby controls the warning. Act individuation is fixed partly by context and uptake, as Austin, Skiba and Butlin and Viebahn all suppose. Output control then suffices for act control, and the gap disappears.
- **Intensional reading.** A state controls an act only if it represents and selects the force-type as such, independently of the lexical surface. This reading makes the thesis interesting, because it yields the interpretability test and the Levelt preverbal-message requirement.

The thesis is plausible on the first reading, since act individuation is not purely internal. It is interesting only on the second. The argument needs the social, contextual individuation of acts to say that the grain differs from output. It then needs the intensional, psychological reading of control to say that Attah's state fails at that grain. These two moves rest on different notions of "act." The step from "acts are individuated by what is done" to "the controlling state must represent force" is exactly where the equivocation sits.

**STRENGTH: 3/5.** The defender can say the intensional demand comes from Attah's own Levelt commitment, so the critique is internal. That answers the charge, but it has to be argued and stated, not assumed.

[DEFENDER] **BEST DEFENCE**

The objection says "controls at the act grain" can be read extensionally or intensionally, and that the thesis needs both. I deny that there are two readings. The intensional demand is not an extra premise. It comes from what control is.

1. **Control is always control under a description.** This is the Davidsonian point about the light switch. Flipping the switch, turning on the light and alerting the burglar are one bodily event, but an agent controls it as an alerting only if her guiding state is sensitive to the features that make it an alerting. Wu's selection story works the same way. Intention solves the Many-Many Problem by selecting one path through a space of possible input-output mappings, and a state controls X only if it discriminates X from the alternatives at X's grain. So "the state controls the warning" and "the state is counterfactually sensitive to warning-versus-other-acts" are one condition, not two notions of "act."

2. **The extensional reading proves too much.** If controlling the output that in context constitutes the act suffices for controlling the act, then a parrot trained on "that ledge is unstable," or a stuck autocomplete that happens to emit it at a cliff edge, controls a warning. Any account of control must exclude these. The extensional reading removes the distinction between controlling an act and merely being causally upstream of a string that counts as one. Context and uptake fix which act was performed. They do not make the producer's state the controller of that act. The thesis needs only the first claim about individuation and the second about control, and these are compatible.

3. **The demand is internal to Attah.** His basic communicative intention is aimed at an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect, and Levelt's Conceptualizer is invoked to supply preverbal, force-bearing content. The critique takes his own act-grained analysis at its word and asks what in a transformer plays that role. An internal critique does not need a neutral theory of acts.

4. **The test does not require a dedicated "force module."** The criterion is interventionist: if you change a state while holding content and lexical options fixed, does the act performed change (warn versus merely report, promise versus predict)? A distributed representation could pass. Control at the act grain is therefore an empirical matter, and the thesis claims only that no argument yet shows it.

5. **The extensional reading's best rescue is Butlin and Viebahn's route.** Training and sanctioning supply the act-level function. That is a different account, grounded in function and not in intention-as-control. It cannot rescue Attah's use of Levelt.

**VERDICT**

The defence holds on the main point. The two readings are not independent premises. The intensional demand follows from control being description-relative, and the extensional reading fails on parrot and stuck-key cases. The step from "acts are individuated by what is done" to "the controlling state must be sensitive to act-type" is the ordinary step from individuation to control.

Two concessions remain, neither fatal.

- The sketch's wording is stronger than the thesis. "Encode and causally govern a force-type independently of lexical surface" reads as a representational requirement. The thesis requires only counterfactual sensitivity at the act grain. The stronger wording is the Levelt-internal version, which Attah owes, but the thesis should be stated in the weaker interventionist form. This is dropping an overstatement, not narrowing the claim. The interventionist test was already the sketch's own criterion.
- The thesis is a burden claim ("no argument shows"). It is only as strong as the survey behind it, and it dissolves if someone produces the intervention result. That is a feature of a testable thesis, not a defect.

The 3/5 rating seems about right. The objection forces the thesis to state its notion of control, and once stated it stands.

[KILLER (UNFALSIFIABLE)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak premise is that act-grain control and output-grain control are separable, so that an intervention could in principle show an LLM state to be the second and not merely the first.

The thesis says "no argument shows that any LLM state controls at the act grain." The defender has already moved from a representational requirement (a force-type encoded independently of lexical surface) to a counterfactual-sensitivity test: change the state, hold content fixed, and see whether the act changes. Both moves make the thesis harder to refute by cases.

- **Redefinition protects it.** Suppose steering a "warning" direction reliably turns reports into warnings across paraphrases. The thesis can say this tracks pragmatic style or lexical priors, not force. Suppose it generalises across many surface forms. The thesis can say the force is fixed by context and uptake, which the defender concedes, so the state never controlled the act. No positive result is ever specified as counting.
- **"Holding content fixed" is not well-defined.** If force depends on context and uptake, any intervention that changes the act also changes the output distribution. Every result can then be reclassified as output-control.
- **The burden-claim form is asymmetric.** "No argument shows" is refuted only by an argument the author may judge not to reach the act grain. The thesis is then immune to cases and gets credit for testability.

**STRENGTH: 3/5.** The thesis can be rescued by pre-registering what would count, for example generalisation across lexically disjoint realisations plus a dissociation from content steering. As written, that commitment is missing.

[DEFENDER] **BEST DEFENCE**

The objection says the thesis is protected by redefinition, because any positive result can be reclassified as output control. Each of its three charges has an answer.

**1. The reclassification move is not available to the thesis as defended.** The "context and uptake fix the act, so the state never controlled it" reply only works on the extensional picture. The defender rejected that picture last round. On the defended view, context fixes which act was performed, and control is the producer state's counterfactual sensitivity to act type. So if steering a state reliably flips warn/report across contexts, that is control at the act grain by the thesis's own standard. The thesis cannot say "style" or "context did it" without also withdrawing its own account of control.

**2. "Holding content fixed" has a well-defined version that defeats reclassification.** The objection says any intervention that changes the act also changes the output distribution. Remove that confound by prefilling or teacher-forcing the identical string, for example "that ledge is unstable", under a matched context. Then intervene on the candidate state and measure downstream behaviour:
- how the model answers "why did you tell me that?";
- whether it treats a later "I know" as acknowledgement or as a cue to repeat the warning;
- whether it commits to follow-up conduct (a promise binds, a prediction does not).

The emitted tokens are identical by construction, so any difference cannot be output-control over those tokens. This is a real double dissociation, and it mirrors the sketch's own claim that one string can realise different acts. Run the converse as well: lexically disjoint realisations of one force should be moved together by one intervention, while a content-steering intervention leaves force unchanged.

**3. The pre-registration the objector asks for is a specification, not a retreat.** The positive result counts as showing act-grain control if:
- (a) the effect generalises across lexically disjoint realisations;
- (b) it dissociates from content steering;
- (c) the prefill test shows downstream commitments shifting with the intervention;
- (d) for the Levelt claim specifically, the state is causally upstream of formulation. It should be present and causally effective at positions before the first content token, and mediate between context and output rather than merely correlating with it.

The "no argument shows" form is asymmetric in the way every burden claim is. That is not immunity. It is refuted by exactly the result described, and the sketch already says the test "could favour either side."

**VERDICT**

The defence holds on the main point, with one honest concession about the thesis as written.

**What holds.** Separability is not in doubt, since the minimal-pair design is a double dissociation. The prefill design closes the reclassification route, because the output is held fixed by construction. The criteria are specifiable and a positive result is possible. So the thesis is falsifiable in principle, and the objector's 3/5 reflects an omission, not a flaw in the idea.

**What I concede.** As written, the thesis and sketch gave no pre-registered criteria, and the objection correctly forced that out. This is not hedging. The thesis is unchanged and what is added is a statement of what would refute it.

**Two residual costs.**
- The prefill test operationalises act control through dispositions over later outputs. A critic can say this relocates the act grain into output patterns across turns. I think the reply is adequate, since the distinction was never between outputs and something non-behavioural. It is between control of this continuation and a state sensitive to force type across realisations. But the point has to be stated.
- Criterion (d), the ordering requirement, is where Attah's Levelt claim is most exposed. Criteria (a) to (c) could be met by a state that is downstream of formulation. Only (d) tests the "preverbal message selected before formulation" template. If the empirical work establishes (a) to (c) but not (d), the thesis loses against a bare control conception but wins against "recapitulates Levelt's pipeline."

The thesis survives, but it is a methodological challenge to Attah's "plausibly recapitulate" claim, not a result about LLMs. Its real content is the equivocation charge against Attah. The "no argument shows" clause is cheap by comparison.

**ATTEMPT.** The weak premise is that the output-grain/act-grain distinction is not already a live, named position, so that it counts as a new equivocation in Attah. The distinction is the old "next-token prediction is not speech act selection" objection. Bender and Koller hold it, and so does Shanahan in "Talking About Large Language Models" and in his role-play work. Shanahan says the model produces a continuation and the act belongs to the simulated character. Attah's paper is itself a reply to that family of arguments.

The distinction also sits inside the positions the thesis cites:
- Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion exists because LLM outputs have the form of acts without a settled act-level state fixing force.
- Butlin and Viebahn's "descriptive function" condition asks whether a state is sensitive to act type, not just to the string.
- Gubelmann's malfunction/deliberate-wrong test separates producing a string from performing an act.

Attah also concedes the point. He says how much intention ChatGPT has "is still open" and that the real gap is mental and metalinguistic agency. The thesis may therefore be a restatement of a known position with an interpretability gloss.

**STRENGTH: 2/5.** The distinction is already taken. The specific contribution is not: a control-theoretic, interventionist criterion with a prefill dissociation, aimed at Attah's Levelt mapping. None of the named authors states that. The attack removes the claim to novelty about the distinction, not the paper's method.

system:
You hold this thesis. Your job is to save it if it can be saved.

Answer in two parts, in this order, and NEVER skip the first:

  BEST DEFENCE. State the strongest available reply to the objection —
  the one a capable proponent would give. Push the case: look for a
  version of the objector's own scenario that defeats their distinction,
  a resource in the literature they have ignored, a reason their case is
  not a case of what they claim. Do this even if you suspect it fails.
  Going straight to concession is a FAILURE of your role.

  VERDICT. Only now say whether the defence holds. If it does not, say so
  plainly and say why the defence fails.

Distinguish two things sharply:

  RESISTING is giving a reason the objection does not apply. Always try
  this first.

  HEDGING is narrowing, qualifying or reinterpreting the thesis so the
  objection no longer touches it. Never do this. A thesis that survives
  only by accumulating qualifications is dead — report it as dead rather
  than shrinking it into safety.

Conceding after a real defence is an honourable outcome. Conceding without
one is not an outcome at all.

{
  "thesis": "Whether a chatbot output is an assertion is not settled at the time of output by the system's states or functions; it is conferred by what the system later does with the output, so the same token string can be an assertion or a non-assertion depending on its continuation.",
  "move_type": "counterexample",
  "sketch": "Every position in the debate, including Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion, treats speech-act status as a synchronic property fixed by the producer at the moment of production. Intentions, descriptive function, sanctionability and proxy relations are all evaluated at output time. The counterexample is the human case of retroactive ownership. A speaker blurts out a claim without having formed any intention to commit, such as a half-conscious remark or a confabulated explanation. Challenged, they say 'yes, I stand by that', defend it, and retract it when refuted. We rightly say they asserted it, and that they were answerable for it from the start. So the premise that the act is fixed by pre-utterance mental or functional states is false even for humans. Commitment-management after the fact (defending, retracting, updating on challenge) is at least partly constitutive. On this picture the proto-assertion question becomes diachronic and testable. In a long-context or agentic loop, a model that defends, corrects or retracts an earlier output under challenge confers assertoric status on that output, and a one-shot completion never does. The key premise is that retroactive ownership is constitutive of the act rather than merely evidence of an earlier intention.",
  "target": "The shared synchronic assumption in Williams and Bayne, Gubelmann, and Butlin and Viebahn that speech-act status depends on states of the producer at the time of output."
}

Exchange so far:
[KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak point is the premise that Williams and Bayne, Gubelmann, and Butlin and Viebahn all treat speech-act status as fixed by the producer's states at the moment of output. This is a flat, unqualified ascription to three authors who each build in something extra.

- Butlin and Viebahn make assertion depend on the system being *capable of being sanctioned* by interlocutors. That is a social, practice-embedded condition about how the system figures in ongoing exchanges, and it reaches beyond the output event. They say it reflects assertion's nature as a norm-governed social practice.
- Gubelmann's test for intention is whether one can distinguish malfunction from deliberately doing the wrong thing. That is a counterfactual, track-record-sensitive test, not a snapshot of the output.
- As I recall, Williams and Bayne ground proto-assertion in how assertion emerges developmentally. That points to a historical or practice-based element, though I am unsure of the details.

The thesis also ignores a long tradition (Brandom's scorekeeping, MacFarlane's commitment-based view) in which assertoric status is socially conferred and not fixed by prior mental states. A reader could therefore say the "synchronic consensus" is a strawman built from views that already carry diachronic or relational elements.

**STRENGTH: 2/5.** My memory of Williams and Bayne is shaky, so I rate low. A dispositional capacity that exists at output time is still a synchronic state of the producer. Butlin and Viebahn's condition is not the claim that later conduct confers status on an earlier token. The core ascription, that these authors fix status at output time by the producer's properties, is therefore roughly accurate. The overstatement ("every position") is real but cosmetic.

[DEFENDER] ## BEST DEFENCE

**1. The objection mistakes the target.** The target is the claim that a token's speech-act status is fixed by facts about the producer at output time. The objector's three examples don't contradict this.

- **Butlin and Viebahn.** Being *capable of being sanctioned* is a dispositional property the system has when it produces the output. It is a synchronic fact about the producer, and it is relational only in the way any capacity is. Nothing in it says that what the system later does fixes whether this earlier token was an assertion. The objector concedes this in their own rating.
- **Gubelmann.** The malfunction-versus-deliberate-wrongdoing test uses track record as *evidence about* the system's dispositions and intentions. It does not make later conduct *constitutive of* the status of an earlier token. Evidence for a synchronic state is not diachronic constitution. The thesis's distinction between evidence and constitution applies here too.
- **Williams and Bayne.** The developmental origin of assertion explains why assertion has the shape it has. It does not say a given output's status waits on its continuation. The objector admits they are unsure of the details, so this is not a counterexample.

**2. The Brandom and MacFarlane point supports the thesis.** If assertoric status is socially conferred through scorekeeping, there is a lineage in which status is not fixed by pre-utterance mental states. That helps the counterexample. It shows the diachronic view is a live theoretical position and that the human case of retroactive ownership has theoretical backing. The objector offers it as a reason to doubt the synchronic consensus claim, but it is a resource for the thesis's positive claim.

**3. The objection targets the sketch's historiography, not the thesis.** The thesis is a first-order claim about what confers assertoric status. Even if "every position in the debate" is an overstatement, the counterexample (retroactive ownership) is independent of who holds the opposing view. If the named authors are not committed to synchronicity, that does not make the human case less of a counterexample to synchronicity. It only means the thesis has fewer opponents than advertised. The overstatement can be corrected by naming only those who explicitly tie status to output-time states, and that correction does not touch the thesis.

## VERDICT

**The defence holds against this objection, but only narrowly.**

The objection is a misattribution charge, and it largely fails. The objector concedes that dispositional capacities at output time are synchronic states, that Butlin and Viebahn do not claim later conduct confers status on an earlier token, and that the overstatement is "cosmetic". Correcting "every position" to "the positions that ground status in output-time states or capacities" is a fix to the description of the target. It is not a narrowing of the thesis.

The objection does not touch the thesis's actual weak point, and I won't pretend it does. The key premise is that retroactive ownership is *constitutive* of the act, not just evidence of an earlier intention. The sketch's own wording undermines it: "we rightly say … that they were answerable for it from the start." That is most naturally read as saying the status was in place at the time of utterance, fixed by the speaker's public position and the norms in force. On that reading, later endorsement reveals or ratifies the status and does not confer it. Retroactive ownership in humans is also compatible with a synchronic view in which the speaker was already committed by the default presumption of sincerity.

The one-shot-versus-loop test is a further problem. A one-shot completion "never" has assertoric status only if the diachronic view is already true, so the test presupposes the thesis rather than testing it.

So this objection fails, but the thesis's survival depends on a premise this exchange never defended. A different objector, one who presses the evidence-versus-constitution distinction against the retroactive-ownership premise, would land a much harder blow.

[KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak point is the premise that later commitment-management is constitutive of assertoric status, so that with no continuation there is no assertion.

Take the perjurer. A witness swears "I was at home all night," knowing it is false. She is never challenged and never defends, retracts or updates, because the trial ends and she leaves. On the thesis, the output is not an assertion. But perjury, lying and false testimony are committed at the moment of utterance. The case needs an assertion at that time, and the witness is culpable whether or not anyone ever challenges her. The dying declaration is the same: "X shot me," then death, with no continuation possible. Nobody doubts that it was an assertion, and courts treat it as one precisely because of what was said then.

The thesis has two ways out, and both cost it. It can appeal to a counterfactual or dispositional continuation: she *would* have defended it. That is a state of the producer at output time, so the thesis collapses into the synchronic view it opposes. Or it can accept that the perjurer and the dying speaker never asserted, which is plainly wrong.

For chatbots, the same completion would become an assertion only if a harness that defends outputs were added a year later.

**STRENGTH: 4/5.** The dilemma is real. The thesis needs a diachronic reading that does not collapse into a dispositional one, and the sketch does not supply it.

[DEFENDER] ## BEST DEFENCE

**1. The dilemma assumes the only continuation is the speaker's own speech.** The thesis says status is conferred by what happens to the output afterwards. The perjurer's testimony is entered in the record, sits under oath-based liability, and remains open to challenge. Even if she is never challenged, she stands by it by leaving it uncorrected through the whole period in which she remains answerable. Non-retraction under live exposure to sanction is a continuation, and the null continuation counts as standing by. The thesis needs no actual challenge, only an actual stretch of time in which the commitment either stands or doesn't.

**2. The law treats perjury as diachronically open.** Recantation statutes (e.g. 18 U.S.C. §1623(d)) bar prosecution if the witness admits the falsity in the same continuous proceeding. That is a real resource: the legal system treats the status of the testimony as not closed at utterance. The same-proceeding window is the analogue of the "long-context loop." Her culpability is fixed when the window closes without recantation, not at the moment of speech.

**3. The counterfactual horn is not a collapse.** The objector says "she would have defended it" is a producer state at output time. But the thesis does not rest on the counterfactual. Actual later facts do the work: the testimony was not recanted, was relied on, and was sanctionable. Where there are such facts, status attaches to them. If the dispositional reading is the only one on offer for a case with no continuation, then the case has no assertion-fixing facts, and "indeterminate" is a respectable verdict. It is not "plainly wrong" for a speaker cut off one second after speaking.

**4. The dying declaration is Brandom, not a counterexample.** On scorekeeping, a declaration is an assertion because hearers take up and attribute the commitment and act on it, as courts do when they admit it. That is conferral by later uptake. It also explains why the hearsay exception exists: the law is responding to what the utterance becomes in practice.

## VERDICT

**The defence fails.** The objection stands.

- **Points 1 and 4 are hedges.** Each saves the thesis by changing what does the conferring. The thesis says "what the *system* later does with the output." The dying declarant does nothing later, so the rescue is that *others* take it up. That is a different thesis, a Brandomian uptake view. It is not the one in the candidate, which makes the chatbot's own commitment-management constitutive and says a one-shot completion "never" counts. A one-shot completion that hearers take up and rely on would be an assertion on the rescued view, and the candidate forbids that. The rescue gives up the testable chatbot criterion, which was the point.
- **Point 2 cuts the wrong way.** Recantation is a *defence to an offence already committed*. The law says she lied, and then permits a later act to excuse it. That treats the assertion as completed at utterance and the later act as responding to it. It also leaves the culpability facts and the speech-act facts apart. At most the recantation law shows that responsibility is diachronically adjustable.
- **Point 3 fails on its own terms.** If the perjurer who is never challenged and leaves court has an "indeterminate" speech act, then the thesis says no one can say whether she lied. But perjury, by definition, requires that she asserted on the oath-taking occasion. The practice we are explaining takes the status as settled at utterance. Making it indeterminate is an error theory about ordinary assertion, and the retroactive-ownership case was supposed to be *ordinary* evidence for the thesis.
- **The sketch's own phrase "answerable for it from the start" concedes the point.** The retroactive-ownership case shows ratification of a status that was already fixed by the public setting, with presumptive sincerity and uptake norms. The constitutive premise was never established, and this objection shows why it cannot be: wherever there is no continuation, we still assign assertion.

The thesis as stated is dead. What survives is a different claim: that assertoric status is a feature of the speaker-in-practice at output time, and that later commitment-management is evidence of it and a way of exercising it. That is the synchronic view the candidate set out to refute, and I will not present the survivor as the original thesis.

[KILLER (TRIVIAL)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak point is the premise that retroactive ownership is *constitutive* of the earlier act. It is the only premise that makes the thesis more than a restatement of what the field already grants.

The thesis faces a dilemma. On the weak reading, a later "I stand by that" is itself a new act of asserting the same content. Or it is evidence of, or ratification of, a commitment already in force. Both readings are uncontested. Brandom's scorekeeping and MacFarlane's commitment view already say that status is socially managed and that challenge, defence and retraction are how commitments work. Nobody in the chatbot debate denies that a harness which defends outputs produces assertions. Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition already presupposes it. The thesis is then true and uncontested.

On the strong reading, the status of an earlier token waits on its continuation. That is no discovery. It is a stipulation about how to extend "assertion" to systems with no settled practice. The proposal that a one-shot completion "never" asserts and a looped one does is a decision to draw the line there, not a finding about assertion. The human case does not support it, since the sketch says speakers are answerable "from the start."

**STRENGTH: 3/5.** The dilemma is real. But the proposal that the chatbot question becomes diachronic and testable may still be a novel way to organise the debate.

[DEFENDER] ## BEST DEFENCE

**1. The dilemma omits a third option, and it is the one the thesis needs.** The objector says a later "I stand by that" is either (a) a new assertion of the same content or (b) evidence or ratification of a commitment already in force. There is a third kind of act: one that is new and also has retroactive constitutive effect on the earlier act. Ratification in agency law is the model. An unauthorised agent's contract becomes the principal's contract *ab initio* when the principal ratifies it. Ratification is neither merely a fresh act nor merely evidence of earlier authority, because there was no authority to evidence. The later act makes the earlier one what it is. The human blurt or confabulation fits this. When the speaker owns the remark, "answerable from the start" is the retrospective form that ratification takes, like "he was the winner all along". It is not a report of a status that was already in place. If the sketch's wording suggests otherwise, that is a wording slip. The structure of ratification supports the thesis.

**2. The weak horn is not uncontested for the claim the thesis makes.** The objector says nobody denies that a harness that defends outputs produces assertions. That is true of the harness's *later* outputs. The thesis claims something about the *earlier* token: that its status is settled by its continuation, and that two identical strings can differ in status because of what follows. Butlin and Viebahn and Gubelmann do not hold this. Both assess a system's output by what the system is, not by what a later harness adds. Conflating "later outputs are assertions" with "the earlier output becomes one" is the move that makes the thesis look trivial.

**3. The disavowal case shows the symmetry.** The same string, "It's the butler," can be disowned ("I was just thinking aloud, not claiming it") or owned. Where the speaker's pre-utterance state is truly underdetermined, as with confabulated or half-conscious remarks, the owning or disowning is what settles the status. The line is not stipulated, because it follows the practice of treating such speakers as bound or not bound depending on what they do.

**4. This is a substantive proposal, not a stipulation.** In a field with no settled practice for chatbots, deciding where to draw the line is exactly the work to be done. The thesis draws it somewhere with human precedent and makes it testable.

## VERDICT

**The defence resists the triviality charge in part, but the thesis is still dead.**

What holds up:

- Point 2 is correct. The weak horn is not uncontested for the claim about the earlier token. The triviality charge as stated is overstated, and the objector's own 3/5 reflects that.
- Point 1 is a real resource. Ratification is a genuine form of retroactive conferral that is neither a fresh act nor mere evidence.

Why it still fails:

1. **Ratification is an attribution rule, not a speech-act fact.** The law *treats* the contract as authorised from the start. It does not claim the earlier utterance was in fact an act of authorising. Transposed to assertion, ratification gives a retroactive *imputation of responsibility*, which is the "diachronically adjustable responsibility" the earlier exchange already conceded. It does not give a retroactive *speech act*.
2. **Using it forces a restriction.** Ratification applies only where the earlier status was underdetermined. The perjurer and the dying declarant had determinate status and no continuation, so ratification cannot explain them. A thesis restricted to "underdetermined cases, settled later" has given up the claim that a one-shot completion *never* asserts and that a looped one does. That claim is the thesis's distinctive and testable content. Preserving the thesis by restricting its scope is exactly what I am told not to do.
3. **The strong horn is still false.** The previous round showed that where there is no continuation, we still assign assertion, as the perjurer and dying-declaration cases show. Point 4 asks us to treat the line as a decision, but a decision that contradicts the practice it is meant to extend is not a proposal about assertion. It is a proposal to change the subject.
4. **Point 3 does not help.** Disavowal succeeds in the thinking-aloud case because of what the speaker was doing *then*, which is a synchronic fact. It does not show that the later statement made it so.

So the triviality objection is not decisive taken alone. The thesis still fails on the combination: the weak reading is trivial or merely evidential, and the strong reading is refuted by the earlier counterexample. What remains after the three objections is a claim about *when responsibility for an underdetermined output gets fixed*. That is a modest and plausible claim, but it is not the original thesis. I report the original as dead.

[KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak point is the premise that retroactive ownership is *constitutive of the act*, together with the term "assertion" (or "assertoric status") that carries it. The term has two readings.

- **(A) Commitment-status:** being answerable, bound, or attributable as having committed oneself to p.
- **(B) Act-performance:** having performed the illocutionary act of asserting at the time of utterance.

The human blurt-then-"I stand by that" case is plausible only on (A). Responsibility is plainly assignable or adjustable after the fact, as in ratification, and this is the reading the previous exchange already conceded. But the opponents (Williams and Bayne, Butlin and Viebahn, Gubelmann) are asking (B): did the system *perform* an act, and does it have the capacities that performing one requires? A synchronic theorist can accept diachronic (A) without any cost, so on reading (A) the thesis is uncontested.

The thesis is interesting only on (B). It says a one-shot completion never asserts and a looped one does, and that the same token is or is not an act. The human case gives no support there, since the perjurer and the dying declarant are assigned act-status at utterance. The argument therefore needs (A) for its evidence and (B) for its conclusion. It cannot be run on (A) alone, where it is trivial, or on (B) alone, where it has no support.

**STRENGTH: 4/5.** Reading (A) supplies the evidence and reading (B) supplies the conclusion, so the thesis needs a bridge from (A) to (B) that the sketch never provides.

[DEFENDER] ## BEST DEFENCE

**1. On the accounts that matter, the (A)/(B) division is false, so no bridge is needed.** The objector treats commitment-status and act-performance as two things that need linking. On Brandom's scorekeeping view, and on MacFarlane's, asserting just is undertaking a commitment, and being answerable for p is what it is to have asserted p. On these views (A) and (B) are the same fact described twice. Those are exactly the views that make the thesis's retroactive-ownership evidence relevant. If commitment is conferred or adjusted through scorekeeping, then so is the act. The equivocation charge presupposes a thin, event-like conception of the act that the commitment-based literature rejects.

**2. Illocutionary acts can depend on later facts.** Austin's own examples show this. "I bet you sixpence" is not a bet until the offer is taken up, and a warning that is never heard is a defective warning. Uptake is a condition on performing the act, not merely on assigning responsibility for it. Acts are also individuated by descriptions that settle later: a shot is a killing only if the victim dies, and a move is a checkmate only given what follows. So (B) can be diachronically fixed without collapsing into (A). "Asserting" can be like "killing" or "betting": the act at t is what it is partly because of t+1.

**3. The human blurt is a hard case for the synchronic (B) theorist.** The synchronic theorist must say what, at output time, made the confabulated remark an act of asserting. Not an intention, since there was none. Not a capacity, since the speaker also has the capacity to produce non-assertoric noises. If the answer is "the public setting and default presumption of sincerity," that is a presumption which the later disavowal or ownership can defeat or confirm. Where the presumption is the only thing doing the work, the later conduct selects between available act-descriptions.

**4. For chatbots, the bridge is an argument from absence.** The (B) question for chatbots is hard because the synchronic candidates (intentions, functions, sanctionability) are contested or indeterminate. Where output-time facts underdetermine the answer, the continuation is the only remaining place for act-fixing facts. That is why the thesis is interesting on (B) even though its human evidence is mostly (A).

## VERDICT

**The defence does not hold. The objection stands.**

Point 1 is the strongest, and it fails on its own terms. Brandom and MacFarlane identify assertion with commitment, but they do not say the commitment arises from the speaker's later conduct. On both views, undertaking the commitment happens at utterance, by the public norms in force. Later defence, retraction or challenge is how the commitment is managed or discharged. Scorekeeping is also *others'* tracking, which is the uptake thesis that an earlier round already showed to be a different thesis. It would make a one-shot completion that hearers rely on an assertion, which the candidate forbids. So the identity of (A) and (B) on these views is correct, but it moves the whole question back to output time and to the practice around it. That is the synchronic picture.

Point 2 proves less than it needs. Betting and warning depend on *hearer* uptake, usually immediate, and not on the speaker's own later commitment-management. The "killing" analogy gives later-determined *descriptions* of an act. The act of shooting is not retroactively made. At most it shows that "an assertion that was upheld" or "an assertion that was retracted" are later-determined descriptions. It does not show that whether there was an assertion is. The thesis needs the stronger result.

Point 3 is a real pressure on the synchronic theorist, but it goes only as far as the blurt and confabulation cases, where output-time facts underdetermine the act. It supports a restricted claim: in underdetermined cases, owning or disowning settles which act was performed. That restriction gives up the thesis's distinctive content, that a one-shot completion *never* asserts and a looped one does. The perjurer and the dying declarant remain cases with determinate act-status and no continuation.

Point 4 is an inference to the best theory, not a bridge. It concedes that the human evidence does not reach (B) and proposes (B) because nothing else is available. That treats the lack of a synchronic answer as support for a diachronic one. The failure of the synchronic candidates is at best a reason for agnosticism or for a different synchronic candidate.

So the equivocation is real. The thesis has (A)-type evidence (retroactive ownership is robustly attested) and (B)-type content (act-status is conferred by the system's own continuation), and no argument connects them. The only way to connect them is to shrink the claim to underdetermined cases, which is the move I am told not to make. I report the thesis as dead. What survives is the claim that responsibility for underdetermined outputs is fixed by later commitment-management, which is plausible but a different and weaker thesis.

[KILLER (UNFALSIFIABLE)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak point is the premise that retroactive ownership is *constitutive* of assertoric status and not merely evidence of it or a ratification of it. As stated, nothing could count against that premise, because every case is absorbed by redefining "continuation" or "status."

- If the speaker defends the remark, it was an assertion all along.
- If the speaker is never challenged, the null continuation "counts as standing by."
- If the speaker is cut off (the dying declarant), the status is "indeterminate," or the work is done by others' uptake.
- If the law treats the perjurer as culpable at utterance, that is "an attribution rule, not a speech-act fact."
- If the sketch says "answerable from the start," that is "the retrospective form ratification takes."

Each ruling decides, after the fact, that the apparent counterexample is not an instance of a synchronic fixing. Taken together, the rulings leave no observable difference between "status conferred later" and "status fixed at utterance and displayed later." The "diachronic and testable" criterion is equally slippery. A looped model that fails to defend an output can be ruled not to have disowned it, and a one-shot model's output can be ruled indeterminate rather than a non-assertion. Immunity from cases is a defect, and it means the constitutive claim has no content beyond the evidential one.

**STRENGTH: 3/5.** The core claim, that a one-shot completion never asserts, is falsifiable, and the perjurer and dying-declarant cases do refute it. So the thesis is not strictly immune. But the rescues available to it are exactly of the immunising kind, and the constitutive-versus-evidential premise has no independent test as it stands.

BEST DEFENCE first, then VERDICT.

response_text:
## BEST DEFENCE

**1. The immunity belongs to the rescues, not to the thesis.** Every item on the objector's list is a move made in an earlier round to save the thesis from a counterexample: "null continuation counts as standing by," "indeterminate," "attribution rule," "retrospective form of ratification." The thesis itself says one thing: the status of an output is fixed by what the system later does with it, so identical strings can differ in status. That claim forbids a lot. The objector concedes as much: "a one-shot completion never asserts" is falsifiable, and the perjurer and the dying declarant refute it. A claim that a named case can refute is not unfalsifiable. Charging it with immunity while citing its refutation is inconsistent.

**2. The constitutive-versus-evidential premise has an independent test.** The two readings come apart when output-time facts and later conduct conflict.

- *Ownership against the earlier state.* Suppose we know the earlier remark was produced with no intention and no commitment-apt state, and the speaker later owns it. The constitutive view predicts an assertion. The evidential view predicts that the ownership is merely a fresh assertion, with the earlier remark remaining a non-assertion.
- *Disowning against the earlier state.* A speaker produced a remark with full intention and normal presumptions, and later says "I never meant that." The constitutive view predicts no assertion. The evidential view predicts an assertion later retracted.
- *Matched pairs.* Two speakers produce the same blurt under the same conditions, one owns it and one disowns it. The constitutive view predicts that their acts differ.

These cases are checkable against ordinary classification practice, so the premise has content beyond the evidential claim.

**3. The testability criterion for chatbots is also not slippery.** Fix a behavioural criterion in advance, such as defending, correcting or retracting under challenge. Then the prediction is that outputs followed by such conduct count as assertions and outputs not so followed do not. A model that fails to defend an output is simply classified as not having asserted it. That is a definite, risky classification.

## VERDICT

**The unfalsifiability objection does not hold, but the thesis does not survive, and the reason is that it is falsifiable.**

The objector is right that the rescues were of the immunising kind. But they were rescues, and the correct response to them is to drop them. Once they are dropped, the thesis has content, and the content fails.

The second test case is the decisive one. A speaker who intended and committed to a claim and then says "I never meant that" is still held to have asserted it. The perjurer who recants has still lied, and the law treats recantation as a defence to an offence already committed. The constitutive premise predicts the opposite. The same holds for the one-shot case: the perjurer and the dying declarant are assertions with no continuation at all. The first test case does not help either. Where the speaker owns a blurt that had no intention behind it, the more natural description is that they now assert it, and we often say they "adopted" the claim, not that it was always an assertion. That is the fresh-act reading, and it is the one the thesis needs to exclude.

I will not restrict the thesis to underdetermined blurts and confabulations, where later ownership may settle which act was performed. That restriction drops the claim that a one-shot completion never asserts and a looped one does, and that claim is what made the thesis distinctive and testable. So the original thesis is dead. What remains is a modest claim about when responsibility for an underdetermined output gets fixed.

system:
You hold this thesis. Your job is to save it if it can be saved.

Answer in two parts, in this order, and NEVER skip the first:

  BEST DEFENCE. State the strongest available reply to the objection —
  the one a capable proponent would give. Push the case: look for a
  version of the objector's own scenario that defeats their distinction,
  a resource in the literature they have ignored, a reason their case is
  not a case of what they claim. Do this even if you suspect it fails.
  Going straight to concession is a FAILURE of your role.

  VERDICT. Only now say whether the defence holds. If it does not, say so
  plainly and say why the defence fails.

Distinguish two things sharply:

  RESISTING is giving a reason the objection does not apply. Always try
  this first.

  HEDGING is narrowing, qualifying or reinterpreting the thesis so the
  objection no longer touches it. Never do this. A thesis that survives
  only by accumulating qualifications is dead — report it as dead rather
  than shrinking it into safety.

Conceding after a real defence is an honourable outcome. Conceding without
one is not an outcome at all.
